slides.headline: ⚠️ The Trap vs The Clean Way
slides.body:
❌ **Common Trap**:
Entering traditional online schools immediately.

✅ **Preferred Approach**:
Launch `Value-Add Courses` similar to Coursera, where market acceptance and scalability are higher.

slides.headline: 🔍 Market Sizing Logic
slides.body:
`India Population = 1.4 Billion`

`Urban Population = 400 Million`

`Upper Middle + Upper Class = 160 Million`

`Age 18-24 = 16 Million`

`Interested Users = 5 Million`

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 1**: Start with `1.4 Billion` population.
**Step 2**: Focus on `400 Million Urban` users.
**Step 3**: Filter to `160 Million UMC + UC` consumers.
**Step 4**: Focus on `18-24 Age Group` → `16 Million`.
**Step 5**: Assume `30%` course adoption → `5 Million Users`.
**Step 6**: `2 Courses/Year × ₹2,000` per course.
**Step 7**: Market Size = `₹20 Billion`.

slides.headline: 🔍 Set-Up Requirements
slides.body:
Key requirements:
• `Licenses & Permissions`
• `Learning Platform`
• `Educators`
• `Support Staff`
• `Marketing & Branding`

Partnerships with coaching institutes can accelerate content creation.

slides.headline: ✨ Key Highlights
slides.body:
• Target segment: `Digital Education`.
• Business model: `Value-Add Courses`.
• Estimated market size: `₹20 Billion`.
• Potential first-year share: `20%`.
• Leverages Airtel's digital ecosystem.
• High-growth industry with scalable demand.

slides.headline: ✅ Recommendations
slides.body:
**Launch Strategy**:
• Build a digital learning platform.
• Partner with top educators and institutes.
• Offer premium certifications.
• Use Airtel's customer base for distribution.

**Risk Mitigation**:
• Monitor `Regulatory Changes`.
• Differentiate through exclusive content.
• Build strong brand credibility.

revisionCards.title: Hotel Chain Entering New Markets
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
A leading Indian premium hotel chain wants to expand internationally because the Indian market is saturated.

Choose between `Brazil`, `Australia`, and `South Africa` by evaluating `Financial Feasibility` and `Operational Feasibility`.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Market Entry Framework**:

Evaluate:
• `Financial Feasibility`
• `Operational Feasibility`

Choose the country that maximizes long-term profits while remaining operationally viable.

slides.headline: 🧠 Financial Feasibility Method
slides.body:
**Calculation Framework**:

`Nights Occupied = Tourists × Avg Stay`

`Target Customers = Nights Occupied × Market Share`

`Profit/Night = Revenue/Night - Cost/Night`

`Profit = Target Customers × Profit/Night - Fixed Cost`

slides.headline: 🔍 Brazil Calculation
slides.body:
`Tourists = 2M`
`Avg Stay = 3 Nights`

`Nights Occupied = 2 × 3 = 6M`

`Market Share = 30%`

`Target Customers = 6 × 30% = 1.8M`

`Profit/Night = $550 - $350 = $200`

`Potential Profit = 1.8M × $200 = $360M`

`Final Profit = $360M - $100M = $260M`

slides.headline: 🔍 Australia Calculation
slides.body:
`Tourists = 4M`
`Avg Stay = 5 Nights`

`Nights Occupied = 4 × 5 = 20M`

`Market Share = 25%`

`Target Customers = 20 × 25% = 5M`

`Profit/Night = $650 - $450 = $200`

`Potential Profit = 5M × $200 = $1B`

`Final Profit = $1B - $300M = $700M`

slides.headline: 🔍 South Africa Calculation
slides.body:
`Tourists = 5M`
`Avg Stay = 4 Nights`

`Nights Occupied = 5 × 4 = 20M`

`Market Share = 25%`

`Target Customers = 20 × 25% = 5M`

`Profit/Night = $600 - $450 = $150`

`Potential Profit = 5M × $150 = $750M`

`Final Profit = $750M - $350M = $400M`

slides.headline: 🔍 Operational Feasibility
slides.body:
**Setup Steps**:
• `Licenses & Permissions`
• `Research Locations`
• `Acquire Land`
• `Build Hotels`
• `Hire Staff`
• `Marketing`
• `Launch Operations`

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 1**: Financial ranking → Australia ($700M) > South Africa ($400M) > Brazil ($260M).
**Step 2**: Brazil had no operational issues.
**Step 3**: Australia could acquire only `50% Land` initially.
**Step 4**: South Africa required an extra `$50M License Cost`.
**Step 5**: Revised Australia Profit = `50% × $700M = $350M`.
**Step 6**: Revised South Africa Profit = `$400M - $50M = $350M`.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Country-Specific Risks
slides.body:
**Brazil**:
• No major issues

**Australia**:
• Foreign land acquisition restricted
• Only `50%` land available initially

**South Africa**:
• Additional premium hotel licenses
• Extra `$50M` investment

slides.headline: ✨ Key Highlights
slides.body:
• Initial profits: `Brazil $260M`, `Australia $700M`, `South Africa $400M`.
• Revised profits: `Australia $350M`, `South Africa $350M`.
• Australia and South Africa tied in short-term profits.
• Australia offers higher `Long-Term Growth Potential`.

slides.headline: ✅ Recommendation
slides.body:
**Recommended Country: Australia**

Reasons:
• Highest original profit potential.
• Equal short-term profits after adjustments.
• Ability to acquire remaining land after `10 Years`.
• Better long-term scalability than South Africa.

revisionCards.title: Solar TV Manufacturer Enters India
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
A US-based `Solar TV Manufacturer` wants to enter India because demand has saturated in its home market.

Evaluate whether entering the Indian market is attractive and identify the best target segment.

slides.headline: 💡 Simplified Analogy
slides.body: Imagine selling battery-powered fans in villages with frequent power cuts. The product becomes valuable because it solves a local problem better than existing alternatives.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Market Entry Framework**:

• `Market Attractiveness`
• `Operational Feasibility`
• `Risks`

This case focuses only on `Market Attractiveness` and revenue potential.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition
slides.body:
The strongest target market is `Rural India` because:

• Limited electricity availability
• High value from solar charging
• Lower total cost than conventional TVs
• No direct competition

slides.headline: 🔍 Revenue Formula
slides.body:
`Revenue = Market Size × Market Share × Price`

Target customers must be estimated before applying the formula.

slides.headline: 🔍 Market Sizing Method
slides.body:
`India Population = 140 Cr`

`Rural Population = 100 Cr`

`Household Size = 5`

`Total Rural Households = 100/5 = 20 Cr`

Income Split:
• `BPL = 8 Cr`
• `LMC + UMC = 10 Cr`
• `UC = 2 Cr`

slides.headline: 🔍 Target Customer Calculation
slides.body:
`BPL` eliminated due to affordability.

`LMC + UMC`:
10 Cr × 80% TV Ownership × 60% Solar Preference
= `4.8 Cr`

`UC`:
2 Cr × 90% TV Ownership × 60% Solar Preference
= `1.08 Cr`

`Total Market Size ≈ 6 Cr Households`

slides.headline: 🔍 Annual Sales Revenue Calculation
slides.body:
`TV Price = ₹7,000`
`TV Life = 5 Years`

Total Revenue = 6 Cr × ₹7,000
= `₹42,000 Cr`

Annual Revenue = ₹42,000 Cr ÷ 5
= `₹8,400 Cr/Year`

slides.headline: 🔍 First-Year Revenue Calculation
slides.body:
`Expected Market Share = 50%`

Sales Revenue:
₹8,400 Cr × 50%
= `₹4,200 Cr`

Maintenance Revenue:
6 Cr × 20% Replacement Rate × 50% Share × ₹7,000
= `₹4,200 Cr`

`Total First-Year Revenue = ₹8,400 Cr`

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 1**: Focus on `Rural India` due to electricity shortages.
**Step 2**: Convert `100 Cr Rural Population` into `20 Cr Households`.
**Step 3**: Remove `BPL Segment` due to affordability constraints.
**Step 4**: Estimate interested households → `~6 Cr`.
**Step 5**: Calculate annual revenue → `₹8,400 Cr`.
**Step 6**: Assume `50% Market Share` in Year 1.
**Step 7**: Total first-year revenue remains `₹8,400 Cr` including maintenance.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Important Assumptions
slides.body:
• `Rural Population = 100 Cr`
• `Household Size = 5`
• `80%` TV ownership in middle class
• `90%` TV ownership in upper class
• `60%` preference for Solar TVs
• `50%` first-year market share
• `5-Year TV Life`

slides.headline: ✨ Key Highlights
slides.body:
• Product solves `Electricity Access Problem`.
• No significant competition.
• Target market size ≈ `6 Cr Households`.
• Annual market revenue ≈ `₹8,400 Cr`.
• Rural India offers the highest adoption potential.

slides.headline: ✅ Recommendation
slides.body:
Enter `Rural India`.

Reasons:
• Strong unmet need.
• Large addressable market.
• Attractive revenue potential.
• Limited competition.
• Solar technology provides a clear value proposition over conventional TVs.

revisionCards.title: Australian Telecom Company Enters India
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
An `Australian Telecom Company` is considering entering the Indian telecom market within the next `2-3 years`.

Develop a comprehensive `Market Entry Strategy` and evaluate whether entering India is attractive.

slides.headline: 💡 Simplified Analogy
slides.body: Entering India's telecom industry is like opening a new food delivery app in a market already dominated by a few giant players. Success depends on market potential, execution capability, and differentiation.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Market Entry Framework**:

• `Financial Feasibility`
• `Operational Feasibility`
• `Risks`

The company should enter only if expected profits justify the investment and risks.

slides.headline: 🧠 Financial Feasibility
slides.body:
**Profit Framework**:

`Total Profit = (Market Size × Market Share × Profit/Unit) - Fixed Costs`

Key variables:
• `Market Size`
• `Market Share`
• `Profit Per Customer`
• `Fixed Costs`

slides.headline: 🔍 Market Size Drivers
slides.body:
Estimate demand using:

• `India Population`
• `Urban vs Rural Split`
• `Telecom Penetration`
• `Mobile Access`
• `Income Levels`
• `Age Distribution`
• `Average Subscription Revenue (ARPU)`

slides.headline: 🔍 Market Share Drivers
slides.body:
Estimate achievable share through:

• `Market Fragmentation`
• `Switching Costs`
• `Network Quality`
• `Pricing Strategy`
• `Brand Awareness`
• `Competitor Strength`

slides.headline: 🧠 Operational Feasibility
slides.body:
**Two-Step Approach**:

`Method` → How to enter
`Manner` → How to execute

This prevents choosing an execution plan before deciding the entry model.

slides.headline: 🔍 Entry Method Options
slides.body:
Possible approaches:

• `Own Operations (Greenfield)`
• `Merger`
• `Acquisition`
• `Joint Venture`
• `Outsourcing`

Selection depends on control, cost, speed, and legal feasibility.

slides.headline: 🔍 Execution Roadmap
slides.body:
Value Chain Setup:

• `Regulatory Certifications`
• `Telecom Towers & Offices`
• `Hire Staff`
• `Distribution Network`
• `Marketing & Advertising`
• `After-Sales Service`

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 1**: Assess `Market Size` and telecom demand.
**Step 2**: Estimate achievable `Market Share`.
**Step 3**: Calculate expected profits using the profitability formula.
**Step 4**: Select entry method (JV, Acquisition, Greenfield, etc.).
**Step 5**: Build telecom infrastructure and distribution.
**Step 6**: Launch marketing and customer acquisition campaigns.
**Step 7**: Evaluate risks before final entry decision.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Risk Assessment
slides.body:
**General Risks**:
• `Cultural & Market Differences`

**Legal Risks**:
• `Licenses & Regulatory Approvals`

**Labour Risks**:
• `Hiring Skilled Workforce`

**Competitive Risks**:
• `Jio, Airtel, Vi Dominance`

**New Entrant Risks**:
• Future price wars and disruption

slides.headline: ✨ Key Highlights
slides.body:
• Analyze `Financial`, `Operational`, and `Risk` dimensions.
• Use profitability formula before committing.
• Evaluate `JV`, `Acquisition`, and `Greenfield` options.
• Build end-to-end telecom value chain.
• Consider strong incumbent competitors.

slides.headline: ✅ Recommendation
slides.body:
Before entering India, perform a detailed market sizing and profitability assessment.

If projected profits exceed investment requirements, a `Joint Venture` or `Acquisition` is likely preferable to a pure greenfield entry because of existing infrastructure, licenses, and market access.

revisionCards.title: Increasing Revenue of a Lemonade Stand
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
A young entrepreneur recently started a `Lemonade Stand` during summer holidays. Despite having enough inventory, sales remain poor.

Identify ways to increase the stand's `Revenue`.

slides.headline: 💡 Simplified Analogy
slides.body: If a food truck has great products but few customers, the solution is not always lowering prices. It may need better timing, location, marketing, or additional sales channels.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Revenue Framework**:

`Revenue = Revenue per Customer × Number of Customers`

To increase revenue, we must either:

• Increase `Number of Customers`
• Increase `Revenue per Customer`
• Or improve both simultaneously.

slides.headline: 🧠 Increase Number of Customers
slides.body:
**Time**
• Extend operating hours
• Identify peak demand periods

**Area**
• Visit schools
• Visit playgrounds
• Cover more neighborhoods

**Quality**
• Improve taste and consistency

**Marketing**
• Flyers and banners
• Family and friends promotion

slides.headline: 🚚 New Sales Channels
slides.body:
Instead of relying only on the cart:

• `Home Delivery`
• `Birthday Party Orders`
• `Community Events`
• `Neighborhood Gatherings`

More channels increase customer reach without changing the core product.

slides.headline: 💰 Increase Revenue per Customer
slides.body:
**Current Price**:
`₹20 per 200ml glass`

Since competitors are supermarkets with higher-priced alternatives, price can potentially be increased to:

`₹25 per glass`

without major demand loss.

slides.headline: 🛒 Increase Volume per Customer
slides.body:
**Discounts**
• Buy 2 Get Discount
• Family Packs

**Cross-Selling**
• Sell `Cookies`
• Sell `Snacks`
• Create `Combo Offers`

Customers spend more per visit.

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 1**: Revenue is low despite excess inventory, indicating a demand-side issue.
**Step 2**: Analyze customer acquisition opportunities through time, area, quality, and marketing.
**Step 3**: Expand sales channels beyond the moving cart.
**Step 4**: Increase price from `₹20` to `₹25` if demand remains stable.
**Step 5**: Increase basket size through discounts and cross-selling.

slides.headline: ⚠️ The Trap vs The Clean Way
slides.body:
❌ **Trap**:
Assuming poor sales require lowering prices.

✅ **Clean Approach**:
First improve `Customer Reach`, `Visibility`, and `Convenience` before changing pricing.

slides.headline: ✨ Key Highlights
slides.body:
• Operates from `2 PM - 5 PM`
• Uses a `Mobile Cart`
• No direct lemonade competitors
• Excess inventory exists
• Revenue can grow through `Time`, `Area`, `Marketing`, and `Channels`
• `Cross-Selling` and `Discounts` increase spending per customer

slides.headline: ✅ Recommendations
slides.body:
**Short-Term Actions**:
• Extend operating hours
• Target schools and playgrounds
• Improve local marketing
• Start home delivery
• Increase price to `₹25`
• Introduce cookies and snack combos

These actions improve both `Customer Count` and `Revenue per Customer`, driving rapid revenue growth.

revisionCards.title: Doubling Revenue of a Biryani Chain in Delhi
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
A premium `Biryani Chain` with `10 outlets in Delhi` wants to increase monthly revenue from `X` in March 2021 to `2X` in April 2021 during the `COVID-19 lockdown`.

Identify practical strategies to achieve this aggressive revenue target.

slides.headline: 💡 Simplified Analogy
slides.body: If an online store wants to double sales in one month, opening new stores isn't feasible. Instead, it must attract more customers and increase spending per customer. The same applies to this restaurant chain.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Revenue Growth Framework**:

`Revenue = Number of Restaurants × Revenue per Restaurant`

Since only `1 month` is available, opening new outlets is unrealistic. The focus should be on increasing `Revenue per Restaurant`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Revenue Driver
slides.body:
`Revenue per Restaurant = Average Number of Orders × Average Bill Value`

To double revenue, we must increase either:

• `Average Number of Orders`
• `Average Bill Value`
• Or both simultaneously

slides.headline: 📦 Increasing Number of Orders
slides.body:
**Supply Side**
• `Increase Kitchen Capacity`
• `Hire More Staff`
• `Improve Kitchen Efficiency`
• `Launch Cloud Kitchens`

**Distribution**
• `Add Swiggy, Zomato, Dineout`
• `Launch Own Delivery Network`
• `Increase Delivery Radius`
• `Increase Delivery Fleet`

slides.headline: 📢 Demand Generation
slides.body:
**Need**
• Position biryani as a `comfort food`

**Awareness**
• Premium placement on food apps
• Search optimization for `Biryani`

**Accessibility**
• Improve last-mile delivery
• Serve relocated suburban/rural customers

**Affordability**
• Coupons
• Festival offers
• Free add-ons

**Experience**
• Luxury packaging
• Safety branding
• Personalized notes
• DIY Biryani Kits

slides.headline: 💰 Increasing Average Bill Value
slides.body:
**Average Price**
• Avoid major price hikes
• Small premium justified through `safety measures`

**Average Order Size**
• `Decoy Pricing`
• `Family Packs`
• `Meal Bundles`
• `Cross-Selling`

**Product Mix**
• Add `Raita`
• Add `Papad`
• Add `Salads`
• Add `North Indian Dishes`

slides.headline: 🎉 Additional Growth Opportunities
slides.body:
Lockdown increased `home-centered celebrations`.

Opportunities:
• Birthday packages
• Anniversary packages
• Promotion celebration combos
• Partner with `Cake Shops`
• Partner with `Party Prop Vendors`
• One-stop celebration solution

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 1**: Revenue doubling cannot come from opening new outlets in one month.
**Step 2**: Focus shifts to increasing revenue per restaurant.
**Step 3**: Increase order volume through supply, distribution, and demand improvements.

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 4**: Increase bill value through bundles, add-ons, and cross-selling.
**Step 5**: Capture lockdown-driven home celebration demand.
**Step 6**: Use cloud kitchens and aggregator channels for rapid scale.

slides.headline: ⚠️ The Trap vs The Clean Way
slides.body:
❌ **Trap**:
Trying to double revenue by simply increasing prices.

✅ **Clean Approach**:
Increase `Orders` + `Order Size` + `Customer Reach` while maintaining premium brand positioning.

slides.headline: ✨ Key Highlights
slides.body:
• `10 outlets` operating in Delhi
• `Premium Biryani Brand`
• Revenue target: `2X in 1 month`
• Lockdown favors delivery-focused growth
• `Cloud Kitchens` offer rapid expansion
• `Decoy Marketing` increases basket size
• Home celebrations create new demand opportunities

slides.headline: ✅ Recommendations
slides.body:
**Immediate Actions**:
• Launch `Cloud Kitchens`
• Expand on `Swiggy/Zomato`
• Increase delivery radius
• Promote premium safety positioning
• Introduce family packs and meal combos
• Add complementary items
• Partner with cake and celebration vendors

Combining these initiatives can significantly increase both `Order Volume` and `Average Bill Value`, creating the fastest path toward the `2X Revenue Goal`.

revisionCards.title: Pricing a Revolutionary Long-Lasting Paint
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
A paint manufacturer has developed a patented paint that lasts `3x longer` than regular paints. The company wants to determine the optimal price to `maximize profits` while ensuring customer adoption.

slides.headline: 💡 Simplified Analogy
slides.body: Imagine a pen that writes for `3x longer` than a normal pen. Customers would pay more for it, but not necessarily `3x the price`, because they value flexibility, future choices, and lower upfront spending.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Pricing Framework**:

Since the product is `patented` and has no direct competitor, pricing can be estimated using:

• `Cost-Based Pricing`
• `Competitor-Based Benchmarking`
• `Value-Based Pricing`
• `Demand-Supply Pricing`

slides.headline: 🧠 Cost-Based Pricing
slides.body:
**Base Manufacturing Cost** = `₹300/L`

**Additional Variable Cost**:
`₹10,000 ÷ 100L = ₹100/L`

**R&D Recovery Cost**:
`₹1,00,00,000 ÷ 50,000L = ₹200/L`

**Total Cost = ₹600/L`

This becomes the `minimum feasible price`.

slides.headline: 📊 Competitor Benchmark
slides.body:
**Regular Paint Price** = `₹350/L`

Since customers would need to repaint `3 times`, equivalent spending becomes:

`₹350 × 3 = ₹1,050`

Additional labour cost:
`₹25 × 2 = ₹50`

**Equivalent Cost ≈ ₹1,100`**

This acts as an external benchmark.

slides.headline: 🎯 Value-Based Pricing
slides.body:
Consumers usually do not value durability proportionally.

Although the paint lasts `3x longer`, customers may value it at roughly `2x` because:

• `Time Value of Money`
• `Large Upfront Payment`
• `Color Preferences Change Over Time`
• `Long-Term Commitment`

Estimated Value:
`₹350 × 2 = ₹700/L`

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 1**: Calculate minimum viable price using production, variable, and R&D recovery costs.
**Step 2**: Benchmark against equivalent spending on traditional paints and repainting costs.
**Step 3**: Estimate customer willingness to pay using value-based pricing.
**Step 4**: Determine pricing range between `₹600/L` and `₹700/L`.
**Step 5**: Select a profit-maximizing price within the range.

slides.headline: ✨ Key Insights
slides.body:
• Product is `Patented`
• No direct competitors exist
• Paint lasts `3x longer`
• `₹600/L` is the minimum feasible price
• Customers value it at approximately `₹700/L`
• Pricing must balance profitability and demand

slides.headline: ✅ Recommendation
slides.body:
**Pricing Range**:
`₹600/L ≤ Price ≤ ₹700/L`

**Recommended Price**:
`₹675/L`

Benefits:
• Generates `₹75/L Profit`
• Higher than industry average margins
• Remains below perceived customer value
• Encourages strong market adoption while maximizing profits

revisionCards.title: Raise the Bar
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
A fitness company wants to open its `first gym` in the North Campus area of New Delhi. The objective is to decide the monthly subscription rate that helps the company `maximize profits` while remaining attractive to students.

slides.headline: 💡 Simplified Analogy
slides.body: Imagine opening a café near a college. You cannot price randomly. You need to check your monthly cost, what students are willing to pay, and what nearby cafés charge. Similarly, the gym price must balance `cost`, `value`, and `competition`.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Pricing Framework**:

To decide the monthly gym subscription, we use:

• `Cost-Based Pricing`
• `Value-Based Pricing`
• `Competitor-Based Pricing`
• `Demand-Supply Pricing`

Demand-supply data is not available, so we mainly rely on the first three approaches.

slides.headline: 🔎 Case Context
slides.body:
The gym is targeting `students in North Campus`.

Key details:

• This is the company’s `first gym`
• Only `one competitor gym` exists nearby
• Gym can serve `40 people at once`
• Open from `5 AM to 10 PM`
• Offers cardio, weights, yoga, personal training, and a health café
• Objective is to `maximize profits`

slides.headline: 🧠 Cost-Based Pricing
slides.body:
**Monthly Equipment Cost**:

• Treadmills/cycles: `₹1,200`
• Weight-training machines: `₹5,000`
• Dumbbells/plates: `₹500`

**Other Monthly Costs** = `₹1,13,300`

**Total Monthly Cost**:
`₹1,200 + ₹5,000 + ₹500 + ₹1,13,300 = ₹1,20,000`

slides.headline: 📊 Break-Even Subscription
slides.body:
**Survey results show that around `80 students` may join the gym.

**Break-even Price**:
`Total Monthly Cost ÷ Number of Subscribers`

`₹1,20,000 ÷ 80 = ₹1,500`

So, `₹1,500/month` is the minimum price needed to cover monthly costs.

slides.headline: 🎯 Value-Based Pricing
slides.body:
Students join gyms mainly to look fitter, healthier, and more confident.

A student may spend around:

• `₹4,000/month` on clothing and appearance
• `₹1,000/month` on healthy diet

So, willingness to spend on fitness can be around `₹3,000/month`.

This gives an upper value-based estimate.

slides.headline: 🏋️ Competitor Benchmark
slides.body:
The nearby competitor gym charges `₹1,800/month`.

Our gym has additional advantages:

• More accessible North Campus location
• Yoga room included
• Health café available
• Personal training option

Because of these extra benefits, charging `₹200–₹300` more than the competitor is reasonable.

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 1**: Identify the objective — maximize profit while targeting students.
**Step 2**: Calculate total monthly cost of running the gym as `₹1,20,000`.
**Step 3**: Use survey demand of `80 students` to find break-even price: `₹1,500/month`.
**Step 4**: Estimate value-based willingness to pay around `₹3,000/month`.
**Step 5**: Compare with competitor pricing of `₹1,800/month`.
**Step 6**: Add premium for better location, yoga room, health café, and facilities.

slides.headline: ✨ Key Insights
slides.body:
• Target users are `North Campus students`
• Monthly cost is `₹1,20,000`
• Expected subscribers are around `80`
• Break-even subscription is `₹1,500/month`
• Competitor charges `₹1,800/month`
• Our gym offers better facilities and location
• Price should be above cost but still student-friendly

slides.headline: ✅ Recommendation
slides.body:
**Pricing Range**:
`₹1,800/month ≤ Price ≤ ₹2,100/month`

**Recommended Price**:
`₹2,000/month`

Why this works:

• Covers the break-even price of `₹1,500`
• Gives `₹500 profit per subscriber`
• Justified by better location and facilities
• Still close to competitor pricing
• Suitable for a student-focused gym

revisionCards.title: Fly Me to the Moon
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
An engineer has invented a patented space jetpack that can take one person to the moon and back. He owns only `1 jetpack`, cannot make more, and wants to decide the ride price that will `maximize profits`.

slides.headline: 💡 Simplified Analogy
slides.body: Imagine owning the only helicopter ride to a private island. Since no one else offers it, normal competitor pricing will not help much. You must first recover your `costs`, then check how many people will buy at different price points.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Pricing Framework**:

To price the moon jetpack ride, we check:

• `Cost-Based Pricing`
• `Competitor-Based Pricing`
• `Value-Based Pricing`
• `Demand-Supply Pricing`

Since the jetpack is `patented` and has no competition, competitor-based pricing is not useful. Value-based pricing is also difficult because no similar lifetime experience exists.

slides.headline: 🔎 Case Context
slides.body:
Key details:

• The engineer has only `1 jetpack`
• No more jetpacks can be made due to scarcity of Zinotium
• The service is `patented`
• No competitor exists
• One ride includes going to the moon, staying there, and returning
• Product life is only `5 years`
• Objective is to `maximize profits`

slides.headline: 🧠 Cost-Based Pricing
slides.body:
**Fixed Development Cost** = `$1 billion`

**Variable Cost per Ride** = `$770,000`

The jetpack lasts for only `5 years`, so the fixed cost must be recovered within this period.

This gives us the `minimum feasible price` below which the business cannot recover its investment.

slides.headline: 📊 Trip Capacity Calculation
slides.body:
The engineer works `10 hours/day` for `350 days/year`.

Due to trip and setup time, he can complete `0.5 trips/hour`.

**Trips per year**:
`0.5 × 10 × 350 = 1,750 trips`

**Trips in 5 years**:
`1,750 × 5 = 8,750 trips`

At `50% capacity`, expected trips become:
`8,750 ÷ 2 = 4,375 trips`

slides.headline: 💰 Lower Price Limit
slides.body:
**Fixed Cost Recovery per Ride**:
`$1,000,000,000 ÷ 4,375 ≈ $230,000`

**Add Variable Cost**:
`$230,000 + $770,000 = $1,000,000`

So, the lower limit of pricing is around `$1 million per ride`.

Charging below this would make it difficult to recover the investment.

slides.headline: 📈 Demand-Supply Pricing
slides.body:
Available demand data:

• At `$1.2 million`, capacity = `80%`
• At `$1.6 million`, capacity = `60%`
• At `$2 million`, capacity = `50%`

Now we compare profits at each price point.

**Profit Formula**:
`Profit = Rides × Profit per Ride - Fixed Cost`

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 1**: Identify that the objective is profit maximization.
**Step 2**: Remove competitor-based pricing because no competition exists.
**Step 3**: Avoid value-based pricing because no similar experience exists.
**Step 4**: Calculate total possible rides over 5 years as `8,750`.
**Step 5**: Find the lower limit using 50% capacity: `$1 million/ride`.
**Step 6**: Compare demand-based price points to select the highest profit option.

slides.headline: 🧮 Profit Comparison
slides.body:
**Case 1**:
Price = `$1.2M`, Capacity = `80%`
Profit ≈ `$2.01B`

**Case 2**:
Price = `$1.6M`, Capacity = `60%`
Profit ≈ `$3.35B`

**Case 3**:
Price = `$2M`, Capacity = `50%`
Profit ≈ `$4.38B`

Even though capacity falls, the higher price generates the maximum profit.

slides.headline: ✨ Key Insights
slides.body:
• Product is `patented`
• No competition exists
• Only `1 jetpack` is available
• Fixed cost is extremely high at `$1B`
• Variable cost is `$770,000/ride`
• Lower price limit is `$1M/ride`
• Demand data shows higher pricing gives better profit
• Profit, not revenue, should be maximized

slides.headline: ✅ Recommendation
slides.body:
**Recommended Price**:
`$2 million per ride`

Why this works:

• Gives the highest estimated profit: `$4.38B`
• Still operates at `50% capacity`
• Stays above the cost-based lower limit of `$1M`
• Best balances exclusivity, scarcity, and profitability

So, the engineer should charge `$2 million` for each moon jetpack ride.

revisionCards.title: Make India Great Again
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
A politician in India wants to increase the number of people who vote in the next municipal election. The election is only `1 week away`, so the focus is on improving voter turnout among people who are already eligible.

slides.headline: 💡 Simplified Analogy
slides.body: Imagine organizing a college event where many students are allowed to attend, but only some actually show up. To increase attendance, you cannot change who is eligible in one week. You must convince interested people and make it easier for them to attend.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Turnout Framework**:

`Votes Cast = Eligible Population × % Wanting to Vote × % Able to Vote`

Since the election is only `1 week away`, eligibility cannot be changed much.

So, the solution focuses on:

• Increasing willingness to vote
• Improving ability to vote
• Reducing practical barriers on election day

slides.headline: 🔎 Case Context
slides.body:
Important case details:

• The election is in `1 week`
• Objective is only to increase voter turnout
• The politician has enough power to implement changes
• Voter ID or eligibility changes are not practical now
• Focus should be on people who are already eligible

This makes the case more about execution than long-term policy.

slides.headline: 🧠 Increasing Willingness
slides.body:
To increase the percentage of people who want to vote, the politician can focus on:

• `Awareness campaigns` through ads, posters, and local announcements
• Clear communication on why voting matters
• More convenient voting centres
• Better booth experience
• Assurance of `anonymity` and voter safety

The goal is to make people feel voting is important, safe, and worth their time.

slides.headline: 🏢 Improving Voting Centres
slides.body:
Voting centres should be easy to access and quick to use.

Possible actions:

• Increase number of voting centres in convenient areas
• Add more counters per centre
• Use EVMs to reduce waiting time
• Provide drinking water and waiting areas
• Ensure washrooms and basic amenities

This reduces friction and makes voting easier for people who already want to vote.

slides.headline: ✅ Improving Ability to Vote
slides.body:
Some people may want to vote but still cannot vote due to practical issues.

Solutions include:

• Choose convenient voting hours
• Extend number of working hours
• Prefer a weekend or holiday
• Provide wheelchair access and ramps
• Make centres elderly and disability-friendly
• Encourage companies to give time off for voting
• Provide one-day daycare support for parents

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 1**: Define the objective — increase number of votes cast.
**Step 2**: Break votes into `eligible population × willingness × ability`.
**Step 3**: Ignore eligibility because the election is only `1 week away`.
**Step 4**: Improve willingness through awareness, safety, anonymity, and convenience.
**Step 5**: Improve ability through timings, accessibility, incentives, and daycare support.
**Step 6**: Prioritize quick, implementable actions before election day.

slides.headline: ✨ Key Insights
slides.body:
• Eligibility cannot be changed quickly
• Focus should be on `willingness` and `ability`
• Awareness improves motivation to vote
• More centres and counters reduce waiting time
• Amenities improve voter experience
• Anonymity increases trust and safety
• Accessibility helps elderly and disabled voters
• Daycare and workplace flexibility reduce personal barriers

slides.headline: ✅ Recommendation
slides.body:
The politician should run a `one-week voter turnout plan` focused on awareness and convenience.

Recommended actions:

• Launch local awareness campaigns
• Increase voting centres and counters
• Ensure water, seating, washrooms, and safety
• Extend voting hours
• Make booths disability-friendly
• Encourage workplace time-off
• Provide temporary daycare support

This directly increases the number of people willing and able to vote.

revisionCards.title: Mo Money, Mo Problems
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
The Government of India wants to increase the number of `digital transactions` in the country as much as possible within the next `6–12 months`, with no major constraints.

slides.headline: 💡 Simplified Analogy
slides.body: Imagine a college wants more students to use online payments in the canteen. Some students do not know how to use it, some do not trust it, and some shops do not accept it. So, the solution must increase both `users` and `usage frequency`.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Digital Transaction Framework**:

`Digital Transactions = Number of People Transacting Digitally × Transactions per Person`

So, we solve the case in two parts:

• Bring more people into digital payments
• Increase how often each person pays digitally

This keeps the approach structured and avoids random suggestions.

slides.headline: 🔎 Case Context
slides.body:
Important details:

• Client is the `Government of India`
• Goal is to increase digital transactions
• Timeline is `6–12 months`
• No major budget or policy constraints
• Digital transactions include UPI, cards, wallets, NEFT, RTGS, etc.

Since the timeline is short, the focus should be on fast adoption and behavior change.

slides.headline: 👥 Increasing Digital Users
slides.body:
To increase the number of people using digital payments, we can use the following levers:

• `Need`
• `Awareness`
• `Accessibility`
• `Affordability`
• `Experience`

The idea is simple: people will shift to digital payments only when they understand the benefit, can access the system easily, and feel safe using it.

slides.headline: 📢 Need & Awareness
slides.body:
First, create a strong need for digital payments.

Possible actions:

• Make digital payments compulsory for large transactions above a limit
• Reduce use of small-denomination cash to nudge digital payments
• Run TV, hoarding, and local awareness campaigns
• Conduct drives in rural shops and government offices
• Promote usage at post offices and ration shops

slides.headline: 📱 Accessibility & Affordability
slides.body:
Digital payments must be easy and affordable.

Actions:

• Push zero-balance bank accounts
• Improve internet and smartphone access
• Create simple BHIM/UPI features using UPI ID and OTP
• Reduce debit and credit card charges
• Subsidize smartphones and data plans for low-income users

This helps more people enter the digital payment ecosystem.

slides.headline: 🔐 Better Experience
slides.body:
Trust is very important for digital payments.

The government can improve experience by:

• Publicly assuring users that digital payments are safe
• Creating quick complaint and refund systems
• Linking digital payments with welfare schemes
• Ensuring compensation in case of fraud or mishandling
• Making apps simple, fast, and available in local languages

A safe experience increases repeat usage.

slides.headline: 🔁 Increasing Transactions/User
slides.body:
After bringing users online, the next step is increasing frequency.

This can be done through:

• Wider merchant acceptance
• Allowing bills like electricity and gas to be paid via UPI
• Cashback and loyalty rewards
• Bill splitting features
• Expense management tools
• More daily-use services inside payment apps

This makes digital payments useful in everyday life.

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 1**: Define digital transactions as UPI, cards, wallets, NEFT, RTGS, etc.
**Step 2**: Break the problem into `users × transactions per user`.
**Step 3**: Increase users through need, awareness, accessibility, affordability, and trust.
**Step 4**: Increase usage through merchant acceptance, incentives, and utility.
**Step 5**: Prioritize quick actions that can work within `6–12 months`.

slides.headline: ✨ Key Insights
slides.body:
• The case is unconventional, so structure matters
• Focus is on both adoption and frequency
• Awareness alone is not enough
• Access to bank accounts, internet, and smartphones is critical
• Trust and security drive repeat usage
• Merchant acceptance increases daily usage
• Incentives and added utility make users transact more often

slides.headline: ✅ Recommendation
slides.body:
The government should follow a two-part strategy:

**1. Increase Digital Users**
Use awareness, bank access, affordability, safety, and simple payment options.

**2. Increase Transactions/User**
Expand merchant acceptance, enable bill payments, offer cashback, and add useful features.

This approach can increase digital transactions quickly while building long-term trust in digital payments.

revisionCards.title: Gold Digger
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
The Ministry of Sports wants to improve India’s performance in Olympic track and field events and increase the gold medal tally to `5 gold medals` by the `2028 Olympics`.

slides.headline: 💡 Simplified Analogy
slides.body: Imagine preparing a college sports team for an inter-college tournament. Winning does not depend only on talent. You need the right players, coaching, equipment, practice, strategy, motivation, and support after the event. Olympic success works the same way, but at a much larger scale.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Olympic Performance Framework**:

To increase gold medals, we divide the plan into three phases:

• `Pre-Event Preparation`
• `During-Event Execution`
• `Post-Event Support`

This structure helps cover athlete selection, training, resources, game-day strategy, motivation, and long-term performance improvement.

slides.headline: 🔎 Case Context
slides.body:
Important details:

• Client is the `Ministry of Sports`
• Focus is on track and field events
• Goal is to reach `5 gold medals`
• Initial target year was 2026, but Olympics happen in 2028
• Final target becomes the `2028 Olympics`
• There are no major constraints

This gives around `7 years` to prepare.

slides.headline: 🏁 Pre-Event: Resources
slides.body:
Before the Olympics, the first focus should be on building strong resources.

Key areas:

• Identify high-potential athletes early
• Decide who to train, how to train, and by when
• Improve sports infrastructure
• Provide world-class equipment
• Hire coaches, physiotherapists, nutritionists, and psychologists
• Build strong support staff around athletes

This creates the foundation for medal-winning performance.

slides.headline: 🏋️ Pre-Event: Implementation
slides.body:
After resources are ready, execution becomes important.

Actions:

• Create event-specific training programs
• Track athlete progress regularly
• Build coordination between athletes, coaches, and support staff
• Improve team chemistry
• Keep athletes motivated through internal rewards
• Send athletes to the host country before the Olympics
• Help them adjust to climate, food, stadiums, and local conditions

slides.headline: 🎯 During-Event Strategy
slides.body:
During the Olympics, small decisions can impact medals.

Focus areas:

• Study opponent strategy and performance patterns
• Prepare athlete-specific game-day plans
• Manage hydration, rest, and nutrition before events
• Avoid unnecessary travel stress
• Ensure smooth scheduling and logistics
• Keep athletes mentally calm and motivated
• Arrange support from Indian fans at stadiums

This helps athletes perform at their peak.

slides.headline: 🏅 Post-Event Support
slides.body:
Post-event support is important for both recognition and future performance.

Actions:

• Give cash bonuses to medal winners
• Offer national sports awards
• Use media coverage to celebrate athletes
• Name stadiums or grounds after top performers
• Provide proper rest before the next training cycle
• Continue support for the next Olympics

This creates motivation for athletes and future talent.

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 1**: Clarify that improving performance means increasing gold medals.
**Step 2**: Correct the target timeline from 2026 to the `2028 Olympics`.
**Step 3**: Break the solution into `pre`, `during`, and `post` phases.
**Step 4**: In the pre phase, focus on athletes, infrastructure, equipment, and staff.
**Step 5**: During the event, focus on opponent strategy, logistics, and motivation.
**Step 6**: Post event, reward athletes and prepare for future Olympics.

slides.headline: ✨ Key Insights
slides.body:
• This is an unconventional case, so structure is important
• The interviewer checks whether you question wrong information
• Olympics should be targeted for `2028`, not 2026
• Medal success needs long-term preparation
• Resources and implementation both matter
• Game-day strategy can impact final performance
• Post-event recognition improves future motivation

slides.headline: ✅ Recommendation
slides.body:
The Ministry should follow a `Pre-During-Post Olympic Plan`.

Recommended approach:

• Build athlete pipeline and support resources
• Invest in infrastructure, equipment, and expert staff
• Create personalized training and progress tracking
• Prepare athletes for host-country conditions
• Use strong game-day strategy and logistics
• Reward medal winners and support future cycles

This gives India the best chance to reach `5 gold medals`.

revisionCards.title: Rating Neil, Nitin and Mukesh
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
An online portal wants to develop a rating framework for Bollywood actors and actresses, similar to an `IMDb-style platform` for the general public.

slides.headline: 💡 Simplified Analogy
slides.body: Imagine rating students for an annual college award. You cannot judge only by marks. You may also look at participation, leadership, discipline, public image, and consistency. Similarly, actors should be rated using multiple dimensions, not just box office numbers.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Actor Rating Framework**:

We can divide the rating into three major buckets:

• `Movies`
• `Recognition`
• `Personality`

Each bucket will have sub-parameters. Then, weights can be assigned based on importance and reliability of the parameter.

slides.headline: 🔎 Case Context
slides.body:
Important details:

• The portal is for the `general public`
• It is similar to IMDb, but focused on actors and actresses
• The client only wants the `rating framework`
• App, website, permissions, and setup are not required
• The framework should be easy to understand and credible

So, the focus is only on rating parameters.

slides.headline: 🎬 Movies Bucket
slides.body:
Under movies, we judge the actor’s professional work.

Key parameters:

• Number of movies done
• Quality and success of movies
• Diversity of roles played
• Number of years in the industry
• Presence outside Bollywood

This shows demand, versatility, experience, and long-term relevance of the actor.

slides.headline: 🏆 Recognition Bucket
slides.body:
Recognition helps measure public and industry-level acceptance.

Key parameters:

• Awards won at Filmfare, IIFA, etc.
• Nominations received
• Popularity among fans
• Social media following
• Google searches and public surveys

Awards are more objective, while popularity captures public interest and mass appeal.

slides.headline: 🌟 Personality Bucket
slides.body:
Actors are also judged by their public image.

Positive factors:

• Charity work
• Social initiatives
• Good public conduct
• Other talents like singing or production

Negative factors:

• Controversies
• Legal issues
• Harmful public behaviour

This makes the rating more complete and not limited only to acting performance.

slides.headline: ⚖️ Weight Assignment
slides.body:
Not all parameters should get equal weight.

Weights should depend on:

• Importance of the parameter
• Reliability of data
• Relevance to public rating

For example, `diversity of roles` may get higher weight than charity events. Similarly, `number of awards` may get more weight than presence outside Bollywood because awards are easier to verify.

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 1**: Clarify that the portal is for the general public.
**Step 2**: Ignore app or website setup because only the framework is needed.
**Step 3**: Divide rating into `Movies`, `Recognition`, and `Personality`.
**Step 4**: Add sub-parameters under each bucket.
**Step 5**: Assign higher weight to important and reliable parameters.
**Step 6**: Use the final weighted score to rate actors.

slides.headline: ✨ Key Insights
slides.body:
• The case is unconventional, so structure matters
• Rating should not depend only on movies
• Recognition adds credibility
• Personality captures public image
• Positive and negative actions both affect rating
• Weights should be based on importance and reliability
• The final framework should be simple enough for public use

slides.headline: ✅ Recommendation
slides.body:
The portal should use a `weighted rating model`.

Suggested buckets:

• Movies: performance, quality, diversity, experience
• Recognition: awards, popularity, fan following
• Personality: social work, conduct, controversies, other talents

Higher weight should go to reliable and important parameters. This creates a balanced, credible, and user-friendly rating system for Bollywood actors and actresses.

revisionCards.title: Left Me High and Dry
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
An online jeans retailer is facing a high churn rate at the `payment gateway`. The task is to identify why customers are dropping off and recommend ways to reduce lost sales.

slides.headline: 💡 Simplified Analogy
slides.body: Imagine reaching the billing counter after choosing clothes, but the cashier takes too long to confirm payment. Even if you liked the product, you may leave. Similarly, users are interested in buying jeans, but friction at the payment stage is making them drop off.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Payment Churn Framework**:

High churn can be broken into two stages:

• `Redirecting to Payment Page`
• `Making the Payment`

For each stage, we check convenience, speed, security, interface, extra charges, and payment success rate.

This helps identify the exact drop-off point.

slides.headline: 🔎 Case Context
slides.body:
Important details:

• Client is an online jeans retailer
• Target users are men and women aged `18–50`
• Churn is high at the payment gateway
• Payment modes include cards, Paytm, and Google Pay
• Drop-off is uniform across payment modes
• A third-party payment gateway is being used
• Competitors do not face this issue

slides.headline: 🚪 Stage 1: Redirecting Page
slides.body:
First, check problems before the payment begins.

Possible issues:

• Obstruction due to banners or pop-ups
• Slow loading of payment page
• Insecure connection warning
• Redirection failure
• Poor success rate while moving to payment gateway

If users cannot reach the payment page smoothly, they may abandon the purchase before payment starts.

slides.headline: 💳 Stage 2: Making Payment
slides.body:
Next, check issues while completing payment.

Possible issues:

• Confusing interface
• Poor navigation between pages
• Too many steps
• Additional hidden charges
• Long OTP delivery time
• Payment failure after entering details

In this case, the key issue is that OTP delivery takes around `3 minutes`, while competitors take only `5–10 seconds`.

slides.headline: 🔐 Root Cause
slides.body:
Since the delay is uniform across cards, Paytm, and Google Pay, the issue is unlikely to be with a single payment mode.

The OTP process can be divided into:

• Information sent from payment partner to wallet/bank
• OTP generated and sent to customer

Because competitors are faster, the problem likely lies with the third-party payment gateway partner.

slides.headline: 🛠️ Immediate Fixes
slides.body:
The company can continue with the same gateway but improve performance.

Actions:

• Ask the gateway partner to improve OTP speed
• Add service-level targets for OTP delivery
• Recover lost sales through penalty clauses
• Use commission-based incentives for better performance
• Add a temporary message saying OTP may take time
• Keep customers informed during the delay

slides.headline: 🔁 Long-Term Fixes
slides.body:
If the issue continues, the company should consider stronger alternatives.

Options:

• Hire a different payment gateway provider
• Build an in-house payment gateway after cost-benefit analysis
• Compare gateway costs, success rates, speed, and reliability
• Track checkout funnel metrics continuously
• Test payment experience across devices and payment modes

This prevents repeated revenue loss.

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 1**: Clarify customer segment, payment modes, and competitor situation.
**Step 2**: Break churn into `redirecting to page` and `making payment`.
**Step 3**: Check issues like obstruction, speed, security, interface, and charges.
**Step 4**: Identify OTP delay as the key problem.
**Step 5**: Compare with competitors taking only `5–10 seconds`.
**Step 6**: Recommend improving, replacing, or building the payment gateway.

slides.headline: ✨ Key Insights
slides.body:
• Churn is happening at payment gateway, not product selection
• Drop-off is uniform across payment modes
• Competitors do not face the same issue
• OTP delay of `3 minutes` is the main problem
• Third-party gateway is likely responsible
• Payment speed directly impacts conversion
• Recommendations should include both immediate and long-term fixes

slides.headline: ✅ Recommendation
slides.body:
The retailer should first improve the current payment gateway’s OTP speed through strict performance targets and penalties.

If the issue continues, it should shift to a better third-party provider or build its own gateway after cost-benefit analysis.

This will reduce payment churn, improve checkout experience, and recover lost sales.

revisionCards.title: Zero Dark Thirty
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
The Government wants to reduce the number of terrorist attacks such as `bomb blasts` and `shootings` in India as much as possible, with no fixed timeline or budget constraint.

slides.headline: 💡 Simplified Analogy
slides.body: Imagine a college wants to prevent theft during a fest. It can either stop problems before they happen through checks and monitoring, or handle them quickly if something goes wrong. Similarly, reducing terrorism needs both `prevention` and `response planning`.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Terrorism Reduction Framework**:

We can divide the solution into two parts:

• `Preventive Measures`
• `Handling the Situation`

Prevention reduces the chance of attacks. Response planning reduces damage if an incident happens.

This makes the approach structured and practical.

slides.headline: 🔎 Case Context
slides.body:
Important details:

• Client is the `Government`
• Terrorism means bomb blasts or shootings
• Goal is to reduce attacks as much as possible
• No fixed timeline is given
• No budget constraint exists

Since the case is broad, we need a structured framework instead of giving random security suggestions.

slides.headline: 🛡️ Preventive Measures
slides.body:
Preventive actions reduce the chance of attacks before they happen.

Key areas:

• Classify threats by geography
• Strengthen border and entry-point security
• Improve coordination between states
• Protect crowded and high-risk public places
• Study past attack patterns
• Increase monitoring around festivals and large gatherings
• Train specialized response teams
• Use strict penalties as deterrence

slides.headline: 🌍 Geography-Based Segmentation
slides.body:
Threats can be segmented by source and location.

For domestic threats:

• Improve inter-state coordination
• Regulate illegal weapons movement
• Increase security at sensitive areas

For cross-border threats:

• Strengthen airports, land borders, and coastal entry points
• Improve identification and screening systems
• Deploy trained security teams at high-risk locations

This helps use resources more effectively.

slides.headline: 📊 Pattern Analysis
slides.body:
Past incidents can reveal when and where risk is higher.

The government can analyze:

• Festival seasons
• Crowded markets
• Malls, hotels, and transport hubs
• Public events and large gatherings
• Sensitive political or religious locations

By identifying high-risk times and places, security teams can stay prepared before incidents occur.

slides.headline: 🚨 Handling the Situation
slides.body:
If an attack happens, the focus should be on reducing damage quickly.

Response actions:

• Identify nearby high-risk areas
• Issue alerts quickly
• Evacuate affected locations
• Reduce approval delays for emergency action
• Control misinformation and panic
• Coordinate police, medical, and emergency teams
• Follow a clear response protocol

A strong response can also discourage future attacks.

slides.headline: 📉 Long-Term Reduction
slides.body:
In the long run, the government should also reduce the factors that allow terrorism to grow.

Focus areas:

• Cut illegal funding channels
• Improve intelligence sharing
• Monitor suspicious networks legally
• Strengthen community trust
• Promote awareness and reporting mechanisms
• Improve rehabilitation and education efforts in vulnerable areas

This addresses both symptoms and root causes.

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 1**: Clarify that terrorism means bomb blasts and shootings.
**Step 2**: Split the approach into `prevention` and `response`.
**Step 3**: Under prevention, classify threats by geography and risk areas.
**Step 4**: Analyze patterns by festivals, crowded places, and sensitive locations.
**Step 5**: Under response, focus on alerts, evacuation, coordination, and protocols.
**Step 6**: Add long-term actions like funding control and intelligence sharing.

slides.headline: ✨ Key Insights
slides.body:
• The case is broad, so structure is essential
• Prevention and response both matter
• Geography-based segmentation improves resource allocation
• Pattern analysis helps predict high-risk situations
• A strong response procedure reduces damage
• Long-term reduction needs funding control and intelligence sharing
• Public trust and awareness can support prevention

slides.headline: ✅ Recommendation
slides.body:
The government should use a `Prevent-Respond-Reduce` strategy.

Recommended approach:

• Prevent attacks through better security, monitoring, and pattern analysis
• Respond quickly through alerts, evacuation, and emergency coordination
• Reduce long-term risk through funding control, intelligence sharing, awareness, and community trust

This creates a complete framework to reduce terrorism in India.

revisionCards.title: Ups and Downs
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
A theme park in Pune is facing long queues for its `roller coaster`. The client wants to reduce waiting time and improve the waiting experience using both short-term and long-term solutions.

slides.headline: 💡 Simplified Analogy
slides.body: Imagine a college fest where one food stall has a huge queue while other stalls are empty. You can either reduce the queue by adding counters, shifting some crowd elsewhere, or make waiting less annoying. The same logic applies to the roller coaster.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Waiting Period Framework**:

We divide the problem into two parts:

• `Reducing Waiting Time`
• `Improving Waiting Experience`

Waiting time depends on:

`People in Queue × Time per Ride ÷ Number of Seats`

So, we can reduce queues by lowering demand, reducing ride cycle time, or increasing capacity.

slides.headline: 🔎 Case Context
slides.body:
Important details:

• Client owns a theme park in Pune
• The park has land rides, water rides, and food stalls
• Complaints are specifically about the `roller coaster`
• Long queues exist at almost all times
• No fixed reduction target is given
• No budget constraint exists
• Both short-term and long-term solutions can be considered

slides.headline: 👥 Reduce People in Queue
slides.body:
First, reduce excess demand for the roller coaster.

Possible actions:

• Charge an additional fee since it is a top attraction
• Promote other rides to distribute crowd better
• Add new thrill rides or 9D cinema
• Create another roller coaster if feasible
• Increase park and ride operating hours
• Introduce age or height requirements only if safety supports it

This spreads demand across the park.

slides.headline: ⏱️ Reduce Time per Ride
slides.body:
Ride cycle time can be reduced across four stages:

• `Boarding`
• `Ride Time`
• `De-boarding`
• `Idle Time`

Actions include training staff, briefing the next batch while the ride is running, using centralized seat-belt checks, reducing ride length slightly, smooth de-boarding, and automating routine safety checks through checklists.

slides.headline: 🎢 Increase Ride Capacity
slides.body:
The third way is to increase the number of seats available per cycle.

Possible actions:

• Add more seats to the roller coaster if technically possible
• Modify machinery after safety checks
• Repair broken or unavailable seats immediately
• Improve occupancy by filling empty seats properly
• Use staff to match smaller groups into vacant seats

Higher capacity reduces waiting time without reducing demand.

slides.headline: 😊 Improve Waiting Experience
slides.body:
Even if waiting cannot be removed fully, the experience can be improved.

Solutions:

• Introduce digital queuing through an app
• Use token systems so people do not stand continuously
• Allow one representative to wait for a group
• Add parades, performers, and mascots near the queue
• Provide shaded waiting areas and drinking water

This makes waiting feel shorter and less frustrating.

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 1**: Clarify that the issue is specifically with the roller coaster.
**Step 2**: Break the solution into `waiting time` and `waiting experience`.
**Step 3**: Use the formula: queue size × ride time ÷ seats.
**Step 4**: Reduce queue size by managing demand and adding alternatives.
**Step 5**: Reduce ride cycle time through better boarding, de-boarding, and checks.
**Step 6**: Improve experience using digital queues, tokens, and entertainment.

slides.headline: ✨ Key Insights
slides.body:
• The problem is limited to the `roller coaster`
• Waiting time has three levers: demand, time, and seats
• Demand can be spread using alternate attractions
• Boarding and de-boarding delays are important
• Capacity can improve through seats and occupancy
• Waiting experience matters even if queues remain
• Digital queuing and token systems reduce frustration

slides.headline: ✅ Recommendation
slides.body:
The theme park should follow a two-part plan.

**Reduce Waiting Time**:
Manage demand, add alternate attractions, improve boarding, reduce idle time, and increase ride capacity.

**Improve Waiting Experience**:
Use digital queues, token systems, representatives, entertainment, shade, and water.

This reduces actual queue time while also making unavoidable waiting more comfortable for visitors.

revisionCards.title: What the Truck!
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
A company wants to enter the transportation business in India and needs to estimate the `cost of running a truck per kilometre`. The focus is only on cost/km, not overall business setup.

slides.headline: 💡 Simplified Analogy
slides.body: Imagine using a bike for delivery. The cost per kilometre is not only petrol. You also include purchase cost, repairs, insurance, and the rider’s salary. Similarly, for a truck, we divide total yearly cost by yearly kilometres travelled.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Truck Cost Framework**:

`Cost/km = Fuel Cost/km + Other Cost/km`

Other costs include:

• `Purchase and financing`
• `Insurance`
• `Driver and helper salary`
• `Servicing and maintenance`

Then, we divide annual non-fuel costs by total kilometres covered in a year.

slides.headline: 🔎 Case Context
slides.body:
Important assumptions:

• Truck is a six-wheel truck
• Purchase price is `₹20 lakh`
• Scrap value after 15 years is `₹2 lakh`
• Useful life is `15 years`
• Total interest payable is `₹6 lakh`
• Truck completes one Mumbai–Delhi round trip per week
• Annual distance is around `1,20,000 km`

slides.headline: 🚚 Distance Calculation
slides.body:
Mumbai to Delhi is around `1,500 km`.

So, one round trip distance:
`1,500 × 2 = 3,000 km`

The truck operates for around `40 weeks/year`.

Annual distance:
`3,000 × 40 = 1,20,000 km`

This distance is used to spread yearly costs and calculate cost per kilometre.

slides.headline: 🧾 Purchase & Financing Cost
slides.body:
**Purchase Cost Allocation**:

Purchase price = `₹20 lakh`
Scrap value = `₹2 lakh`

Net cost:
`₹20L - ₹2L = ₹18L`

Annual purchase cost:
`₹18L ÷ 15 = ₹1.2L/year`

**Financing Cost**:
Total interest = `₹6L`

Annual financing cost:
`₹6L ÷ 15 = ₹40,000/year`

slides.headline: 👷 Labour & Maintenance
slides.body:
**Labour Cost**:

Driver salary = `₹25,000/month`
Helper salary = `₹20,000/month`

Annual staff cost:
`₹45,000 × 12 = ₹5.4L/year`

**Maintenance Cost**:

Truck is serviced `4 times/year`.
Cost per service = `₹10,000`

Annual maintenance:
`4 × ₹10,000 = ₹40,000/year`

slides.headline: 🛡️ Insurance & Other Cost/km
slides.body:
**Insurance Cost**:

Insurance premium is around `3%` of purchase price.

`3% of ₹20L = ₹60,000/year`

Total annual non-fuel cost:

`₹1.2L + ₹40,000 + ₹5.4L + ₹40,000 + ₹60,000 = ₹8L`

Other cost per km:

`₹8L ÷ 1,20,000 = ₹6.67/km`

slides.headline: ⛽ Fuel Cost/km
slides.body:
**Fuel Cost Formula**:

`Fuel Cost/km = Diesel Price per Litre ÷ Mileage`

Diesel price = `₹80/litre`

Truck mileage = `8 km/litre`

Fuel cost per km:

`₹80 ÷ 8 = ₹10/km`

Fuel is the largest direct running cost and must be added separately to other annual costs.

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 1**: Clarify that the goal is only cost per kilometre.
**Step 2**: Estimate annual distance as `1,20,000 km`.
**Step 3**: Calculate annual purchase allocation as `₹1.2L`.
**Step 4**: Add financing, insurance, labour, and maintenance costs.
**Step 5**: Divide total non-fuel cost of `₹8L` by annual distance.
**Step 6**: Add fuel cost of `₹10/km` to get final cost/km.

slides.headline: ✨ Key Insights
slides.body:
• Cost/km includes both fuel and non-fuel costs
• Annual distance is important for cost allocation
• Purchase cost must be adjusted for scrap value
• Financing and insurance should not be ignored
• Labour is a major recurring cost
• Maintenance should be added separately
• Final cost depends heavily on mileage and diesel price

slides.headline: ✅ Final Estimate
slides.body:
**Other Cost/km**:
`₹6.67/km`

**Fuel Cost/km**:
`₹10/km`

**Total Cost/km**:
`₹6.67 + ₹10 = ₹16.67/km`

So, the estimated cost of running a six-wheel truck in India is around:

`₹16.67 per kilometre`

This includes purchase, financing, insurance, labour, maintenance, and fuel costs.

revisionCards.title: An Apple a Day Keeps the Doctor Away
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
The Ministry of Health wants to improve the general well-being of Indian citizens across the country. The solution can include both `short-term` and `long-term` measures, with no major constraints.

slides.headline: 💡 Simplified Analogy
slides.body: Imagine improving health in a school. You can prevent students from falling sick through hygiene, awareness, vaccines, and clean water. But if someone still falls ill, they need quick diagnosis, proper treatment, medicines, and follow-ups. A country’s healthcare system works similarly.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Health Improvement Framework**:

We can divide the approach into two parts:

• `Preventive Measures`
• `Curative Measures`

Preventive measures reduce the chances of illness.

Curative measures improve diagnosis, admission, treatment, and recovery after someone becomes sick.

slides.headline: 🔎 Case Context
slides.body:
Important details:

• Client is the `Ministry of Health`
• Objective is to improve general well-being
• Scope is across India
• Both short-term and long-term solutions are allowed
• No budget constraint is given
• No specific region is mentioned

So, we should give a broad national-level healthcare framework.

slides.headline: 🛡️ Preventive Measures
slides.body:
Preventive measures help reduce disease before treatment is needed.

Key actions:

• Run awareness campaigns on common diseases
• Promote vaccination and regular check-ups
• Encourage employers to provide medical insurance
• Invest in hospitals, labs, research, and medicine access
• Improve cleanliness and hygiene
• Control pollution and ensure safe drinking water

This reduces both disease frequency and severity.

slides.headline: 📢 Awareness & Encouragement
slides.body:
People must know how to stay healthy and when to seek help.

Actions:

• Use TV, radio, and digital campaigns
• Spread awareness about diseases like tuberculosis
• Encourage healthy lifestyle habits
• Promote vaccination drives
• Encourage regular health check-ups
• Make employers support preventive healthcare

This builds better health behaviour at the citizen level.

slides.headline: 🏥 Curative Measures
slides.body:
Curative measures focus on helping people once they are sick.

The healthcare journey can be divided into:

• `Diagnosis`
• `Admission`
• `Treatment`
• `Post-Treatment`

Each stage should be improved so that patients can access care quickly, affordably, and safely.

slides.headline: 🩺 Diagnosis & Admission
slides.body:
**Diagnosis**:

• Encourage people to visit clinics early
• Cap consultation fees for affordability
• Subsidize rural consultations
• Improve access to diagnostic labs

**Admission**:

• Reduce unnecessary paperwork
• Ensure availability of beds
• Improve staff availability
• Make hospital entry faster and simpler

Early diagnosis and smooth admission reduce complications.

slides.headline: 💊 Treatment & Recovery
slides.body:
**Treatment**:

• Increase availability of doctors
• Set up more medical institutes
• Maintain quality standards for doctors and nurses
• Keep hospitals sanitized
• Limit disease spread inside hospitals

**Post-Treatment**:

• Schedule regular follow-ups
• Ensure availability of general and specialized medicines
• Track whether patients take prescribed medicines properly

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 1**: Clarify that the goal is general well-being across India.
**Step 2**: Split the solution into `preventive` and `curative` measures.
**Step 3**: Under prevention, focus on awareness, incentives, investments, lifestyle, and externalities.
**Step 4**: Under cure, break the journey into diagnosis, admission, treatment, and post-treatment.
**Step 5**: Recommend both short-term access improvements and long-term healthcare investment.

slides.headline: ✨ Key Insights
slides.body:
• Health improvement needs both prevention and cure
• Awareness helps citizens make better choices
• Vaccination and check-ups reduce disease burden
• Clean water, hygiene, and pollution control matter
• Diagnosis should be early and affordable
• Hospital admission should be simple
• Treatment quality depends on doctors, medicines, and hygiene
• Follow-ups support proper recovery

slides.headline: ✅ Recommendation
slides.body:
The Ministry should follow a `Prevent-Cure-Recover` strategy.

Recommended actions:

• Increase health awareness and vaccination
• Improve hygiene, water safety, and pollution control
• Invest in hospitals, labs, medicines, and medical institutes
• Make diagnosis affordable and early
• Improve beds, staff, and treatment quality
• Ensure medicines and regular follow-ups

This improves both short-term care and long-term public health.

revisionCards.title: Bad Teacher
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
The Education Ministry of Rajasthan wants to improve the `pass percentage` of class 10 and class 12 students in local state board public schools as soon as possible.

slides.headline: 💡 Simplified Analogy
slides.body: Imagine a school wants more students to pass final exams. You cannot only focus on the exam day. You need to check whether students are eligible, whether they prepared well, whether the exam process is accessible, and whether checking is fair.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Board Result Improvement Framework**:

We can divide the student journey into four stages:

• `Eligibility`
• `Preparation`
• `Examination`
• `Evaluation`

Since the goal is to improve pass percentage, we focus on already enrolled students and increase the percentage of students who clear the board exams.

slides.headline: 🔎 Case Context
slides.body:
Important details:

• Client is the `Education Ministry of Rajasthan`
• Focus is on class `10` and class `12`
• Scope is local state board only
• Only public schools are considered
• Goal is to increase pass percentage
• Solutions should be implemented as soon as possible
• No budget constraint is given

slides.headline: ✅ Stage 1: Eligibility
slides.body:
Eligibility ensures that only prepared students reach board exams.

For new admissions:

• Set minimum required academic standards
• Revise standards where needed

For already enrolled students:

• Conduct strict readiness checks in classes 9 and 11
• Promote students only when they are prepared
• Identify weak students early
• Provide remedial support before board year

This improves the quality of students appearing for exams.

slides.headline: 📚 Stage 2: Preparation
slides.body:
Preparation is the most important stage.

It can be improved through:

• Better infrastructure
• Teacher training
• Stronger course design
• Student motivation

Infrastructure includes classrooms, libraries, computer labs, science labs, hygiene, and extracurricular opportunities.

This gives students a better learning environment before they appear for board exams.

slides.headline: 👩‍🏫 Teachers & Course
slides.body:
Teacher-side improvements:

• Train teachers regularly
• Evaluate teacher performance
• Maintain optimum student-teacher ratio
• Ensure students get enough attention

Course-side improvements:

• Reduce unnecessary passing marks pressure
• Revise syllabus for board relevance
• Provide recorded lectures and flexible timetable
• Conduct pre-boards and chapter-wise tests
• Allow multiple attempts where possible

slides.headline: 🌟 Motivation
slides.body:
Students need motivation to perform better.

Possible actions:

• Give scholarships to strong performers
• Provide free uniforms or fee waivers
• Recognize toppers publicly
• Highlight successful alumni who studied in the same schools
• Give awards to consistent performers
• Create healthy competition between schools

Motivation makes students take preparation more seriously.

slides.headline: 📝 Stage 3: Examination
slides.body:
The exam process should be accessible and fair.

Actions:

• Allow more languages for writing exams
• Improve facilities for disabled students
• Ensure accessible and quality exam centres
• Reduce confusion on exam day
• Provide clear instructions to students
• Improve seating, lighting, and basic facilities

A smoother exam environment helps students perform according to their preparation.

slides.headline: 📊 Stage 4: Evaluation
slides.body:
Evaluation should be fair, transparent, and accountable.

Possible actions:

• Allow revaluation of answer sheets
• Create accountability for examiners
• Penalize misconduct or careless checking
• Use moderation checks for consistency
• Train evaluators before checking begins
• Track school-wise result gaps after evaluation

This ensures students are not unfairly failed due to process issues.

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 1**: Clarify that improvement means increasing pass percentage.
**Step 2**: Restrict scope to Rajasthan state board public schools.
**Step 3**: Break the journey into eligibility, preparation, examination, and evaluation.
**Step 4**: Improve preparation through infrastructure, teachers, course, and motivation.
**Step 5**: Make exams accessible and student-friendly.
**Step 6**: Ensure fair evaluation through rechecking and examiner accountability.

slides.headline: ✨ Key Insights
slides.body:
• Focus is on public schools only
• Pass percentage depends on the full student journey
• Eligibility checks prevent unprepared promotion
• Preparation needs teachers, infrastructure, course, and motivation
• Exam centres must be accessible and fair
• Evaluation should be transparent
• Disability-friendly exam centres and multiple language options are strong brownie points

slides.headline: ✅ Recommendation
slides.body:
The ministry should follow a `Student Journey Improvement Plan`.

Recommended actions:

• Identify weak students early
• Improve school infrastructure and hygiene
• Train and evaluate teachers
• Revise syllabus and conduct regular mocks
• Motivate students through scholarships and recognition
• Improve exam centres and accessibility
• Ensure fair evaluation and revaluation

This can improve board results in a structured way.

revisionCards.title: Where’s Perry?
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Mr. Perry, a senior partner, has recently started arriving `30 minutes late` to the office every day. The firm wants to identify the reason without directly asking him and recommend practical solutions.

slides.headline: 💡 Simplified Analogy
slides.body: Imagine a student who was always punctual suddenly starts reaching class late. Instead of assuming laziness, you check their full morning journey: waking up, getting ready, travel, entry gate, and reaching class. The delay usually lies in one broken step.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Journey Mapping Framework**:

Mr. Perry’s arrival can be broken into:

• `Waking Up`
• `Morning Routine`
• `Travel to Office`
• `Arrival at Office`
• `Reaching Desk`

Since personal and work-related issues are ruled out, we focus on the travel journey and identify where time has increased.

slides.headline: 🔎 Case Context
slides.body:
Important details:

• The case is set in `2016`
• Mr. Perry has been late for the last `2 weeks`
• He arrives `30 minutes late`
• He leaves office on time
• Work satisfaction and role have not changed
• No personal issues are suspected
• He is the only senior partner facing this issue

So, the problem is likely external.

slides.headline: 🚗 Commute Breakdown
slides.body:
Commute time can be calculated as:

`Time Taken = Distance Travelled ÷ Average Speed + Time Spent in Stoppages`

Possible causes:

• Route distance may have increased
• Road quality may have worsened
• Traffic may have increased
• Speed limits or signals may have changed
• Time spent at stoppages may have gone up

The case reveals that stoppage time has increased.

slides.headline: 🛑 Toll Booth Analysis
slides.body:
The delay is happening at the toll booth.

Toll booth time depends on:

`Number of Cars ÷ Number of Booths × Turnover Time per Car`

Possible causes:

• More cars waiting
• Fewer toll booths operating
• Higher time per car

The case reveals that the `turnover time per car` has increased, so we analyze why each transaction is taking longer.

slides.headline: 💳 Transaction Delay
slides.body:
Turnover time at the toll booth can increase because of:

• Poor staff efficiency
• Faulty toll system
• Policy changes
• Payment transaction delays

Under transaction delays, possible reasons are:

• Card machines not working
• Lack of change with Mr. Perry
• Lack of change at the toll booth
• Difficulty issuing tickets

The main clue is the year: `2016`.

slides.headline: 🧩 Root Cause
slides.body:
The key insight is `2016 demonetization`.

Demonetization caused a shortage of cash change across India. This increased transaction time at toll booths.

Mr. Perry was delayed not because of personal issues, motivation, or office problems, but because toll booth payments became slower due to lack of change and transaction delays.

slides.headline: 🛠️ Recommendations
slides.body:
Mr. Perry can reduce the delay by:

• Keeping sufficient change in advance
• Using digital payment options where available
• Buying a monthly or yearly toll pass
• Taking an express pass if available
• Leaving slightly earlier until the issue stabilizes
• Choosing an alternate route if it saves time

The best solution is a pass because it directly reduces toll transaction time.

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 1**: Rule out personal, work, and motivation-related reasons.
**Step 2**: Map Mr. Perry’s full morning journey.
**Step 3**: Identify that the issue lies in travel time.
**Step 4**: Break commute into distance, speed, and stoppage time.
**Step 5**: Find that toll booth turnover time has increased.
**Step 6**: Connect the year `2016` to demonetization and cash-change issues.

slides.headline: ✨ Key Insights
slides.body:
• Do not assume the person is careless
• Rule out personal and professional causes first
• Journey mapping helps locate the exact delay point
• Commute time depends on distance, speed, and stoppages
• Toll booth delay is caused by transaction time
• The year `2016` is the biggest clue
• Demonetization explains the sudden lack of change

slides.headline: ✅ Recommendation
slides.body:
The firm should conclude that Mr. Perry’s lateness is due to increased toll booth transaction time after demonetization.

Recommended actions:

• Ask him to keep change in advance
• Suggest a monthly/yearly toll pass
• Use digital payment or express pass options
• Consider an alternate route temporarily

This solves the issue without directly blaming or questioning Mr. Perry.

revisionCards.title: Money Heist
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
The Professor’s team has robbed the Royal Mint of Spain and needs to transport `€2.4 billion` in cash to a safe-house `15 km` away. Estimate the number of `mini-trucks` required for one trip.
