slides.headline: 💡 Simplified Analogy
slides.body: Imagine shifting a huge pile of books using small vans. First, you estimate the space taken by one book, then the total number of books, and finally how much space one van has. Similarly, here we compare `total cash volume` with `mini-truck volume`.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Mini-Truck Requirement Framework**:

`Mini-trucks required = Total Volume of Notes ÷ Volume of One Mini-Truck`

Total volume of notes depends on:

• `Number of notes`
• `Volume of one note`

Truck volume depends on:

• `Length`
• `Breadth`
• `Height`

We assume one trip and no space wastage.

slides.headline: 🔎 Case Context
slides.body:
Important details:

• Total cash = `€2.4 billion`
• Currency denomination = `€100 notes`
• Money must be transported in `one trip`
• Notes are loosely transported
• Safe-house is `15 km` away
• Mini-truck can carry the load safely
• No space wastage is assumed

So, the problem mainly becomes a volume-based guesstimate.

slides.headline: 💶 Number of Notes
slides.body:
**Number of Notes**:

`Total Amount ÷ Denomination per Note`

`€2.4 billion ÷ €100`

`= 2.4 × 10⁹ ÷ 10²`

`= 2.4 × 10⁷ notes`

So, the team needs to transport approximately `24 million` currency notes.

slides.headline: 📏 Volume of One Note
slides.body:
Assume one `€100 note` has dimensions similar to a currency note:

• Length = `15 cm`
• Width = `7 cm`
• Thickness = `0.01 cm`

**Volume of One Note**:

`15 × 7 × 0.01 = 1.05 cm³`

For simplicity, we approximate it as:

`1 cm³ per note`

slides.headline: 📦 Total Volume of Notes
slides.body:
**Total Volume of Notes**:

`Number of Notes × Volume of One Note`

`2.4 × 10⁷ × 1 cm³`

`= 2.4 × 10⁷ cm³`

So, the entire loot will occupy approximately:

`2.4 × 10⁷ cm³`

This is the total space required inside the trucks.

slides.headline: 🚚 Volume of One Mini-Truck
slides.body:
Assume the mini-truck is similar to a small cargo vehicle like Tata Ace.

Cargo body dimensions:

• Length = `300 cm`
• Breadth = `150 cm`
• Height = `180 cm`

**Truck Volume**:

`300 × 150 × 180`

`= 8.1 × 10⁶ cm³`

Approximate volume:

`8 × 10⁶ cm³`

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 1**: Clarify amount, denomination, number of trips, and packing style.
**Step 2**: Calculate number of notes as `2.4 × 10⁷`.
**Step 3**: Estimate one note’s volume using length, width, and thickness.
**Step 4**: Calculate total note volume as `2.4 × 10⁷ cm³`.
**Step 5**: Estimate one mini-truck volume as `8 × 10⁶ cm³`.
**Step 6**: Divide total note volume by truck volume.

slides.headline: 🧮 Final Calculation
slides.body:
**Mini-Trucks Required**:

`Total Volume of Notes ÷ Volume of One Truck`

`(2.4 × 10⁷) ÷ (8 × 10⁶)`

`= 3`

Therefore, the Professor would need approximately:

`3 mini-trucks`

This assumes full space utilization and that weight is not a limiting factor.

slides.headline: ✨ Key Insights
slides.body:
• This is a volume-based guesstimate
• Ask about denomination and number of trips first
• `€100` notes reduce the number of notes needed
• One note is approximated as `1 cm³`
• Total cash volume is around `2.4 × 10⁷ cm³`
• One mini-truck holds around `8 × 10⁶ cm³`
• Final answer is `3 mini-trucks`

slides.headline: ✅ Final Estimate
slides.body:
**Estimated Number of Mini-Trucks**:
`3 mini-trucks`

Why this works:

• Total amount = `€2.4 billion`
• Denomination = `€100`
• Total notes = `2.4 × 10⁷`
• Total note volume = `2.4 × 10⁷ cm³`
• One truck volume = `8 × 10⁶ cm³`

So, `3 mini-trucks` should be enough to transport the loot in one trip.

revisionCards.title: Don’t Do Coke
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the volume of `Pepsi sold` during an IPL match between Royal Challengers Bangalore and Mumbai Indians at Wankhede Stadium, Mumbai, assuming pre-COVID full stadium conditions.

slides.headline: 💡 Simplified Analogy
slides.body: Imagine estimating how much cold drink is sold at a college fest. First, count how many people attend. Then estimate how many buy a drink, how many choose Pepsi, and how much each person drinks. The stadium case follows the same logic.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Pepsi Sales Framework**:

`Volume Sold = Seats × Occupancy × % Buying Soft Drinks × % Buying Pepsi × Volume per Person`

So, we estimate:

• Total stadium capacity
• Match occupancy
• Share buying soft drinks
• Share choosing Pepsi
• Average quantity consumed per buyer

slides.headline: 🔎 Case Context
slides.body:
Important details:

• Match is at `Wankhede Stadium, Mumbai`
• It is an `IPL match`
• Teams are RCB and Mumbai Indians
• Assume year is `2019`, before COVID restrictions
• Weather is pleasant, not too hot or too cold
• Crowd is allowed inside the stadium

This makes it a high-profile match with strong attendance.

slides.headline: 🏟️ Stadium Capacity
slides.body:
Wankhede is an average-sized Indian stadium.

Assume:

• Number of stands = `8`
• Seats per stand = `4,000`

**Total Seats**:
`8 × 4,000 = 32,000`

Since it is a popular IPL match with RCB and Mumbai Indians, we assume high occupancy.

**Occupancy**:
`90%`

Expected crowd:
`32,000 × 90% = 28,800 people`

slides.headline: 🥤 Soft Drink Buyers
slides.body:
Not everyone will buy a soft drink.

We filter buyers using three factors:

• Income-friendly audience: `50%`
• Not health-conscious: `70%`
• Mood to drink: `80%`

**Soft drink buyer share**:
`50% × 70% × 80% ≈ 30%`

So, around `30%` of the crowd may buy a soft drink during the match.

slides.headline: 🔵 Pepsi Preference
slides.body:
Assume there are around `4 major soft drink options` available at the stadium.

If preference were uniform, Pepsi would get:
`25% share`

But Pepsi is popular, so we adjust upward.

**Pepsi buyer share**:
`40%`

This means out of the people buying soft drinks, around `40%` may choose Pepsi.

slides.headline: 🥛 Volume per Person
slides.body:
Assume most Pepsi buyers consume around `1 glass`.

Some people may buy a second glass, so we estimate:

**Average glasses per buyer**:
`1.25 glasses`

Each glass is around:
`300 ml`

**Average volume per Pepsi buyer**:
`1.25 × 300 ml = 375 ml`

This is the average quantity consumed by each Pepsi buyer.

slides.headline: 🔍 Dry Run Trace
steps: **Step 1**: Clarify match type, stadium, year, and weather.
**Step 2**: Estimate stadium capacity as `32,000 seats`.
**Step 3**: Apply `90% occupancy` for a high-profile IPL match.
**Step 4**: Estimate soft drink buyers using income, health, and mood filters.
**Step 5**: Estimate Pepsi preference as `40%` among soft drink buyers.
**Step 6**: Multiply by `375 ml` average consumption per Pepsi buyer.

slides.headline: ✨ Key Insights
slides.body:
• This is a demand-based guesstimate
• Clarifying match type and weather is important
• IPL match means high occupancy
• Not every spectator buys a soft drink
• Income, health, and mood filters help estimate buyers
• Pepsi share is adjusted upward due to popularity
• Average consumption is around `375 ml/person`
• Final estimate is around `1,300 litres`

slides.headline: ✅ Final Estimate
slides.body:
**Estimated Pepsi Sold**:
`1,300 litres`

Why this works:

• Stadium capacity = `32,000`
• Occupancy = `90%`
• Soft drink buyers = `30%`
• Pepsi preference = `40%`
• Average Pepsi consumed = `375 ml/person`

So, approximately `1,300 litres of Pepsi` may be sold during the IPL match at Wankhede Stadium.

revisionCards.title: ACs Sold in India
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the number of ACs sold in India.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine AC demand is like electricity usage. Homes, offices, malls, cafes, and public spaces use ACs differently, so we estimate each segment separately and add them.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate annual AC sales in India.
2. Consumers are divided into households, offices, malls, restaurants, and public spaces.
3. Since ACs last for multiple years, we estimate total AC demand and convert it into yearly sales using average lifetime.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Segment-Based Estimation**:
Instead of guessing total AC sales directly, we estimate AC ownership across major consumer segments. Then we add the demand and adjust using AC lifetime.
`Annual Sales = Total AC Demand ÷ Average AC Lifetime`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Consumer Segments:**
Total population = `150 Cr`.
Average family size = `4`, so households = `37.5 Cr`.
Urban households = `40%`, rural households = `60%`.
Only urban households are considered for AC ownership. Other segments include corporate offices, cafes, restaurants, malls, showrooms, lodges, and public gathering spots.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Households:**
Total households = `37.5 Cr`
Urban households = `40%`
AC ownership in urban homes = `35%`
Calculation:
`37.5 × 0.40 × 0.35`
= **5.25 Cr ACs**

**Step 2: Corporate Offices:**
Office-going population = `11.25 Cr`
Small companies = `1L`, corporations = `35,000`
Assume `10 ACs` per small company and `100 branches × 10 ACs` per corporation.
Total = **3.52 Cr ACs**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Cafes and Restaurants:**
In 50 metro cities, assume `400 cafes` with `3 ACs` each and `800 restaurants` with `5 ACs` each.
Calculation:
`50 × (400×3 + 800×5)`
= **2.6L ACs**

**Step 4: Towns and Lodges:**
Small towns/villages add around **0.6L ACs**.
Lodges: `50 × 800 + 10000 × 10 + 5L × 1 × 50%`
= **3.2L ACs**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Showrooms, Malls and Public Spots:**
Malls in metro and Tier 1 cities contribute around **24.9L ACs**.
Other public gathering spots like libraries, classrooms, museums, and tourist places contribute around **0.5 Cr ACs**.

**Step 6: Final Estimate:**
Commercial/public demand:
`3.52 Cr + 2.6L + 0.6L + 3.2L + 24.9L + 0.5 Cr`
= **4.33 Cr ACs**
Assuming an average AC lifetime of `10 years`, yearly sales are estimated around **4.33 Cr ACs/year**.

revisionCards.title: Revenue Generated by a Single Petrol Pump in India
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the amount of revenue generated by a single petrol pump in India.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine a petrol pump like a shop where different vehicles buy different amounts of fuel. Highways get heavy vehicles, while cities get more bikes and cars, so we estimate both separately.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate daily revenue for one petrol pump.
2. Location is not fixed, so we consider both highway and city petrol pumps.
3. Vehicles are divided into bikes, cars, buses, trucks, and transport vehicles because fuel purchase differs by vehicle type.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Vehicle-Based Revenue**:
Instead of guessing revenue directly, we estimate how many vehicles visit a petrol pump and how much fuel money each type spends. Then we calculate highway and city revenue separately and take an average.
`Revenue = Vehicles × Average Fuel Spend`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Fuel and Location Segments:**
Average petrol price = `₹100/litre`.
Average diesel price = `₹90/litre`.
Highway pumps get more trucks, buses, and transport vehicles.
City pumps get more bikes, scooters, cars, SUVs, buses, and tempos.
Revenue is estimated for `1 day`.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Highway Heavy Vehicles:**
Daily vehicles = `200 trucks + 100 tempos + 100 buses`
Heavy vehicle fuel spend split:
`30% × ₹5,000`, `50% × ₹10,000`, `20% × ₹20,000`
Calculation:
`400 × (0.30×5000 + 0.50×10000 + 0.20×20000)`
= **₹42 lakh**

**Step 2: Highway Cars and SUVs:**
Daily vehicles = `50 cars + 50 SUVs = 100`
Fuel spend split:
`20% × ₹500`, `40% × ₹1500`, `40% × ₹2500`
Calculation:
`100 × (0.20×500 + 0.40×1500 + 0.40×2500)`
= **₹1.7 lakh**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Total Highway Revenue:**
Heavy vehicle revenue = `₹42 lakh`
Cars and SUVs revenue = `₹1.7 lakh`
Total highway revenue
= `42 + 1.7`
= **₹43.7 lakh/day**

**Step 4: Tier 1 City Pump:**
Vehicles: `500 bikes`, `200 cars/SUVs`, `50 buses`, `20 tempos`
Bike spend split: `40%×₹100`, `30%×₹250`, `30%×₹500`
Cars/SUVs spend = `₹1000`
Buses/tempos spend = `₹1500`

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: City Revenue Estimate:**
Tier 1 revenue:
`500×(0.40×100 + 0.30×250 + 0.30×500) + 200×1000 + 70×1500`
= **₹4,37,500**
Tier 2 revenue = `60% of Tier 1`
Tier 3 revenue = `5% of Tier 1`
Average city revenue = **₹2,40,625/day**

**Step 6: Final Average Revenue:**
Highway revenue = `₹43.7 lakh/day`
City revenue = `₹2.41 lakh/day`
Average revenue:
`(43.7 + 2.41) ÷ 2`
= **₹23.05 lakh/day**

revisionCards.title: Foreign Tourists in India Per Year
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the number of foreign tourists in India per year.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine tourists entering India like students entering through school gates. We estimate how many flights arrive daily, how many passengers they carry, and what fraction are foreign tourists.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate foreign tourists visiting India in one year.
2. Only international flights arriving at Indian airports are considered.
3. We assume foreign passengers arriving through these flights are tourists.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Flight-Based Estimation**:
Instead of guessing tourists directly, we estimate daily international flights, average passengers per flight, and the share of foreigners. Then we convert daily tourists into yearly tourists.
`Tourists/year = Flights/day × Avg passengers × Foreign share × 365`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Flight Segments:**
International airports in India = `40`.
Each airport hosts `20` international arrivals daily.
Total international flights/day = `40 × 20 = 800`.
Large flights = `40%`, capacity = `1000 passengers`.
Small flights = `60%`, capacity = `400 passengers`.
Foreign passenger share = `30%`.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Flights Per Day:**
International airports = `40`
Flights per airport per day = `20`
Calculation:
`40 × 20`
= **800 flights/day**

**Step 2: Average Passenger Capacity:**
Large flights = `40% × 1000`
Small flights = `60% × 400`
Average passengers/flight:
`0.40×1000 + 0.60×400`
= **640 passengers**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Foreign Passengers Per Day:**
Total flights/day = `800`
Average passengers/flight = `640`
Foreign passenger share = `30%`
Calculation:
`800 × 640 × 0.30`
= **1,53,600 tourists/day**

**Step 4: Yearly Tourists:**
Daily foreign tourists = `1,53,600`
Days in a year = `365`
Calculation:
`1,53,600 × 365`
= **5,60,64,000 tourists/year**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Final Estimate:**
Total foreign tourists visiting India in a year
= **5,60,64,000**
≈ **5.6 Cr foreign tourists/year**

revisionCards.title: Footballs Sold in India Per Year
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the number of footballs sold in India.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine football sales like stationery sales. Some are bought by children, some by young adults, and some by schools, colleges, and clubs, so we estimate each group separately and add them.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate footballs sold in India in one year.
2. Buyers are divided into students, young adults, sports clubs, schools, and colleges.
3. Both personal purchases and institutional purchases are included.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Consumer-Based Estimation**:
Instead of guessing total football sales directly, we estimate purchases by each consumer group. Children and young adults buy for personal play, while schools, colleges, and clubs buy in bulk.
`Total Sales = Personal Sales + Institutional Sales`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Consumer Segments:**
Indian population = `150 Cr = 15000L`.
Students = `20%` of population.
Young adults aged 18–26 = `15%` of population.
Personal buyers are students and young adults.
Institutional buyers include sports clubs, schools, and colleges.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Students:**
Student population = `20% × 15000L`
Assume `1 football per 20 children`
Calculation:
`20% × 15000L ÷ 20`
= **150L footballs/year**

**Step 2: Young Adults:**
Young adults = `15% × 15000L`
Assume only `0.5%` buy a football yearly
Calculation:
`15% × 15000L × 0.5%`
= **11.25L ≈ 10L footballs/year**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Sports Clubs:**
Tier 1 cities = `8`, with `200 clubs each`
Tier 2 cities = `100`, with `50% × 20 clubs each`
Each club buys `25 footballs/year`
Calculation:
`(200×8 + 50%×100×20) × 25`
= **0.65L footballs/year**

**Step 4: Schools:**
School-going population = `24 Cr`
Tier 1 schools buy `10` footballs/year
Tier 2/rest schools buy `5` footballs/year
Total school demand = **22.4L footballs/year**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Colleges:**
College students = `15% × 75% × 150 Cr = 16.88 Cr`
Average college strength = `750 students`
Number of colleges = `16.88 Cr ÷ 750 = 2.25L`
Each college buys `10 footballs/year`
Total = **22.5L footballs/year**

**Step 6: Final Total:**
Students = `150L`
Young adults = `10L`
Institutions = `0.65L + 22.4L + 22.5L = 45.5L`
Total = **205L footballs/year**

revisionCards.title: Chapatis Consumed at Balaji Temple in a Day
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the number of chapatis consumed at Balaji Temple in a day.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine temple food like a community meal. Different age groups eat different numbers of chapatis, so we estimate chapati consumption age-wise and add everything.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate chapatis consumed at Balaji Temple in one day.
2. Daily pilgrims are assumed to be `1.5 lakh`.
3. Pilgrims are divided by age because appetite and chapati consumption vary across age groups.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Age-Based Consumption**:
Instead of guessing total chapatis directly, we divide pilgrims into age groups. For each group, we estimate how many people eat 1, 2, 3, or 4 chapatis, then add all group totals.
`Total Chapatis = Pilgrims × Age Share × Avg Chapatis`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Age Segments:**
Daily pilgrims = `1.5 lakh`.
Age split: `0–10 years = 10%`, `10–18 years = 15%`, `18–30 years = 25%`, `30–50 years = 35%`, `50+ years = 15%`.
Since the temple is in South India, some pilgrims prefer rice, reducing chapati consumption.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: 0–10 Years:**
Age share = `10%`
50% eat `0.5 chapati`
10% eat `1 chapati`
Calculation:
`1.5L × 10% × (50%×0.5 + 10%×1)`
≈ **0.05L chapatis**

**Step 2: 10–18 Years:**
Age share = `15%`
30% eat `1 chapati`
40% eat `2 chapatis`
30% eat `3 chapatis`
Calculation:
`1.5L × 15% × (30%×1 + 40%×2 + 30%×3)`
≈ **0.45L chapatis**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: 18–30 Years:**
Age share = `25%`
10% eat `2 chapatis`
30% eat `3 chapatis`
60% eat `4 chapatis`
Calculation:
`1.5L × 25% × (10%×2 + 30%×3 + 60%×4)`
≈ **1.31L chapatis**

**Step 4: 30–50 Years:**
Age share = `35%`
20% eat `2 chapatis`
40% eat `3 chapatis`
40% eat `4 chapatis`
Calculation:
`1.5L × 35% × (20%×2 + 40%×3 + 40%×4)`
≈ **1.68L chapatis**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: 50+ Years:**
Age share = `15%`
40% eat `1 chapati`
30% eat `2 chapatis`
30% eat `3 chapatis`
Calculation:
`1.5L × 15% × (40%×1 + 30%×2 + 30%×3)`
≈ **0.43L chapatis**

**Step 6: Final Total:**
Total = `0.05L + 0.45L + 1.31L + 1.68L + 0.43L`
= **3.92L chapatis/day**

revisionCards.title: Average Sleep Hours of Indian Students
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the average number of hours of sleep Indian students take per day.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine student sleep like study schedules. School students usually sleep more regularly, while college students have different weekday and weekend sleep patterns, so we estimate both separately.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate average daily sleep hours of Indian students.
2. Students are divided into school and college students.
3. College students are further split into weekday and weekend sleep patterns because their schedules vary more.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Weighted Average Estimation**:
Instead of guessing average sleep directly, we estimate sleep hours for school and college students separately. Then we combine them using their population shares.
`Average Sleep = School Share × Sleep + College Share × Sleep`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Student Segments:**
Indian population = `150 Cr`.
Students = `20%` of population = `30 Cr`.
School students = `60%` of students.
College students = `40%` of students.
School students sleep around `7 hours/day`. College students have different weekday and weekend sleep patterns.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: School Students:**
School student share = `60%`
They usually sleep from around `11 pm to 6 am`.
Average sleep = **7 hours/day**

**Step 2: College Weekday Sleep:**
50% sleep `6 hours`
30% sleep `5 hours`
10% sleep `7 hours`
10% sleep `4 hours`
Calculation:
`0.50×6 + 0.30×5 + 0.10×7 + 0.10×4`
= **5.6 hours**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: College Weekend Sleep:**
25% sleep `6 hours`
40% sleep `5 hours`
35% sleep `4 hours`
Calculation:
`0.25×6 + 0.40×5 + 0.35×4`
= **4.9 hours**

**Step 4: Average College Sleep:**
Weekdays = `5 days`, weekends = `2 days`
Calculation:
`(5×5.6 + 2×4.9) ÷ 7`
= **5.4 hours/day**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Final Average:**
School students = `60%`, sleep = `7 hours`
College students = `40%`, sleep = `5.4 hours`
Calculation:
`0.60×7 + 0.40×5.4`
= `4.2 + 2.16`
= **6.36 hours/day**

**Final Estimate:**
Average sleep of Indian students is around **6 to 6.5 hours per day**.

revisionCards.title: Non-Fiction Books Sold in India Per Month
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the number of non-fiction books sold in India per month.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine book sales like snack buying. Some people buy many books, some buy a few, and some rarely buy, so we estimate reading habits group-wise and add them.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate non-fiction books sold in India per month.
2. Both physical books and e-books are included.
3. Readers are divided by age and reading habit because book purchase frequency differs across groups.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Reading-Habit Estimation**:
Instead of guessing total book sales directly, we first estimate India’s literate reader base. Then we divide readers by age group and classify them as reading addicts, average readers, or inactive readers.
`Books Sold = Readers × Books Bought Per Month`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Reader Segments:**
Indian population = `150 Cr`.
Literacy rate = `75%`, so potential readers = `112.5 Cr`.
Age split among readers:
`0–18 years = 50%`, `18–30 years = 30%`, `30–60 years = 15%`, `60–80 years = 5%`.
E-books are included, but physical books form the major share.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: 0–18 Years:**
Reader share = `50%`
20% buy `5 books/month`
30% buy `3 books/month`
50% buy `1 book/month`
Calculation:
`112.5 × 0.50 × (0.20×5 + 0.30×3 + 0.50×1)`
= **135 Cr books/month**

**Step 2: 18–30 Years:**
Reader share = `30%`
10% buy `3 books/month`
40% buy `2 books/month`
50% buy `1 book/month`
Calculation:
`112.5 × 0.30 × (0.10×3 + 0.40×2 + 0.50×1)`
= **54 Cr books/month**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: 30–60 Years:**
Reader share = `15%`
30% buy `3 books/month`
30% buy `2 books/month`
40% buy `1 book/month`
Calculation:
`112.5 × 0.15 × (0.30×3 + 0.30×2 + 0.40×1)`
≈ **32 Cr books/month**

**Step 4: 60–80 Years:**
Reader share = `5%`
40% buy `2 books/month`
60% do not read regularly
Calculation:
`112.5 × 0.05 × 0.40 × 2`
= **4.5 Cr books/month**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Final Total:**
0–18 years = `135 Cr`
18–30 years = `54 Cr`
30–60 years = `32 Cr`
60–80 years = `4.5 Cr`
Total = `135 + 54 + 32 + 4.5`
≈ **226 Cr books/month**

**Step 6: E-book Note:**
Since India is still growing in e-book adoption, assume around `10%` of total purchases are e-books, included within the same total.

revisionCards.title: Coffees Ordered in CCD in Mumbai in a Day
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the number of coffees ordered in CCD in Mumbai.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine CCD orders like traffic in a café. Some hours are slow, some are peak snack hours, so we estimate orders time-slot wise and add them.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate coffee orders in CCD outlets in Mumbai for one day.
2. The number of CCD outlets is assumed to be `150`.
3. Working hours are considered from `10:00 AM` to `10:00 PM`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Outlet + Time-Slot Estimation**:
Instead of guessing total orders directly, we divide CCD outlets into busy and less busy locations. Then we estimate orders per hour in each time slot and add all orders.
`Total Orders = Outlets × Orders/hour × Hours`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Outlet and Customer Segments:**
Total CCD outlets in Mumbai = `150`.
Busy outlets = `100`, less busy outlets = `50`.
Target customers are mainly working professionals and youngsters aged `18–40 years`.
Time slots: `10–12`, `12–3`, `3–6`, and `6–10`.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: 10:00 AM–12:00 PM:**
Busy outlets = `100`, orders = `10/hour`
Less busy outlets = `50`, orders = `5/hour`
Duration = `2 hours`
Calculation:
`10×2×100 + 5×2×50`
= **2500 orders**

**Step 2: 12:00 PM–3:00 PM:**
Busy outlets = `100`, orders = `7/hour`
Less busy outlets = `50`, orders = `3/hour`
Duration = `3 hours`
Calculation:
`7×3×100 + 3×3×50`
= **2550 orders**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: 3:00 PM–6:00 PM:**
Busy outlets = `100`, orders = `15/hour`
Less busy outlets = `50`, orders = `10/hour`
Duration = `3 hours`
Calculation:
`15×3×100 + 10×3×50`
= **6000 orders**

**Step 4: 6:00 PM–10:00 PM:**
Busy outlets = `100`, orders = `10/hour`
Less busy outlets = `50`, orders = `3/hour`
Duration = `4 hours`
Calculation:
`10×4×100 + 3×4×50`
= **4600 orders**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Final Total:**
Morning orders = `2500`
Lunch orders = `2550`
Snack-time orders = `6000`
Evening orders = `4600`
Total = `2500 + 2550 + 6000 + 4600`
= **15,650 coffee orders/day**

revisionCards.title: Online Shopping Packages Received by a Household in India
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the number of online shopping packages received by households in India.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine online packages like monthly groceries. Some households order often, some occasionally, and some rarely, so we divide households by income, region, and shopping frequency.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate packages received by Indian households in one day.
2. Food parcels are excluded.
3. Packages from Amazon, Flipkart, Myntra, Meesho, Nykaa, Blinkit-type grocery deliveries, etc. are included.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Household Shopping Segmentation**:
Instead of estimating packages directly, we first estimate internet-access households. Then we split them by income, urban/rural location, and shopping behaviour.
`Daily Packages = Monthly Packages ÷ 30`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Household Segments:**
Indian population = `150 Cr`.
Average household size = `4`, so households = `37.5 Cr`.
Households with internet access = `75% × 37.5 = 28.125 Cr`.
Income split: low = `40%`, middle = `35%`, high = `25%`.
Each income group has `50% urban` and `50% rural` households.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: High-Income Households:**
High-income share = `25%`
Urban = `12.5%`, rural = `12.5%`
Urban shopper split = `60%, 30%, 10%`
Rural shopper split = `45%, 30%, 25%`
Calculation:
`28.125 × [(0.125×(0.60×4 + 0.30×3 + 0.10×1)) + (0.125×(0.45×2 + 0.30×1))]`
= **16.17 Cr/month**

**Step 2: Middle-Income Households:**
Middle-income share = `35%`
Urban = `17.5%`, rural = `17.5%`
Urban shopper split = `50%, 30%, 20%`
Rural shopper split = `20%, 30%, 50%`

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Middle-Income Calculation:**
Urban: active shoppers buy every `10 days`, average shoppers buy monthly, below-average shoppers buy every `2 months`.
Rural: active shoppers buy monthly, average shoppers buy every `2 months`, below-average shoppers buy none.
Calculation:
`28.125 × [(0.175×(0.50×3 + 0.30×1 + 0.20×0.5)) + (0.175×(0.20×1 + 0.30×0.5))]`
= **11.07 Cr/month**

**Step 4: Low-Income Households:**
Low-income households are assumed to order very rarely, around once in `4 months`, so their daily contribution is considered negligible.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Final Total:**
High-income packages = `16.17 Cr/month`
Middle-income packages = `11.07 Cr/month`
Total monthly packages = `16.17 + 11.07`
= **27.24 Cr/month**

**Step 6: Daily Packages:**
Daily packages = `27.24 ÷ 30`
= `0.908 Cr/day`
= **90.8 lakh packages/day**

revisionCards.title: Smartphone Users with 5G in India
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the number of smartphone users with 5G in India.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine 5G access is like a new facility available first in bigger cities. Tier 1 cities adopt it fastest, Tier 2 moderately, and Tier 3 slower, so we estimate users tier-wise.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate smartphone users with 5G access in India.
2. Only people with internet access are considered.
3. The population is divided into Tier 1, Tier 2, and Tier 3 regions because 5G adoption varies by city development.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Internet + City-Tier Adoption**:
Instead of guessing 5G users directly, we first estimate internet users. Then we divide them by city tier and apply age eligibility plus 5G adoption rates.
`5G Users = Internet Users × Tier Share × Eligible Age Share × 5G Access Rate`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**User Segments:**
Indian population = `150 Cr`.
Internet access = `60%`, so internet users = `90 Cr`.
Tier split: Tier 1 = `40%`, Tier 2 = `30%`, Tier 3 = `30%`.
Only age groups `18–30` and `30–50` are considered active 5G smartphone users.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Internet Users:**
Total population = `150 Cr`
Internet access = `60%`
Calculation:
`150 × 0.60`
= **90 Cr internet users**

**Step 2: Eligible Age Share:**
0–18 and 50–80 years are assumed to have negligible 5G access.
Eligible groups are `18–30` and `30–50`.
Tier 1 eligible share = `30% + 35% = 65%`
Tier 2 eligible share = `30% + 30% = 60%`
Tier 3 eligible share = `30% + 30% = 60%`

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Tier-wise 5G Access:**
Tier 1 share = `40%`, eligible share = `65%`, 5G access = `100%`
Tier 2 share = `30%`, eligible share = `60%`, 5G access = `80%`
Tier 3 share = `30%`, eligible share = `60%`, 5G access = `50%`

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Final Estimate:**
Based on tier-wise adoption and eligible age groups:
Total 5G smartphone users in India
= **44.46 Cr users**

revisionCards.title: Average Household Electricity Consumption in India
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate average electricity consumption in an Indian household in a day.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine electricity use like daily water use. Urban homes use more appliances, rural homes use fewer, so we estimate both separately and take a weighted average.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate average daily electricity consumption per household in India.
2. Households are divided into urban and rural lifestyles.
3. Consumption is based on common appliances like fans, fridge, TV, lights, AC, heaters, washing machines, and charging devices.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Appliance-Based Estimation**:
Instead of guessing electricity use directly, we estimate appliance usage hours and power rating. Then we calculate urban and rural household consumption separately and combine them using population share.
`Electricity = Power × Usage Hours`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Household Segments:**
Urban households = `40%`, rural households = `60%`.
Urban homes use more appliances like ACs and washing machines.
Rural homes use fewer appliances and fewer fans.
Seasons are split equally: summer, winter, and rainy season are each assumed to last `4 months`.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Appliance Power Ratings:**
Charging devices = `40W/hr`
Fans = `80W/hr`
AC = `1000W/hr`
Water heater = `1500W/hr`
TV = `150W/hr`
Lights = `30W/hr`
Fridge = `500W/hr`
Washing machine = `1000W/hr`

**Step 2: Urban Household Usage:**
Fans = `16×3×4/12 hours`
Fridge = `24 hours`
Heater = `2×8/12 hours`
Charging = `40 hours`
Washing machine = `(4×4/12 + 2×8/12) hours`
AC = `0.4×8×4/12 hours`
Lights = `80 hours`

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 4: Rural Household Usage:**
Rural homes have fewer appliances.
Fans = `2 fans`, charging devices = `2`, no AC, fridge used `24 hours`, washing machine used by `30%` households, and desert coolers used in summer.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 6: Final Average:**
Urban = `40%`, rural = `60%`
Average household consumption:
`0.40×23 + 0.60×20`
= **21.2 kWh/day per household**

revisionCards.title: SUVs Sold in India in a Year
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the number of SUVs sold in India in a year.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine SUVs are like premium family cars. Larger and higher-income families are more likely to buy them, so we estimate SUV ownership by family size, income, and region.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate SUVs sold in India in one year.
2. SUVs are mainly purchased by economically stronger families.
3. Families are segmented by size, region, and income because SUV affordability and need vary across these groups.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Family-Based Estimation**:
Instead of guessing SUV sales directly, we estimate families likely to own SUVs. Larger families and high-income households have higher SUV ownership. Then we divide total SUV stock by average SUV life.
`Annual Sales = SUV Owners ÷ Vehicle Life`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Family Segments:**
Indian population = `150 Cr`.
10% people live separately, so they are excluded.
80% live in nuclear families of `3`.
20% live in families of `4, 5, or 6`.
SUV buyer focus is on high-income families. Average SUV life = `10 years`.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Family of 6:**
Share among large families = `16.7%`
Urban = `40%`, rural = `60%`
High-income share: urban = `70%`, rural = `60%`
Assume `100%` high-income families of 6 buy SUVs.
Contribution:
`0.167 × (40%×70% + 60%×60%)`

**Step 2: Family of 5:**
Share among large families = `20%`
Urban = `40%`, rural = `60%`
High-income share: urban = `50%`, rural = `40%`
Assume `40%` high-income families of 5 buy SUVs.
Contribution:
`0.2 × 40% × (40%×50% + 60%×40%)`

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Family of 4:**
Share among large families = `25%`
Urban = `40%`, rural = `60%`
High-income share: urban = `40%`, rural = `30%`
Assume `20%` high-income families of 4 buy SUVs.
Contribution:
`0.25 × 20% × (40%×40% + 60%×30%)`

**Step 4: Total SUV Stock:**
Eligible population share = `20%`
Calculation:
`150 × 20% × [family of 6 + family of 5 + family of 4]`
≈ **4.3 Cr SUVs**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Annual SUV Sales:**
Total SUV stock = `4.3 Cr`
Average SUV life = `10 years`
Annual sales:
`4.3 Cr ÷ 10`
= `0.43 Cr`
= **43 lakh SUVs/year**

**Final Estimate:**
Number of SUVs sold in India in a year is approximately **43 lakh**.

revisionCards.title: Ball Pens Sold in India in a Day
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the number of ball pens sold in India in a day.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine ball pens like daily-use items. Students and professionals buy them regularly, while colleges and companies buy them in bulk, so we estimate both individual and bulk purchases.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate ball pens sold in India in one day.
2. Main buyers are students, working professionals, colleges, and companies.
3. Both personal purchases and bulk customized pen purchases are included.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Consumer-Based Estimation**:
Instead of guessing total pen sales directly, we estimate individual purchases by students and professionals first. Then we add bulk purchases made by colleges and companies.
`Total Pens = Individual Purchases + Bulk Purchases`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Consumer Segments:**
Indian population = `150 Cr`.
Students aged `0–25 years` form around `40%` of the population.
Literacy rate in this group = `90%`.
So, active student/professional users considered = `36% × 150 = 54 Cr` people.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Individual Pen Buyers:**
Eligible users = `54 Cr`
Assume `20%` buy a ball pen daily.
Calculation:
`20% × 54`
= **10.8 Cr pens/day**

**Step 2: College Bulk Purchases:**
Out of `54 Cr` students, assume `40%` study in colleges.
Colleges and students buy customized or regular pens in bulk.
Estimated college contribution
= **0.12 Cr pens/day**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Company Bulk Purchases:**
Companies also buy customized ball pens for employees, events, and branding.
Assume company purchases are `50 times` the college bulk purchase.
Calculation:
`50 × 0.12`
= **6 Cr pens/day**

**Step 4: Final Total:**
Individual purchases = `10.8 Cr`
College purchases = `0.12 Cr`
Company purchases = `6 Cr`
Total = `10.8 + 0.12 + 6`
= **16.92 Cr pens/day**

revisionCards.title: Instagram Reels Scrolled Per Person in India
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the average number of Instagram reels scrolled in India per person in a day.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine reels like short videos watched during free time. Some users scroll a lot, some moderately, and some very little, so we estimate usage group-wise and average it.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate average Instagram reels scrolled per person in India in one day.
2. Only people with internet access can use Instagram.
3. Internet users are divided into addicted, average, and below-average Instagram users.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Usage-Based Estimation**:
Instead of guessing reels directly, we estimate daily Instagram time for different user groups. Then we divide total time by average reel duration.
`Reels = Total Instagram Time ÷ Reel Duration`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**User Segments:**
Indian population = `150 Cr`.
Internet access = `60%`.
Instagram users are divided as:
Addicted users = `50%`, using Instagram `6 hours/day`.
Average users = `30%`, using Instagram `4 hours/day`.
Below-average users = `20%`, using Instagram `3 hours/day`.
Average reel duration = `40 seconds`.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Internet Users:**
Total population = `150 Cr`
Internet access = `60%`
Internet users = `150 × 0.60`
= **90 Cr users**

**Step 2: Weighted Instagram Time:**
Addicted users: `50% × 6 hours`
Average users: `30% × 4 hours`
Below-average users: `20% × 3 hours`
Weighted time = `0.50×6 + 0.30×4 + 0.20×3`
= **4.8 hours/day**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Reels Per Internet User:**
Average Instagram time = `4.8 hours/day`
Convert to seconds:
`4.8 × 60 × 60 = 17,280 seconds`
Average reel duration = `40 seconds`
Reels per internet user:
`17,280 ÷ 40`
= **432 reels/day**

**Step 4: Average Across India:**
Only `60%` people have internet access.
Average reels per person in India:
`432 × 0.60`
= **259.2 reels/day**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Final Estimate:**
Average Instagram reels scrolled per person in India per day
≈ **260 reels/day**

revisionCards.title: Packaged Water Bottles Sold in India Per Day
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the number of packaged water bottles sold in India per day.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine water bottle sales like daily travel needs. People buy bottles while travelling by train, road, or visiting eateries, so we estimate each situation separately.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate packaged water bottles sold in India in one day.
2. Main purchase occasions are train travel, road travel, and eateries.
3. Household water usage is excluded because we focus only on packaged bottle purchases.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Occasion-Based Estimation**:
Instead of guessing total bottle sales directly, we estimate where people commonly buy packaged water. Then we calculate bottles bought during train travel, road travel, and eatery visits.
`Total Bottles = Train + Road + Eateries`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Purchase Segments:**
People buy packaged water mainly while travelling or eating outside.
For trains, we consider Tier 1 stations and daily train traffic.
For roads, we consider car-owning households travelling daily.
For eateries, we consider restaurants and cafes across Tier 1 and Tier 2 cities.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Train Travellers:**
Tier 1 cities = `8`
Stations/city = `5`
Platforms/station = `10`
Trains/platform/day = `40`
Total trains = `8×5×10×40 = 16000`
Passengers/train = `15 wagons × 40 seats = 600`
Travellers = `16000×600 = 96 lakh/day`

**Step 2: Bottles in Trains:**
10% buy `1 bottle`
30% buy `2 bottles`
60% buy `3 bottles`
Calculation:
`96 lakh × (0.10×1 + 0.30×2 + 0.60×3)`
= **240 lakh = 2.4 Cr bottles**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Road Travellers:**
10% households own cars and 5% of them travel daily.
Average household size = `4`
Calculation:
`0.10×150 Cr÷4×0.05`
= **18.75 lakh travellers**

**Step 4: Bottles on Roads:**
30% buy `2 bottles`
40% buy `3 bottles`
30% buy `4 bottles`
Calculation:
`18.75 lakh × (0.30×2 + 0.40×3 + 0.30×4)`
= **56.25 lakh bottles**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Eateries:**
Tier 1: `8 cities`, each with `5000 cafes + 2000 restaurants`, selling `50 bottles/day`
Calculation:
`8×(5000+2000)×50`
= **28 lakh bottles**
Tier 2: `200 cities`, each with `2500 cafes + 1000 restaurants`, selling `20 bottles/day`
= **1.4 Cr bottles**

**Step 6: Final Total:**
Trains = `2.4 Cr`
Roads = `56.25 lakh = 0.5625 Cr`
Eateries = `0.28 + 1.4 = 1.68 Cr`
Total = `2.4 + 0.5625 + 1.68`
≈ **4.64 Cr bottles/day**

revisionCards.title: Revenue of OTT Platforms in India in 2024
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the revenue of OTT platforms in India in 2024.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine OTT revenue like subscription fees collected from different viewer groups. Some users pay more, some less, so we estimate subscribers first and then multiply by monthly plan prices.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate revenue from video OTT platforms in India.
2. Audio streaming platforms are excluded.
3. Major players considered are Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, Disney+ Hotstar, JioCinema, Zee5, and other similar platforms.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Subscriber × Price Estimation**:
Instead of guessing revenue directly, we first estimate OTT subscribers from the internet-access population. Then we divide them by platform market share and multiply by average monthly subscription price.
`Revenue = Subscribers × Subscription Price`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Market Segments:**
Indian population = `150 Cr`.
Internet access = `60%`, so internet users = `90 Cr`.
OTT target age group is mainly `18–50 years`, taken as `60%` of internet users.
Users are divided by income and interest in OTT content.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: OTT Subscriber Base:**
Internet users = `90 Cr`
18–50 age group = `60%`
Income split: low = `50%`, middle = `30%`, high = `20%`
Subscriber assumption:
Low income = `20% × 60%`
Middle income = `50% × 50%`
High income = `30% × 50%`

**Step 2: Subscriber Calculation:**
Calculation:
`90 × 0.60 × (0.20×0.60 + 0.50×0.30 + 0.30×0.50)`
= **12.15 Cr subscribers**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Platform Market Share:**
Netflix = `20%`, avg price = `₹200/month`
Amazon Prime = `20%`, avg price = `₹300/month`
Disney+ Hotstar = `40%`, avg price = `₹50/month`
Other platforms = `20%`, avg price = `₹180/month`

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Yearly Revenue:**
Monthly revenue = `₹1895.4 Cr`
Yearly revenue:
`1895.4 × 12`
= **₹22,744.8 Cr/year**

**Final Estimate:**
Revenue of OTT platforms in India in 2024 is approximately **₹22,745 Cr/year**.

revisionCards.title: Market Size of Formal Ties in India
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the market size of formal ties in India on an annual basis.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine formal ties like office dress-code items. Not everyone needs them, so we narrow the population to employed urban professionals whose jobs require formal attire.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate the annual market size of formal ties in India.
2. Formal ties are mainly bought by corporate and office-going professionals.
3. We focus on employed urban adults whose jobs require formal dressing.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Workforce-Based Estimation**:
Instead of considering the whole population, we filter people step by step. We first take the working-age population, then employed people, then urban workers, and finally those whose jobs require formal ties.
`Market Size = Population × Working Age × Employment × Urban Share × Formal Job Share`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**User Segments:**
Total Indian population = `150 Cr`.
Working-age group `18–50 years` = `50%`.
Employment rate = `75%`.
Urban population share = `30%`.
Among urban workers, around `40%` have jobs where formal ties may be used.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Working-Age Population:**
Total population = `150 Cr`
Working-age share = `50%`
Calculation:
`150 × 0.50`
= **75 Cr people**

**Step 2: Employed Population:**
Employment rate = `75%`
Calculation:
`75 × 0.75`
= **56.25 Cr employed people**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Urban Employed Population:**
Urban share = `30%`
Calculation:
`56.25 × 0.30`
= **16.875 Cr urban employed people**

**Step 4: Formal Tie Users:**
Jobs requiring formal ties = `40%`
Calculation:
`16.875 × 0.40`
= **6.75 Cr potential tie users**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Final Estimate:**
Formula:
`150 × 50% × 75% × 30% × 40%`
= **6.75 Cr**
So, the annual market size of formal ties in India is approximately **6.75 Cr ties/users**.

revisionCards.title: Shampoo Bottles Sold in India in a Year
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the number of shampoo bottles sold in India in a year.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine shampoo bottles like daily-use household items. Families usually buy large bottles, while people living alone may buy smaller bottles, so we estimate both groups separately.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate shampoo bottles sold in India in one year.
2. Shampoo bottles of `50ml`, `100ml`, and `500ml` are considered.
3. Users are divided into families and individuals because bottle size and usage frequency differ.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Usage-Based Estimation**:
Instead of guessing total shampoo bottles directly, we divide people into family users and individual users. Families buy larger bottles, while individuals buy smaller bottles more frequently.
`Total Bottles = Family Bottles + Individual Bottles`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Consumer Segments:**
Indian population = `150 Cr`.
60% people live in families.
Average family size = `5`, so families = `(60% × 150) ÷ 5 = 18 Cr`.
Remaining 40% people are considered individual users. Families buy `500ml` bottles, while individuals buy `50ml` or `100ml` bottles.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Family Users:**
People living in families = `60% × 150 Cr`
Average family size = `5`
Number of families:
`60% × 150 ÷ 5`
= **18 Cr families**

**Step 2: Family Bottle Usage:**
A `500ml` shampoo bottle lasts around `2 months` for a family.
Bottles used per family per year = `12 ÷ 2 = 6`
Calculation:
`18 × 6`
= **108 Cr bottles/year**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Individual Users:**
Individual users = `40% × 150 Cr`
50% buy `50ml` bottles, lasting `1 month`
50% buy `100ml` bottles, lasting `2 months`

**Step 4: Individual Bottle Usage:**
50ml bottles/year = `40% × 50% × 150 × 12`
100ml bottles/year = `40% × 50% × 150 × 6`
Total:
`40% × 50% × 150 × (12 + 6)`
= **540 Cr bottles/year**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Final Total:**
Family bottles = `108 Cr`
Individual bottles = `540 Cr`
Total = `108 + 540`
= **648 Cr shampoo bottles/year**

revisionCards.title: Laptop Bags Sold in Kolkata Per Year
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the number of laptop bags sold in Kolkata per year.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine laptop bags like laptop accessories. Only people who use laptops regularly need them, so we estimate laptop users among students and employees, then adjust for bag replacement cycle.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate laptop bags sold in Kolkata in one year.
2. Kolkata population is assumed to be `50 lakh`.
3. Main buyers are STEM students and corporate employees because they are more likely to use laptops regularly.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Laptop-User Estimation**:
Instead of guessing laptop bag sales directly, we first estimate people likely to own laptops. Then we assume laptop bags are replaced along with laptops over an average life cycle.
`Annual Bag Sales = Laptop Users ÷ Average Laptop Life`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**User Segments:**
Population of Kolkata = `50 lakh`.
Age split: `0–18 years = 20%`, `18–22 years = 20%`, `22–50 years = 40%`, `50+ years = 20%`.
Among 18–22 years, STEM students = `25%`.
Among 22–50 years, corporate employees = `45%`.
Average laptop life = `5 years`.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: STEM Students:**
Population = `50 lakh`
18–22 age group = `20%`
STEM students = `25%`
Calculation:
`50 × 20% × 25%`
= **2.5 lakh laptop users**

**Step 2: Corporate Employees:**
Population = `50 lakh`
22–50 age group = `40%`
Corporate employees = `45%`
Calculation:
`50 × 40% × 45%`
= **9 lakh laptop users**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Total Laptop Users:**
STEM student laptop users = `2.5 lakh`
Corporate employee laptop users = `9 lakh`
Total laptop users = `2.5 + 9`
= **11.5 lakh users**

**Step 4: Annual Laptop Bag Sales:**
Average laptop life = `5 years`
Assume laptop bags are usually bought with laptops.
Calculation:
`11.5 ÷ 5`
= **2.3 lakh bags/year**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Final Estimate:**
Formula:
`50 lakh × (20%×25% + 40%×45%) ÷ 5`
= **2.3 lakh laptop bags/year**
So, around **2.3 lakh laptop bags** are sold in Kolkata per year.

revisionCards.title: LCD/LED TVs Sold in India Per Year
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the number of LCD/LED TVs sold per year in India.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine TVs like long-term household appliances. Most homes already own one, so yearly sales mainly depend on replacement after the TV’s average life.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate LCD/LED TVs sold in India in one year.
2. Second-hand TVs are included.
3. TVs are mainly purchased by households, so we estimate household count and replacement demand.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Household Replacement Estimation**:
Instead of guessing annual TV sales directly, we estimate how many TVs exist across income groups. Then we divide by average TV life to estimate yearly purchases.
`Annual TV Sales = Total TVs Owned ÷ Average TV Life`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Household Segments:**
Indian population = `150 Cr`.
Average family size = `4`.
Total households = `150 ÷ 4 = 37.5 Cr`.
Low income = `45%`, middle income = `40%`, high income = `15%`.
Low and middle-income homes own `1 TV`, while high-income homes own `2 TVs`.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Total Households:**
Indian population = `150 Cr`
Average family size = `4`
Calculation:
`150 ÷ 4`
= **37.5 Cr households**

**Step 2: Middle + High Income TVs:**
Middle income = `40%`, with `1 TV/home`
High income = `15%`, with `2 TVs/home`
Average TV life = `10 years`
Calculation:
`(40%×37.5×1 + 15%×37.5×2) ÷ 10`
= **2.625 Cr TVs/year**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Low-Income TVs:**
Low income = `45%`, with `1 TV/home`
These may include second-hand TVs.
Average TV life = `10 years`
Calculation:
`45% × 37.5 ÷ 10`
= **1.6875 Cr TVs/year**

**Step 4: Final Total:**
Middle + high income = `2.625 Cr`
Low income = `1.6875 Cr`
Total = `2.625 + 1.6875`
= **4.31 Cr TVs/year**

revisionCards.title: Water Coolers Sold in Delhi in a Year
revisionCards.explanation:

Estimate the number of water coolers sold in Delhi in a year.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine water coolers like summer appliances. Homes buy them for daily use, while schools and colleges buy them in bulk, so we estimate both separately.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate water coolers sold in Delhi in one year.
2. Delhi’s population is assumed to be `3 Cr`.
3. Main buyers are households, schools, and colleges because they have regular cooling needs.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Consumer-Based Estimation**:
Instead of guessing total sales directly, we estimate demand from households and institutions separately. Households buy individually, while schools and colleges buy multiple coolers over a replacement cycle.
`Total Sales = Household Sales + School Sales + College Sales`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Consumer Segments:**
Delhi population = `3 Cr`.
Average household size = `4`, so households = `0.75 Cr = 75 lakh`.
10% households buy water coolers yearly.
Literacy rate = `80%`.
Age split: `0–18 years = 30%`, `18–25 years = 20%`.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Household Demand:**
Total households = `75 lakh`
Households buying yearly = `10%`
Calculation:
`75 lakh × 10%`
= **7.5 lakh coolers/year**

**Step 2: School Demand:**
School-going population = `80% × 30% × 3 Cr`
Average students per school = `1000`
Each school buys `10 coolers once in 5 years`
Estimated demand ≈ **14,400 coolers/year**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: College Demand:**
College-going population = `80% × 20% × 3 Cr`
Average students per college = `2500`
Each college buys `30 coolers once in 5 years`
Estimated demand ≈ **1,920 coolers/year**

**Step 4: Final Total:**
Household demand = `7.5 lakh`
School demand = `14,400`
College demand = `1,920`
Total ≈ **7.7 lakh water coolers/year**

revisionCards.title: Gym Goers in India
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the number of gym goers in India.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine gym-going is like a fitness habit. Some people are highly fitness-focused, some are moderately interested, and some are not interested, so we estimate each group separately.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate the number of gym goers in India.
2. The main target group is adults aged `18–40 years`.
3. People are divided by interest in fitness because gym adoption depends mainly on fitness awareness and motivation.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Interest-Based Estimation**:
Instead of considering the entire population, we first focus on adults. Then we divide them into fitness freaks, average fitness enthusiasts, and people not interested in fitness.
`Gym Goers = Adult Population × Fitness Interest × Gym Adoption`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Adult Segments:**
Indian population = `150 Cr`.
Adults aged `18–40 years` = `40%` of population = `60 Cr`.
Fitness freaks = `45%`.
Average fitness enthusiasts = `30%`.
Ignorant/not interested people = `25%`.
Ignorant people are assumed not to go to gyms.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Adult Population:**
Total population = `150 Cr`
Adults aged 18–40 years = `40%`
Calculation:
`150 × 40%`
= **60 Cr adults**

**Step 2: Fitness Freaks:**
Fitness freaks = `45%` of adults
Gym adoption = `90%`
Calculation:
`60 × 45% × 90%`
= **24.3 Cr gym goers**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Average Fitness Enthusiasts:**
Average enthusiasts = `30%` of adults
50% go to gyms
Out of them, 70% are regular visitors
Calculation:
`60 × 30% × 50% × 70%`
= **6.3 Cr gym goers**

**Step 4: Ignorant Group:**
Ignorant group = `25%` of adults
Gym adoption = `0%`
Contribution = **0 Cr**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Final Total:**
Fitness freaks = `24.3 Cr`
Average enthusiasts = `6.3 Cr`
Ignorant group = `0 Cr`
Total = `24.3 + 6.3`
= **30.6 Cr gym goers**

revisionCards.title: LPG Gas Usage in a Household Per Month in India
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate LPG gas usage in a household per month in India.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine LPG usage like monthly grocery consumption. Bigger families cook more food and finish cylinders faster, so we estimate cylinder usage by family size.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate LPG usage in India per month.
2. Final answer is calculated in terms of LPG cylinders.
3. LPG is assumed to be mainly used for cooking, and household usage depends on family size.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Family-Size Based Estimation**:
Instead of guessing total LPG usage directly, we divide households by family size. Larger families consume cylinders faster, so we calculate yearly usage for each group and convert it into monthly usage.
`Monthly Usage = Yearly Cylinders ÷ 12`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Household Segments:**
Indian population = `150 Cr`.
Families of 4 people = `25%`.
Families of 5 people = `35%`.
Families of 6 people = `40%`.
A 4-member family uses `1 cylinder in 3 months`, a 5-member family uses `1 cylinder in 2 months`, and a 6-member family uses `1 cylinder/month`.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Households of 4:**
Population share = `25%`
People = `150 × 25% = 37.5 Cr`
Households = `37.5 ÷ 4 = 9.37 Cr`
Usage = `4 cylinders/year`
Total = `9.37 × 4`
= **37.48 Cr cylinders/year**

**Step 2: Households of 5:**
Population share = `35%`
People = `150 × 35% = 52.5 Cr`
Households = `52.5 ÷ 5 = 10.5 Cr`
Usage = `6 cylinders/year`
Total = `10.5 × 6`
= **63 Cr cylinders/year**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Households of 6:**
Population share = `40%`
People = `150 × 40% = 60 Cr`
Households = `60 ÷ 6 = 10 Cr`
Usage = `12 cylinders/year`
Total = `10 × 12`
= **120 Cr cylinders/year**

**Step 4: Total Yearly Usage:**
Family of 4 = `37.48 Cr`
Family of 5 = `63 Cr`
Family of 6 = `120 Cr`
Total = `37.48 + 63 + 120`
= **220.48 Cr cylinders/year**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Monthly Usage:**
Yearly LPG cylinder usage = `220.48 Cr`
Monthly usage:
`220.48 ÷ 12`
= **18.37 Cr cylinders/month**

**Final Estimate:**
Around **18.37 Cr LPG cylinders** are used monthly in India.

revisionCards.title: Families Visiting Restaurants Once a Week in India
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the number of families visiting restaurants once a week in India.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine restaurant visits like weekly outings. Higher-income families go more often, middle-income families sometimes, and low-income families rarely, so we estimate by family size and income.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate families in India visiting restaurants once a week.
2. Families are divided by size: 4, 5, and 6 members.
3. Restaurant visits are estimated mainly by income level because affordability strongly affects weekly dining out.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Family-Size + Income Estimation**:
Instead of guessing total restaurant-going families directly, we estimate household count by family size. Then we apply income distribution and weekly restaurant visit probability.
`Restaurant Families = Households × Income Share × Visit Share`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Household Segments:**
Indian population = `150 Cr`.
Families of 4 = `25%`, families of 5 = `35%`, families of 6 = `40%`.
Household counts: family of 4 = `9.37 Cr`, family of 5 = `10.5 Cr`, family of 6 = `10 Cr`.
Low-income families are assumed not to visit restaurants weekly.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: High-Income Families:**
Assume every high-income family visits restaurants once a week.
High-income share:
Family of 4 = `25%`
Family of 5 = `20%`
Family of 6 = `20%`
Calculation:
`25%×9.37 + 20%×10.5 + 20%×10`
= **6.44 Cr families**

**Step 2: Middle-Income Families:**
Weekly visit share:
Family of 4 = `40%`
Family of 5 = `50%`
Family of 6 = `50%`

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Middle-Income Calculation:**
Middle-income share:
Family of 4 = `35%`
Family of 5 = `30%`
Family of 6 = `35%`
Calculation:
`40%×35%×9.37 + 50%×30%×10.5 + 50%×35%×10`
= **4.63 Cr families**

**Step 4: Low-Income Families:**
Low-income families are assumed to rarely visit restaurants once every week.
Contribution = **0 Cr**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Final Total:**
High-income restaurant-going families = `6.44 Cr`
Middle-income restaurant-going families = `4.63 Cr`
Low-income families = `0 Cr`
Total = `6.44 + 4.63`
= **11.07 Cr families/week**

revisionCards.title: Water Heaters Sold Per Year
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the number of water heaters sold per year.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine water heaters like winter household appliances. Some families rarely buy them, while middle and high-income families replace or upgrade them more often.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate water heaters sold in India in one year.
2. Both immersion rods and geysers are included.
3. Sales are estimated through Indian households, divided by income level because affordability affects purchase behaviour.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Household Income Segmentation**:
Instead of guessing total sales directly, we estimate total households first. Then we divide them into low, middle, and high-income groups and apply water heater ownership and yearly purchase rates.
`Sales = Households × User Share × Annual Purchase Rate`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Household Segments:**
Indian population = `150 Cr`.
Average household size = `4`, so households = `150 ÷ 4 = 37.5 Cr`.
Low-income households = `30%`, middle-income households = `45%`, high-income households = `25%`.
Water heaters are mainly bought during rainy and winter seasons.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Low-Income Households:**
Household share = `30%`
70% use water heaters
10% of users buy annually
Calculation:
`37.5 × 30% × 70% × 10%`
= **0.79 Cr heaters/year**

**Step 2: Middle-Income Households:**
Household share = `45%`
20% households buy a water heater yearly
Calculation:
`37.5 × 45% × 20%`
= **3.38 Cr heaters/year**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: High-Income Households:**
Household share = `25%`
20% use geysers
20% of geyser users buy yearly
Calculation:
`37.5 × 25% × 20% × 20%`
= **0.38 Cr heaters/year**

**Step 4: Final Total:**
Low-income = `0.79 Cr`
Middle-income = `3.38 Cr`
High-income = `0.38 Cr`
Total = `0.79 + 3.38 + 0.38`
≈ **4.54 Cr water heaters/year**

revisionCards.title: Market Size of Cricket Bat Industry in India
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the market size of the cricket bat industry in India.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine cricket bats are like sports notebooks. Some are bought by children, some by adults, and some in bulk by schools, colleges, and clubs, so we estimate each buyer group separately.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate cricket bats bought in India.
2. Buyers are divided into children, enthusiastic adults, schools, colleges, and sports clubs.
3. Both individual purchases and institutional purchases are included.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Consumer-Based Estimation**:
Instead of guessing total bat sales directly, we estimate demand from major consumer groups. Children and adults buy personally, while schools, colleges, and clubs buy in bulk.
`Total Market Size = Individual Demand + Institutional Demand`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Consumer Segments:**
Indian population = `150 Cr`.
Children aged `0–18 years` = `20%`.
Adults aged `18–35 years` = `15%`.
Among children, `70%` are cricket enthusiasts.
Among adults, `30%` are assumed to actively play cricket and own bats.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Children:**
Children share = `20%`
Cricket enthusiast share = `70%`
Calculation:
`150 × 20% × 70%`
= **21 Cr bats**

**Step 2: Enthusiastic Adults:**
Adult share = `15%`
Active cricket players = `30%`
Calculation:
`150 × 15% × 30%`
= **6.75 Cr bats**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Schools:**
School-going population = `20% × 80% × 150 Cr`
Average school size = `1000 students`
Each school buys `5 bats`
Calculation:
`20% × 80% × 150 Cr ÷ 1000 × 5`
= **12 lakh bats**

**Step 4: Colleges:**
College-age population = `15% × 75% × 150 Cr`
Average college size = `2500 students`
Each college buys `20 bats`
Calculation:
`15% × 75% × 150 Cr ÷ 2500 × 20`
= **13.5 lakh bats**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Sports Clubs:**
Tier 1 clubs = `200 × 8`
Tier 2 clubs = `50 × 100`
Each club buys `25 bats`
Calculation:
`(200×8 + 50×100) × 25`
= **1.65 lakh bats**

**Step 6: Final Total:**
Children = `21 Cr`
Adults = `6.75 Cr`
Schools + colleges + clubs ≈ `0.27 Cr`
Total ≈ **28 Cr cricket bats**

revisionCards.title: Weddings Conducted Per Year in India
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the number of weddings conducted per year in India.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine weddings are like yearly admissions. Only people in a certain age group are likely to marry, so we estimate eligible males and females and take the smaller count.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate weddings conducted in India in one year.
2. Court marriages are included.
3. Since one wedding involves one male and one female, we estimate eligible males and females separately and take the limiting side.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Marriage-Eligible Population**:
Instead of guessing weddings directly, we estimate people in the common marriage age group. Then we remove those already married and calculate the share planning marriage this year.
`Weddings = Min(Eligible Males, Eligible Females) + Court Marriages`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Marriage Segments:**
Indian population = `150 Cr`.
Sex ratio is assumed nearly `50:50`.
Marriage age group for males = `25–30 years`.
Marriage age group for females = `23–30 years`.
Major wedding seasons are `Nov–Jan` and `Apr–Jun`.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Eligible Males:**
Males aged 25–30 = `20%` of population
Already married = `50%`
Planning marriage this year = `25%`
Calculation:
`150 × 50% × 20% × 25%`
= **3.75 Cr males**

**Step 2: Eligible Females:**
Females aged 23–30 = `20%` of population
Already married = `50%`
Planning marriage this year = `40%`
Calculation:
`150 × 50% × 20% × 40%`
= **6 Cr females**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Regular Marriages:**
Male estimate = `3.75 Cr`
Female estimate = `6 Cr`
Since one wedding needs one male and one female, take the smaller count.
Regular marriages ≈ **3.75 Cr**

**Step 4: Court Marriages Add-on:**
Court marriages are included separately.
Assume court marriages = `10%` of regular marriages
Calculation:
`3.75 × 10%`
= **0.375 Cr**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Final Total:**
Regular marriages = `3.75 Cr`
Court marriages = `0.375 Cr`
Total = `3.75 + 0.375`
= **4.125 Cr weddings/year**
≈ **4.18 Cr weddings/year**

revisionCards.title: Revenue of McDonald’s Outlets from Burger Sales
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the revenue of McDonald’s outlets from burger sales in one day.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine McDonald’s revenue is like daily shop sales. Some outlets get more orders, especially on weekends, so we estimate orders city-wise and multiply by burger price.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate revenue for one day.
2. Only burger sales are considered.
3. Only dine-in orders are included.
4. Outlets are divided into Tier 1 and Tier 2 cities because order volume differs by location.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Outlet-Based Revenue Estimation**:
Instead of guessing revenue directly, we first estimate the number of McDonald’s outlets. Then we estimate weekday and weekend burger orders and multiply average daily orders by burger price.
`Revenue = Orders × Average Burger Price`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Outlet Segments:**
Tier 1 cities = `8`, with `50 outlets` each.
Tier 2 cities = `100`, with `1 outlet` each.
Total outlets = `8×50 + 100×1 = 500`.
Weekends have higher orders than weekdays.
Average burger price = `₹150`.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Total Outlets:**
Tier 1 outlets = `8 × 50 = 400`
Tier 2 outlets = `100 × 1 = 100`
Total outlets = `400 + 100`
= **500 outlets**

**Step 2: Weekday Orders:**
Tier 1 outlet orders = `200/day`
Tier 2 outlet orders = `100/day`
Weekday orders:
`400×200 + 100×100`
= **90,000 orders/day**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Weekend Orders:**
Tier 1 outlet orders = `400/day`
Tier 2 outlet orders = `200/day`
Weekend orders:
`400×400 + 100×200`
= **1,80,000 orders/day**

**Step 4: Average Daily Orders:**
Weekdays = `5 days`, weekends = `2 days`
Average orders:
`(90,000×5 + 1,80,000×2) ÷ 7`
≈ **1.15 lakh orders/day**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Final Revenue:**
Average daily orders = `1.15 lakh`
Average burger price = `₹150`
Revenue:
`1.15 lakh × 150`
= **₹1.72 Cr/day**

**Final Estimate:**
McDonald’s outlets generate approximately **₹1.72 Cr/day** from burger sales.

revisionCards.title: Soaps Sold Per Day in India
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the number of soaps sold per day in India.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine soap usage like daily household essentials. Larger families finish soaps faster, so we estimate usage by household size and then add liquid soap demand.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate soaps sold in India per day.
2. Only bathing soaps are considered.
3. Both normal solid soaps and liquid bathing soaps are included, while washing soaps are excluded.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Household Usage Estimation**:
Instead of guessing soap sales directly, we divide the population into household sizes. Larger households finish soaps faster, so we estimate monthly soap usage for each group and convert it into daily sales.
`Daily Sales = Monthly Soap Usage ÷ 30`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Household Segments:**
Indian population = `150 Cr`.
Households of 2 = `10%`, households of 4 = `40%`, households of 5 = `30%`, households of 6 = `20%`.
Liquid soaps are assumed to be `10%` of total solid soap sales.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Household Count:**
Family of 2: `150×10%÷2 = 7.5 Cr`
Family of 4: `150×40%÷4 = 15 Cr`
Family of 5: `150×30%÷5 = 9 Cr`
Family of 6: `150×20%÷6 = 5 Cr`

**Step 2: Monthly Solid Soap Usage:**
Family of 2 uses `1 soap/month`
Family of 4 uses `2 soaps/month`
Family of 5 uses `2.5 soaps/month`
Family of 6 uses `3 soaps/month`

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Solid Soaps Per Month:**
Calculation:
`7.5×1 + 15×2 + 9×2.5 + 5×3`
= `7.5 + 30 + 22.5 + 15`
= **75 Cr soaps/month**

**Step 4: Solid Soaps Per Day:**
Monthly solid soaps = `75 Cr`
Daily solid soaps:
`75 ÷ 30`
= **2.5 Cr soaps/day**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Liquid Soap Add-on:**
Liquid soaps = `10%` of solid soap sales
Calculation:
`10% × 2.5 Cr`
= **0.25 Cr soaps/day**

**Step 6: Final Total:**
Solid soaps = `2.5 Cr/day`
Liquid soaps = `0.25 Cr/day`
Total = `2.5 + 0.25`
= **2.75 Cr soaps/day**

revisionCards.title: People in India with Passport
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the number of people in India with passport.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine passport ownership is like access to international travel. Urban, literate, and higher-income people are more likely to own passports, so we filter the population step by step.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate the number of passport holders in India.
2. Rural passport ownership is assumed negligible.
3. Urban literate population is considered the main base because passport ownership depends on literacy, income, and travel need.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Population Funnel Estimation**:
Instead of guessing passport holders directly, we filter India’s population into urban and literate users. Then we divide them by income because passport ownership rises with affordability and travel exposure.
`Passport Holders = Urban Literate Population × Income-wise Passport Share`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**Population Segments:**
Indian population = `150 Cr`.
Rural population = `60%`, urban population = `40%`.
Literacy rate = `75%`.
Urban literate population = `150 × 40% × 75% = 45 Cr`.
Passport ownership is estimated only among urban literate people.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: Urban Literate Population:**
Total population = `150 Cr`
Urban share = `40%`
Literacy rate = `75%`
Calculation:
`150 × 40% × 75%`
= **45 Cr people**

**Step 2: Low-Income Group:**
Income less than `5 LPA` = `20%`
Assume negligible passport ownership.
Contribution:
`45 × 20% × 0%`
= **0 Cr**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Middle-Income Group:**
Income `5–20 LPA` = `50%`
Passport ownership = `30%`
Calculation:
`45 × 50% × 30%`
= **6.75 Cr passport holders**

**Step 4: High-Income Group:**
Income above `20 LPA` = `30%`
Assume everyone has a passport.
Calculation:
`45 × 30% × 100%`
= **13.5 Cr passport holders**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Final Total:**
Low-income passport holders = `0 Cr`
Middle-income passport holders = `6.75 Cr`
High-income passport holders = `13.5 Cr`
Total = `0 + 6.75 + 13.5`
= **20.25 Cr passport holders**

revisionCards.title: Total Gmail Accounts in India
revisionCards.explanation:
**Problem Statement**:
Estimate the total number of Gmail accounts in India.

💡 **Simplified Analogy**:
Imagine Gmail accounts like digital notebooks. Most internet users have one, while students and employees often maintain multiple accounts for personal, academic, and work purposes.

slides.headline: 💡 The Mental Model
slides.body:
**Clarifications & Scope**:
1. We estimate total Gmail accounts in India.
2. People with internet access are assumed to have at least one Gmail account.
3. High school students, college students, and corporate employees may have multiple Gmail accounts.

slides.headline: 🧠 Core Intuition & Approach
slides.body:
**Intuition: Age-Based Account Estimation**:
Instead of guessing total Gmail accounts directly, we divide users into age groups. Some groups have multiple accounts, while the remaining population mostly maintains one account.
`Total Gmail Accounts = Age-group Accounts + Remaining User Accounts`

slides.headline: Assumptions
slides.body:
**User Segments:**
Indian population = `150 Cr`.
High school students aged `14–18` = `5%`.
College students aged `18–22` = `10%`, with `90%` literacy.
Corporate employees aged `22–40` = `40%`.
These groups are assumed to have around `90%` internet access.

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 1: High School Students:**
Population share = `5%`
Accounts per person = `2`
Calculation:
`150 × 5% × 2`
= **15 Cr accounts**

**Step 2: College Students:**
Population share = `10%`
Literacy/access rate = `90%`
Accounts per person = `3`
Calculation:
`150 × 10% × 90% × 3`
= **40.5 Cr accounts**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 3: Corporate Employees:**
Population share = `40%`
Accounts per person = `3`
Calculation:
`150 × 40% × 3`
= **180 Cr accounts**

**Step 4: Internet Access Adjustment:**
For the above groups, assume `90%` have internet access.
Calculation:
`90% × (15 + 40.5 + 180)`
= **211.95 Cr accounts**

slides.headline: 🧮Numerical Estimation
steps:
**Step 5: Remaining Population:**
