slides.body: • An interviewer might ask: *"Does LRU suffer from Belady's Anomaly?"* **No!** Because LRU is a stack algorithm. Only non-stack algorithms like FIFO suffer from it.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• More frames = more page faults.

• Occurs in FIFO.

• Stack algorithms (LRU, OPT) are immune.

revisionCards.title: Numericals
revisionCards.explanation: Given the page reference string: `[7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0]` and **3 memory frames**, find the number of page faults using **LRU** replacement.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body:
Trace the first references: 

• `7` ➔ Fault ➔ Frames: `[7]` 

• `0` ➔ Fault ➔ Frames: `[7, 0]` 

• `1` ➔ Fault ➔ Frames: `[7, 0, 1]` (3 page faults so far).

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body:
Trace next references: 

• `2` ➔ Fault. Replaces `7` (least recently used) ➔ Frames: `[2, 0, 1]`. 

• `0` ➔ Hit. Frames: `[2, 1, 0]` (update `0` to most recently used).

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body:
Trace final references: 

• `3` ➔ Fault. Replaces `1` (least recently used) ➔ Frames: `[2, 0, 3]`. 

• `0` ➔ Hit. Frames: `[2, 3, 0]` (update `0` to most recently used).

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: Total Page Faults = **5**

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: Verification tip: Keep track of page access times. When replacing for `3` at step 3, check history backwards: `0` was used at t=5, `2` at t=4, `1` at t=3. Since `1` is the oldest, it must be replaced.

revisionCards.title: File Concept
revisionCards.explanation: A **File** is an abstract logical storage unit mapped by the OS onto physical secondary storage devices.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Hides sector-level hardware complexities from applications.

• Attributes: Name, Identifier, Type, Location, Size, Protection, Timestamps.

• Operations: Create, Write, Read, Reposition (seek), Delete, Truncate.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • To the OS, a file is just a stream of raw bytes. It is the application (like a text editor or image viewer) that interprets these bytes as formatted text or pixels.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Logical abstraction of storage.

• OS maps files to physical sectors.

• Attributes tracked in directory structures.

revisionCards.title: Directory Structure
revisionCards.explanation: A **Directory** is a special file containing a list of file names, attributes, and physical addresses.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Single-Level**: All files in one directory (naming conflicts, no grouping).

• **Two-Level**: Directory per user (isolated, but no folder hierarchies).

• **Tree-Structured**: Directory contains files and subdirectories (standard in modern OS).

• **Acyclic Graph**: Allows directories to share files/folders via links (symlinks).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Directory lookups must be fast. OS use Hash Tables or B-Trees to search directories instead of linear lists, preventing file search lag.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Maps file names to metadata/addresses.

• Tree-structure is the modern standard.

• Acyclic graphs allow file sharing.

revisionCards.title: File Allocation Methods
revisionCards.explanation: File allocation defines how blocks of secondary storage are allocated to files.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Contiguous**: File blocks are stored in a continuous line on disk. Fast read/write, but suffers from external fragmentation.

• **Linked**: Blocks are scattered; each block points to the next. No fragmentation, but slow random access (must traverse link chain).

• **Indexed**: An **Index Block** stores pointers to all file blocks. Fast random access and no fragmentation. Used in Unix/Linux inodes.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • If asked: *"How does Unix implement file allocation?"* Answer: **Indexed Allocation**. It uses an **inode** containing direct block pointers and indirect pointers for large files.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Contiguous: Fast, but fragmentation issues.

• Linked: No fragmentation, but slow random access.

• Indexed: Fast, no fragmentation (used in Linux inodes).

revisionCards.title: Free Space Management
revisionCards.explanation: The OS must track all free disk blocks to allocate them efficiently when new files are created.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Bit Vector (Bitmap)**: An array of bits where `1` represents free and `0` represents allocated. Fast search, but takes memory.

• **Linked List**: Free blocks are linked together. No memory overhead, but slow search.

• **Grouping**: First free block stores addresses of next $N$ free blocks.

• **Counting**: Tracks starting address of contiguous free blocks and count of free blocks.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Bitmap is preferred for modern SSDs because it allows processors to quickly find contiguous blocks of free space using specialized CPU bitwise search instructions.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Bitmap: Fast, requires RAM storage.

• Linked List: Zero memory overhead, slow.

• Counting: Good for contiguous allocation.

revisionCards.title: File Protection
revisionCards.explanation: File protection regulates who can access files and what operations (Read, Write, Execute) they can perform.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Access Control List (ACL)**: Lists user accounts and permissions for each file. Secure, but directory size increases.

• **Unix/Linux Owner/Group/Public Model**: Compact 9-bit mask representing permissions for Owner, Group, and Others (e.g., `rwxr-xr-x`).

• Enforced by OS kernel during file open system calls.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Linux `chmod 755 file` translates to binary `111 101 101`, giving read/write/execute to owner, and read/execute to group and others.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Enforces security privileges.

• ACL vs Owner-Group-Other models.

• Controls Read (r), Write (w), and Execute (x).

revisionCards.title: FCFS
revisionCards.explanation: **First-Come, First-Served (FCFS)** disk scheduling services sector read/write requests in the exact order they arrive.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Fair; no starvation.

• Highly inefficient: disk head swings back and forth across track cylinders.

• No optimization for head movement overhead.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • FCFS is only useful when the disk request load is very light. Under heavy loads, the disk head will thrash back and forth across the platters, degrading performance.

revisionCards.title: SSTF
revisionCards.explanation: **Shortest Seek Time First (SSTF)** disk scheduling services the request closest to the current head position next.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Minimizes disk head seek time.

• Can cause **Starvation**: requests far away from the head may wait indefinitely if new, closer requests arrive.

slides.headline: Dry Run
slides.body:
• Queue: `[98, 183, 37, 122]` | Initial head = 53 

• Closest to 53 is 37 (dist: 16). Head moves to 37. 

• Closest to 37 is 98 (dist: 61). Head moves to 98. 

• Closest to 98 is 122 (dist: 24). Head moves to 122. 

• Head moves to 183. Total movement = `16 + 61 + 24 + 61 = 162 cylinders`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • SSTF is similar to Shortest Job First (SJF) scheduling: it is optimal for local execution but introduces starvation risk.

revisionCards.title: SCAN
revisionCards.explanation: The **SCAN** (or Elevator) algorithm moves the disk head in one direction servicing requests, then reverses direction on reaching the boundary.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Simulates an elevator: goes floor to floor in one direction, then reverses.

• Eliminates starvation.

• **Major Drawback**: Requests that just arrived behind the head must wait until it sweeps back.

slides.headline: Dry Run
slides.body:
• Queue: `[98, 183, 37, 122]` | Head = 53 (moving towards 0), cylinders = 0-199 

• Head path: `53 ➔ 37 ➔ 0` (boundary) ➔ `98 ➔ 122 ➔ 183`. 

• Total movement = `(53 - 0) + (183 - 0) = 236 cylinders`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Remember that SCAN **must touch the boundary** (0 or 199) even if there are no requests there, which wastes head movement cylinders.

revisionCards.title: C-SCAN
revisionCards.explanation: **Circular SCAN (C-SCAN)** moves the disk head in one direction servicing requests, then wraps around to the beginning track without servicing requests on the return.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Provides a more uniform waiting time than SCAN.

• Disk head returns to the starting boundary instantly once it reaches the end cylinder.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Why wrap without servicing? Because the tracks at the beginning have been waiting the longest. Servicing them immediately yields consistent latency.

revisionCards.title: LOOK
revisionCards.explanation: **LOOK** is an optimization of SCAN that reverses head direction when there are no more requests ahead, without visiting the boundary.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Head "looks" ahead to see if there are more requests in the current direction.

• Saves seek cylinders by avoiding empty sweeps to boundary tracks `0` or `199`.

slides.headline: Dry Run
slides.body:
• Queue: `[98, 183, 37, 122]` | Head = 53 (moving towards 0) 

• Path: `53 ➔ 37` (reverses here because 37 is the smallest request) ➔ `98 ➔ 122 ➔ 183`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • If asked: *"What is the difference between SCAN and LOOK?"* Answer: SCAN always goes to the boundary cylinder (`0` or `199`), whereas LOOK reverses immediately upon reaching the last request in that direction.

revisionCards.title: C-LOOK
revisionCards.explanation: **C-LOOK** is an optimization of C-SCAN that wraps around immediately upon reaching the last request, instead of traveling to the boundary.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body: • Head travels only as far as the last request in the current direction, then wraps around to the lowest request.

slides.headline: Dry Run
slides.body:
• Queue: `[98, 183, 37, 122]` | Head = 53 (moving towards 199) 

• Path: `53 ➔ 98 ➔ 122 ➔ 183` (reverses) ➔ `37` (lowest request). 

• Total seek: `(183 - 53) + (183 - 37) [wrap] + (37 - 37) = 130 + 146 + 0 = 276 cylinders`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • C-LOOK minimizes wasteful seek times because it skips boundary visits both on the forward sweep and the return wrap.

revisionCards.title: Numericals
revisionCards.explanation: Given the request queue: `[98, 183, 37, 122]` and **initial head position = 53**. Find the total seek time (in cylinders) using the **LOOK** algorithm (moving towards larger tracks first).

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body:
Identify tracks and sorting sequence: 

• Initial head = 53. 

• Requests: `[37, 98, 122, 183]`. 

• Direction: towards larger tracks (right).

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body:
Trace head movement to the right: 

• Head visits: `53 ➔ 98 ➔ 122 ➔ 183`. 

• Seek distance = `(183 - 53) = 130 cylinders`.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body:
Reverse direction to service the remaining left requests: 

• Head visits `37` (largest to smallest remaining). 

• Seek distance = `(183 - 37) = 146 cylinders`.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: Total head movement = `130 + 146 = 276 cylinders`

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: Quick calculation tip: For LOOK (single direction sweep with reverse), the formula is `(Max_request - Initial_head) + (Max_request - Min_request)`. Here: `(183 - 53) + (183 - 37) = 130 + 146 = 276`.

revisionCards.title: Shared Memory
revisionCards.explanation: **Shared Memory** is an IPC mechanism where a region of memory is mapped into the address spaces of multiple processes.

slides.headline: 💡 How It Works
slides.body:
• Processes read and write directly to the shared region.

• Fastest IPC mechanism (no system call overhead during data transfer).

• **Responsibility**: Processes must manually synchronize access (using Mutex/Semaphores) to prevent race conditions.

slides.headline: Code Snippet
🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Why is Shared Memory faster than Message Passing? Because it maps memory directly. Message passing requires copying data from user space to kernel buffer, then back to target user space (2 system calls per message).

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Fastest IPC mechanism.

• Direct memory mapping.

• Requires manual mutual exclusion.

revisionCards.title: Message Passing
revisionCards.explanation: **Message Passing** is an IPC mechanism where processes communicate by sending and receiving messages via a kernel mailbox.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Enforced by OS system calls: `send(message)` and `receive(message)`.

• Good for exchanging smaller data amounts and distributed systems.

• No manual synchronization needed (OS handles queuing and locking).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Can be synchronous (blocking send/receive) or asynchronous (non-blocking). If synchronous, sender blocks until message is received, ensuring strict process synchronization.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Safe communication (no shared state).

• OS manages synchronization.

• Incurs system call copy overhead.

revisionCards.title: Pipes
revisionCards.explanation: A **Pipe** is a unidirectional communication channel in Unix systems.

slides.headline: 💡 How It Works
slides.body:
• Operates as a FIFO queue with two file descriptors: `fd[0]` (read end) and `fd[1]` (write end).

• **Ordinary (Anonymous) Pipes**: Restricted to parent-child communication. Destroyed on process termination.

• **Named Pipes (FIFOs)**: Appear as files in filesystem; can be used by unrelated processes.

slides.headline: Code Snippet
🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Pipes are half-duplex (data flows in one direction). For bidirectional communication, you must instantiate **two pipes**.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Unidirectional communication channel.

• Anonymous (related processes) vs Named (unrelated).

• Uses standard file descriptors.

revisionCards.title: Message Queues
revisionCards.explanation: A **Message Queue** is a kernel-linked list of messages that allows asynchronous communication.

slides.headline: 💡 How It Works
slides.body:
• Messages are retrieved by type, not just FIFO order.

• Persistent in kernel until deleted or system reboot.

• Uses system calls: `msgget` (create/get), `msgsnd` (send), and `msgrcv` (receive).

slides.headline: Code Snippet
🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Unlike pipes which read stream bytes, message queues preserve **message boundaries**. A receiver reads a complete, structured message block.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Message boundaries preserved.

• Asynchronous, typed communication.

• Persistent in OS memory.

revisionCards.title: Signals
revisionCards.explanation: A **Signal** is a software interrupt sent by the OS kernel to notify a process of an event.

slides.headline: 💡 How It Works
slides.body:
• Process can handle signals by: Catching (custom handler), Ignoring, or Default OS action.

• Common signals: `SIGINT` (Ctrl+C), `SIGKILL` (force terminate), `SIGSEGV` (invalid memory).

• Sent using the `kill(pid, signal)` system call.

slides.headline: Code Snippet
🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Can all signals be caught? **No!** `SIGKILL` (PID kill) and `SIGSTOP` (pause) cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored. They guarantee OS process control.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Software interrupt notification.

• Custom handler overrides.

• SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be blocked.

revisionCards.title: Sockets
revisionCards.explanation: A **Socket** is a bidirectional endpoint for communication over a network or local loopback.

slides.headline: 💡 How It Works
slides.body:
• Allows communication between processes running on different machines.

• Identified by IP address and Port number.

• Uses connection-oriented TCP (`SOCK_STREAM`) or connectionless UDP (`SOCK_DGRAM`).

slides.headline: Code Snippet
🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Sockets are the foundation of all client-server architecture (HTTP, FTP, database connections).

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Network-based communication.

• Endpoint pair: IP address + Port.

• Supports TCP and UDP.

revisionCards.title: fork()
revisionCards.explanation: The `fork()` system call creates a child process by copying the parent.

slides.headline: 💡 How It Works
slides.body:
• Duplicates parent's stack, heap, files, and registers.

• Enforces Copy-on-Write (COW) optimization.

• Both processes run concurrently starting at the instruction right after `fork()`.

slides.headline: Code Snippet
🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • **Fork Returns Twice**: It returns `0` inside the child process, and returns the child's `PID` inside the parent process.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Creates child process.

• Returns 0 to child; child's PID to parent.

• Independent memory space.

revisionCards.title: exec()
revisionCards.explanation: The `exec()` family of system calls replaces the current process memory image with a new program.

slides.headline: 💡 How It Works
slides.body:
• Discards current stack, heap, and code segment.

• Loads the new executable program file into memory.

• Does not create a new process; PID remains unchanged.

slides.headline: Code Snippet
🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Why does code after `exec()` not run? Because the entire process binary image is wiped and replaced by the new executable. The original program ceases to exist.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Replaces current process image.

• No PID change.

• Code after successful exec is unreachable.

revisionCards.title: wait()
revisionCards.explanation: The `wait()` system call blocks the calling parent process until one of its child processes terminates.

slides.headline: 💡 How It Works
slides.body:
• Enables parents to retrieve child exit codes.

• Cleans up terminated child process entries, preventing zombie accumulation.

slides.headline: Code Snippet
🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • If a process has no children, `wait()` returns `-1` immediately. If a child is already a zombie, `wait()` reaps it and returns immediately without blocking.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Blocks parent until child exits.

• Reaps child processes (destroys zombies).

• Returns terminated child PID.

revisionCards.title: pipe()
revisionCards.explanation: The `pipe()` system call instantiates a unidirectional data channel in the kernel.

slides.headline: 💡 How It Works
slides.body:
• Takes an array of two integers: `fd[0]` (read endpoint) and `fd[1]` (write endpoint).

• Data written to `fd[1]` is queued in kernel buffer and read from `fd[0]`.

slides.headline: Code Snippet
🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Standard shell redirection like `ls | grep txt` works by having the shell create a pipe, fork two processes, map `ls` standard output (`stdout`) to `fd[1]`, and map `grep` standard input (`stdin`) to `fd[0]` using `dup2()`.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Creates unidirectional channel.

• fd[0] is read end | fd[1] is write end.

• Used for shell pipeline redirection.

revisionCards.title: Signals
revisionCards.explanation: Linux processes use signals to communicate asynchronous control events.

slides.headline: 💡 How It Works
slides.body:
• Sent by terminal shortcuts (Ctrl+C sends `SIGINT`), CPU traps (`SIGSEGV`), or user code (`kill`).

• Handled by custom signal handlers.

slides.headline: Code Snippet
🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Interview question: *"Can you ignore SIGKILL?"* **No**. `SIGKILL` and `SIGSTOP` bypass handler interception to ensure administrative control.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Asynchronous notifications.

• Can be ignored, caught, or defaulted.

• SIGKILL bypasses code interception.

revisionCards.title: Basic Linux Commands
revisionCards.explanation: These are the standard Linux commands for system diagnostics and process management.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• `ps`: Displays snapshot of current running processes.

• `top` / `htop`: Real-time system monitor showing CPU/RAM/process usage.

• `kill <PID>`: Sends `SIGTERM` signal to process. Use `kill -9 <PID>` to send unignorable `SIGKILL`.

• `lsof`: Lists all open files and active network ports.

• `free -m`: Displays available and used physical RAM and swap space.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Knowing these commands is essential for backend engineering and system administration interviews.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• ps: List processes.

• top: Interactive usage stats.

• kill -9: Unignorable termination.

revisionCards.title: Process vs Thread
revisionCards.explanation: This is the most common OS interview question. It checks if you understand memory isolation and execution overhead.

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: Process
slides.body:
• Private virtual address space.

• No direct sharing (isolated).

• Context switches are heavy (restores page tables, CPU state).

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: Thread
slides.body:
• Shares parent process's address space.

• Shares static variable data and open files.

• Context switches are very fast (swaps only registers and stack pointer).

slides.headline: Comparison Table
slides.body:
• **Address Space**: Private isolated virtual space ➔ Shared parent process space

• **Context Switch**: Heavy context swap (virtual map change) ➔ Fast thread swap (registers only)

• **Communication**: Heavyweight IPC required ➔ Fast shared variables and pointers

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Always summarize: *"A process is an allocating unit of resources, whereas a thread is a scheduling unit of execution."*

revisionCards.title: Mutex vs Semaphore
revisionCards.explanation: This comparison tests your understanding of mutual exclusion vs counting signals.

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: Mutex
slides.body:
• A locking mechanism.

• Binary state (Locked/Unlocked).

• Strict ownership: Lock-holder must release the lock.

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: Semaphore
slides.body:
• A signaling mechanism.

• Integer value (can track N resources).

• No ownership: Any thread can signal (increment) it.

slides.headline: Comparison Table
slides.body:
• **Mechanism**: Locking mechanism (resource locking) ➔ Signaling mechanism (resource counts)

• **Ownership**: Has a strict owner thread ➔ No ownership constraints

• **Concurrency**: Only 1 thread in critical section ➔ Up to N threads concurrently

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Use the toilet key analogy: Mutex = single key to restroom stall. Semaphore = key-rack containing N keys for N identical stalls.

revisionCards.title: Paging vs Segmentation
revisionCards.explanation: This comparison tests your knowledge of fixed division vs logical division memory designs.

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: Paging
slides.body:
• Fixed-size blocks (Pages/Frames).

• Eliminates external fragmentation.

• Invisible to programmer.

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: Segmentation
slides.body:
• Variable-sized logical segments.

• Saves blocks according to programmer's logical view.

• Enforces logical security (e.g. read-only code segments).

slides.headline: Comparison Table
slides.body:
• **Block Size**: Fixed-size divisions ➔ Variable-size logical segments

• **Fragmentation**: Internal fragmentation risk ➔ External fragmentation risk

• **Logical Scheme**: 1D linear memory addresses ➔ 2D structural segments

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Modern OS combine both into **Paged Segmentation** (logical segments subdivided into pages) to get best properties of both.

revisionCards.title: Internal vs External Fragmentation
revisionCards.explanation: This question tests if you understand why memory is wasted under different allocation designs.

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: Internal Fragmentation
slides.body:
• Occurs when allocated memory block is larger than requested.

• Wasted space resides **inside** the process's allocated memory block.

• Caused by fixed partition limits.

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: External Fragmentation
slides.body:
• Occurs when total free memory fits request, but is split into tiny non-contiguous blocks.

• Wasted space resides **between** allocated memory blocks.

• Caused by variable partition allocation.

slides.headline: Comparison Table
slides.body:
• **Wasted space location**: Inside allocated block ➔ Outside allocated blocks (between holes)

• **Resolution**: Decrease fixed frame/block size ➔ Perform compaction or use Paging

• **Allocation Cause**: Fixed-partition allocation ➔ Dynamic variable partition sizing

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Paging solves external fragmentation because it allows physical frames to be non-contiguous, meaning any page fits anywhere.

revisionCards.title: Zombie vs Orphan
revisionCards.explanation: This tests process termination hierarchy and reaping dynamics.

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: Zombie Process
slides.body:
• Child process has terminated but parent has not called `wait()`.

• Occupies PID slot in the Process Table.

• Cannot be killed because it is already dead.

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: Orphan Process
slides.body:
• Parent process has exited/crashed while child is still running.

• Adopted by `init` process (PID 1).

• Runs normally in background; reaped automatically on exit.

slides.headline: Comparison Table
slides.body:
• **Process State**: Terminated (already dead) ➔ Active execution (alive)

• **Resource leaked**: PID slot in process table ➔ Consumes active CPU/memory resources

• **Guardian / Reaping**: Parent must call `wait()` ➔ Root `init` process (PID 1) reaps it

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • A zombie process is a dead process waiting for its funeral. An orphan is an active child whose parent passed away, now adopted by the system guardian (PID 1).

revisionCards.title: Deadlock vs Starvation
revisionCards.explanation: This question tests if you understand system blocking vs scheduling bias.

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: Deadlock
slides.body:
• Two or more processes are blocked waiting for resources held by each other.

• Execution is completely frozen.

• Requires OS intervention to resolve.

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: Starvation
slides.body:
• A process is ready to run but is continuously ignored by the CPU scheduler.

• Execution could continue if CPU was allocated.

• Resolved by the **Aging** mechanism.

slides.headline: Comparison Table
slides.body:
• **Process State**: Blocked/Waiting (cannot run) ➔ Ready to Run (executable)

• **System execution**: Entire deadlock loop is frozen ➔ Other high-priority tasks executing

• **Recovery**: Process termination or rollback ➔ Aging priority scheduling

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • In Deadlock, processes are stuck in a mutual lock loop. In Starvation, the process is ready to run but is repeatedly cut in line by higher priority processes.

revisionCards.title: Virtual Memory
revisionCards.explanation: Virtual Memory abstracts physical RAM limits by utilizing disk storage.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Separates logical programmer view of memory from actual physical RAM frames.

• Allows programs to execute even if they exceed physical RAM size.

• Implemented using **Demand Paging**.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Virtual memory improves multiprogramming by letting the OS load only the active code pages of multiple applications simultaneously, swapping out inactive ones.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Bypasses physical RAM size constraints.

• Enables execution of partially loaded processes.

• Uses demand paging.

revisionCards.title: TLB
revisionCards.explanation: The Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) is a fast memory cache for page translations.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• CPU checks TLB first for virtual-to-physical address mapping.

• If hit, address is resolved instantly. If miss, page table in RAM is accessed.

• Hit rate is typically >95% due to program temporal locality.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Without TLB, virtual memory would be twice as slow because every variable load would require 2 RAM operations (Page Table access + Data access).

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Associative MMU hardware cache.

• Resolves address translations in parallel.

• Reduces memory access overhead.

revisionCards.title: Context Switching
revisionCards.explanation: Context switching swaps the execution state of processes on the CPU.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Saves current process state to its PCB, and loads next process state from its PCB.

• Pure system overhead (no user computations are performed during switch).

• Triggered by timer interrupts, system calls, or I/O waits.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • OS designers keep context switches to a minimum. Swapping page tables and flushing CPU caches degrades processor pipelines.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Multitasking mechanism.

• Pure OS overhead.

• Saves/restores process states via PCB.

revisionCards.title: Copy on Write
revisionCards.explanation: Copy on Write (COW) optimizes process creation by sharing parent physical pages.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Parent and child share read-only memory pages initially on `fork()`.

• If either writes, a page fault copies that page, mapping it to the modifying process.

• Avoids copying the parent address space when child calls `exec()` immediately.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • COW makes `fork()` call almost instantaneous because only pointers are duplicated, delaying resource allocation until writes occur.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Parent-child memory share.

• Duplicates pages only on modification.

• Optimizes fork-exec pipelines.

revisionCards.explanation: A **Computer Network** is a set of interconnected nodes (devices) that communicate with each other using shared protocols over physical links.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Enables sharing of hardware, software, files, and processing power.

• Uses standard rules (protocols) to format, transmit, and check for errors in packets.

• Physical links can be guided (cables) or unguided (wireless).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • An interviewer expects nodes to mean hosts, routers, switches, gateways, etc., rather than just PCs. Think of the network as a graph: nodes are devices, edges are communication links.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Primary purpose: resource sharing and data communication.

• Devices are called **Nodes**; links are called **Channels**.

• Protocols govern nodes behavior.

revisionCards.title: What is a Computer Network

revisionCards.explanation: Networks are categorized by their geographic span, ownership, and transmission speed.

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: LAN (Local Area Network)
slides.body:
• Spans small areas like homes, offices, or labs.

• Very high data transfer rates (Gbps/10Gbps).

• Private ownership with extremely low propagation delay.

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: WAN (Wide Area Network)
slides.body:
• Spans massive geographic regions (countries/continents).

• Relatively lower speeds and higher propagation delay.

• Owned by public companies or telecom providers (e.g., Internet).

slides.headline: Comparison Table
slides.body:
• **Scope**: Small (LAN) ➔ Medium (MAN) ➔ Continental (WAN)

• **Speed**: High (Gbps) ➔ Medium (Mbps) ➔ Variable

• **Error Rate**: Very low ➔ Moderate ➔ High

• **Examples**: Home Wi-Fi ➔ City Cable network ➔ The Internet

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Understand that the key differences are **propagation delay** and **packet loss rate**. LANs are clean and fast, WANs are noisy, slower, and route-dense.

revisionCards.title: Network Types (LAN, MAN, WAN)

revisionCards.explanation: A **Network Topology** describes the geometric arrangement or physical connection of devices in a network.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Mesh**: Every node connects directly to every other node. Fully redundant, most expensive.

• **Star**: Every node connects to a central Hub/Switch. Single point of failure (Hub), easy installation.

• **Bus**: Nodes share a single transmission line (backbone). Easy setup, cabling breakdown stops all.

• **Ring**: Nodes connect in a closed circular loop. Token passing required, unidirectional flow.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Mesh topology formulas are high-frequency: A fully connected mesh of N nodes requires `N * (N - 1) / 2` duplex links, and each node needs `N - 1` I/O ports.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Mesh has max redundancy, Star has central dependency, Bus has backbone dependency.

• Star is most common in modern LAN setups.

revisionCards.title: Network Topologies

revisionCards.explanation: Interconnecting networks requires specialized hardware operating at different layers of the OSI model.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Repeater / Hub**: Physical layer devices. Regenerate signals; Hub broadcasts to all ports.

• **Bridge / Switch**: Data Link layer devices. Switch filters and forwards frames using MAC addresses.

• **Router**: Network layer device. Forwards packets across distinct networks using IP addresses.

• **Gateway**: Application layer. Connects heterogeneous networks using different protocol families.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Remember collision vs broadcast domains. Hub: 1 collision, 1 broadcast. Switch: N collision domains (1 per port), 1 broadcast domain. Router: N collision domains, N broadcast domains.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Hub = Broadcast (Physical Layer).

• Switch = MAC based switching (Data Link Layer).

• Router = IP routing (Network Layer).

revisionCards.title: Network Devices

revisionCards.explanation: Transmission mode defines the direction of signal flow between two connected devices.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Simplex**: Unidirectional communication. One device transmits, the other only receives (e.g., Keyboard, TV).

• **Half-Duplex**: Bidirectional communication, but **not simultaneously**. Devices must take turns (e.g., Walkie-Talkie).

• **Full-Duplex**: Simultaneous bidirectional communication. Both devices can send/receive at the same time (e.g., Mobile Phone).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Half-duplex channels require arbitration (collision detection, e.g., CSMA/CD). Full-duplex channels split bandwidth into two separate paths, avoiding collisions.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Simplex: One-way street.

• Half-Duplex: Single lane bridge (one direction at a time).

• Full-Duplex: Two-way highway.

revisionCards.title: Transmission Modes

revisionCards.explanation: The **OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) Model** is a 7-layer conceptual framework developed by the ISO to standardize network communications.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Abstracts system interactions into distinct, independent layers.

• Each layer provides services to the layer above it and requests services from the layer below.

• Enables multivendor hardware compatibility.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • OSI is a **logical model**, not a physical implementation. Memorize layers from bottom to top: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application (Mnemonic: **P**lease **D**o **N**ot **T**hrow **S**ausage **P**izza **A**way).

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• 7-layer conceptual framework.

• Each layer has unique headers and trailer (Data Link).

• Standardized communication interfaces.

revisionCards.title: Introduction to OSI

revisionCards.explanation: The **Physical Layer (Layer 1)** deals with the physical connection of devices and raw bit stream transmission over physical media.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Defines connectors, pins, voltage levels, cabling types, and line coding.

• Handles bit synchronization (sender/receiver clocks alignment).

• Defines physical transmission rates (bps) and topologies.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • This layer deals with bits (`1`s and `0`s) as electrical/optical/radio signals. It has no concept of packets, frames, or destinations.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Unit: **Bits**.

• Responsibilities: Pin configurations, signaling, encoding, bit rate control.

• Devices: Cables, Repeaters, Hubs, Modems.

revisionCards.title: Physical Layer

revisionCards.explanation: The **Data Link Layer (Layer 2)** provides reliable hop-to-hop node communication over a physical link.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Framing**: Packages bits from physical layer into logical units called frames.

• **Physical Addressing**: Adds MAC addresses of sender and receiver to the frame header.

• **Flow Control**: Prevents fast senders from overwhelming slow receivers.

• **Error Control**: Appends checksum/CRC trailer to detect corrupted bits.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Data Link Layer handles **local delivery** on the same subnet. Routers strip Layer 2 headers/trailers and rewrite them at each hop, while IP remains unchanged.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Unit: **Frames**.

• Responsibilities: Framing, Error/Flow control, MAC addressing.

• Sublayers: LLC (Logical Link Control) and MAC (Media Access Control).

revisionCards.title: Data Link Layer

revisionCards.explanation: The **Network Layer (Layer 3)** manages host-to-host packet delivery across distinct, heterogeneous networks.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Routing**: Determines the optimal path from source to destination across multiple networks.

• **Logical Addressing**: Uses IP addresses to identify devices globally.

• **Fragmentation**: Splits packets if they exceed the link's Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • While Layer 2 manages hop-to-hop link delivery, Layer 3 handles **end-to-end logical delivery**. Routers use IP headers to make path decisions.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Unit: **Packets**.

• Responsibilities: Logical addressing (IP), Routing, Fragmentation/Reassembly.

• Protocols: IPv4, IPv6, ICMP, ARP.

revisionCards.title: Network Layer

revisionCards.explanation: The **Transport Layer (Layer 4)** provides process-to-process reliable, end-to-end data delivery.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Port Addressing**: Directs packet stream to specific applications using port numbers.

• **Segmentation & Reassembly**: Splits message into segments at source and reconstructs them at destination.

• **Connection Control**: Manages setup and teardown (connection-oriented vs connectionless).

• **Flow & Congestion Control**: Matches transfer speed and throttles sender during network congestion.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • The Transport Layer is responsible for **process-to-process delivery** (using Port numbers, e.g., HTTP = 80). Layer 3 only gets it to the destination machine, Layer 4 gets it to the correct running program.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Unit: **Segments** (TCP) / **Datagrams** (UDP).

• Responsibilities: Process addressing, Reliability, Flow/Congestion control.

• Key Protocols: TCP and UDP.

revisionCards.title: Transport Layer

revisionCards.explanation: The **Session Layer (Layer 5)** establishes, manages, synchronizes, and terminates dialogs between network applications.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Dialog Control**: Determines full-duplex or half-duplex turn-taking dialog.

• **Synchronization**: Injects checkpoints into streams so transfers can resume from the last point after a crash.

• **Session Restoration**: Re-establishes broken transport connections seamlessly.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Think of downloading a 2GB file. If connection drops at 1.5GB, the Session layer uses checkpoints to resume downloading rather than restarting from zero.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Responsibilities: Dialog control, Synchronization checkpoints.

• Rarely implemented as a distinct protocol in TCP/IP (merged into Application).

revisionCards.title: Session Layer

revisionCards.explanation: The **Presentation Layer (Layer 6)** manages syntax and semantics of the transmitted information.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Translation**: Converts data from application formats to common network formats (e.g., ASCII/EBCDIC).

• **Encryption/Decryption**: Encrypts data for security before transmission.

• **Compression**: Reduces data size for bandwidth efficiency.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • This is the "translator" layer. It formats data (JSON, XML, Encryption like SSL/TLS) so the Application layer can read it.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Responsibilities: Translation, Encryption/Decryption, Compression.

• Acts as the data format translator.

revisionCards.title: Presentation Layer

revisionCards.explanation: The **Application Layer (Layer 7)** provides direct network services to user applications and software interfaces.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Acts as the window through which software interacts with the network.

• Provides services like file transfer, email client support, database access, and remote terminal connections.

• Common interfaces: Browsers, Email Clients.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Note: This layer is **not** the web browser itself, but the protocol (like HTTP) that the browser calls to perform web transfers.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Responsibilities: User interface, file/mail transfer support.

• Key Protocols: HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, DNS, SMTP.

revisionCards.title: Application Layer

revisionCards.explanation: The **TCP/IP Model** (Internet Protocol Suite) is a 4-layer functional framework used to run the modern Internet.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Link Layer**: Handles physical transmission and network interfaces (combines OSI Layers 1 and 2).

• **Internet Layer**: Handles logical addressing and global packet routing (OSI Layer 3).

• **Transport Layer**: Manages host-to-host process communication (OSI Layer 4).

• **Application Layer**: Exposes communication interfaces to applications (combines OSI Layers 5, 6, 7).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • TCP/IP is a practical, protocol-driven architecture. Unlike OSI, it was created after its protocols (TCP, IP, UDP) were already running successfully.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• 4-layer architecture.

• The foundation of the modern Internet.

• Simpler and more direct than OSI.

revisionCards.title: TCP/IP Architecture

revisionCards.explanation: While OSI is an academic reference model, TCP/IP is the actual operational model of the Internet.

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: OSI Model
slides.body:
• 7 logical layers (strict boundaries).

• Independent of specific protocols.

• Distinguishes strictly between services, interfaces, and protocols.

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: TCP/IP Model
slides.body:
• 4 layers (more relaxed and practical).

• Protocol-dependent (centered around IP and TCP).

• Combines physical/link layers and application/presentation/session layers.

slides.headline: Comparison Table
slides.body:
• **Layer Count**: 7 layers ➔ 4 layers

• **Approach**: Theoretical/Academic ➔ Practical/Implementation

• **Data Delivery**: Connectionless & Connection-oriented (Network Layer) ➔ Connectionless only (Network/Internet Layer)

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • In interviews, state that OSI is excellent for theoretical learning and diagnostics, whereas TCP/IP is the actual standard that devices execute.

revisionCards.title: OSI vs TCP/IP

revisionCards.explanation: Data flows down the sender stack (Encapsulation) and up the receiver stack (Decapsulation), changing unit wrappers at each layer.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Encapsulation**: At each layer, header information is prepended to the data payload from above. The Data Link Layer also appends a trailer (FCS).

• **Decapsulation**: The receiver reads, processes, and strips off the layer header as the payload moves up the stack.

• Each layer only interacts with its peer layer on the remote host.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Think of sending a letter: you write it (Application Data), put it in an envelope (Transport Segment), write the address (Network Packet), and load it into a shipping box (Data Link Frame).

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Encapsulation = Adding headers downwards.

• Decapsulation = Stripping headers upwards.

• Maintains logical peer-to-peer layer conversations.

revisionCards.title: Encapsulation & Decapsulation

revisionCards.explanation: Transmission media carries the raw bit signals across physical channels between sender and receiver.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Twisted Pair**: Copper wires twisted together to reduce electromagnetic interference (crosstalk). Common in Ethernet.

• **Coaxial Cable**: Solid copper core wrapped in shielding. High bandwidth, common in TV cable.

• **Fiber Optic**: Glass/plastic cores conducting light pulses. Maximum bandwidth, lowest attenuation, immune to noise.

• **Wireless**: Unguided media using electromagnetic waves (Radio, Microwave, Infrared) to transmit signals.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Fiber optics utilize **Total Internal Reflection** to guide light beams over thousands of miles with negligible loss. It is the backbone of global subsea cables.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Guided: Twisted pair, Coaxial, Fiber.

• Unguided: Radio waves, Microwaves, Infrared.

• Fiber optic offers the highest throughput and distance.

revisionCards.title: Transmission Media

revisionCards.explanation: Switching is the process of forwarding signals through intermediate nodes from source to destination.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Circuit Switching**: Establishes a dedicated physical path between nodes. Bandwidth is reserved and guaranteed.

• **Packet Switching**: Divides data into packets routed independently. Resources are shared dynamically (statistical multiplexing).

• **Message Switching**: Sends the entire message block, storing and forwarding it at each intermediate node. (Largely deprecated).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Compare a phone call (Circuit: dedicated line, busy tone if occupied) vs web browsing (Packet: shared link, packets from different users interleave).

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Circuit Switching = Dedicated path, reserved resource.

• Packet Switching = Shared path, dynamic routing, store-and-forward delay.

revisionCards.title: Switching Techniques

revisionCards.explanation: Circuit and packet switching manage network bandwidth and routing under fundamentally different constraints.

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: Circuit Switching
slides.body:
• Connection setup phase required before transmission.

• Zero queueing delay; dedicated path bandwidth.

• Inefficient for bursty traffic (idle links waste resources).

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: Packet Switching
slides.body:
• No prior connection path reservation (connectionless routing).

• Packets experience queueing, serialization, and propagation delays.

• Highly efficient; handles bursty data traffic cleanly.

slides.headline: Comparison Table
slides.body:
• **Bandwidth Reservation**: Yes ➔ No (Dynamic)

• **Setup Phase**: Required ➔ None

• **Congestion**: Cannot occur once connection is set ➔ Occurs in queues (packet drop)

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Circuit switching is optimized for real-time constant voice/video feeds. Packet switching is optimized for dynamic, bursty, data-heavy web traffic.

revisionCards.title: Circuit vs Packet Switching

revisionCards.explanation: Framing is the process of encapsulating packet data into distinct frames with markers so the receiver can detect boundaries.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Character Count**: Header field specifies frame length. Risk: if count gets corrupted, all subsequent frames desynchronize.

• **Byte Stuffing**: Uses flag bytes (e.g., `ESC`) to wrap frame data. Escape bytes are stuffed before flags inside data.

• **Bit Stuffing**: Inserts a `0` bit after five consecutive `1`s in data to prevent it from matching the flag bit pattern (`01111110`).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • In bit stuffing: Sender checks data stream. If it sees `11111`, it inserts a `0` immediately. Receiver sees `11111`, checks the next bit: if `0`, it strips it; if `1` and next is `0`, it is a Flag.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Prevents receivers from misinterpreting raw bits.

• Bit stuffing is bit-level boundary demarcation.

• Byte stuffing is byte-level boundary demarcation.

revisionCards.title: Framing

revisionCards.explanation: Error detection techniques add redundant bits to frames so the receiver can verify if data was modified during transit.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Simple Parity**: Appends a single bit to make total `1`s count even or odd. Cannot detect even-numbered bit errors.

• **Checksum**: Sender splits frame into 16-bit integers, sums them using 1s complement arithmetic, and appends complement. Receiver verifies sum is all `1`s.

• **Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC)**: Uses binary polynomial division. Highly robust, implemented in hardware.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Note: Error **detection** simply drops corrupted frames. Error **correction** (e.g., Hamming Code) corrects minor bit flips but has higher bit overhead.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Parity: Simple, low overhead, weak.

• Checksum: Software friendly (used in IP/TCP headers).

• CRC: Hardware friendly, mathematically robust.

revisionCards.title: Error Detection Techniques

revisionCards.explanation: Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) uses binary division modulo 2 to calculate a remainder appended to the frame.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Identify the divisor polynomial of degree G. Append G zero bits to the sender data frame.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: Perform modulo 2 division (XOR operations instead of subtraction) of the modified frame by the divisor.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body: Extract the remainder of size G bits, replace the appended zeroes at the end of the frame with this remainder.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: Sender transmits: Frame + Remainder. Receiver divides the incoming frame by the same divisor. If remainder is 0, no errors occurred; else, packet is dropped.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: Modulo 2 XOR rule: `0 XOR 0 = 0`, `1 XOR 1 = 0`, `0 XOR 1 = 1`, `1 XOR 0 = 1`. Do not carry over arithmetic borrows.

revisionCards.title: CRC

revisionCards.explanation: A **MAC (Media Access Control) Address** is a 48-bit physical identifier burned into the Network Interface Card (NIC).

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Unique address for hop-to-hop communication on local subnets.

• Written in hexadecimal notation (e.g., `00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E`).

• **OUI (Organizationally Unique Identifier)**: First 24 bits identify vendor. Remaining 24 bits are device specific.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • IP address changes when you connect to different Wi-Fi routers. MAC address is physical and never changes; it is the unique hardware fingerprint of the network interface.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• 48-bit physical address (Layer 2).

• OUI (Vendor code) + NIC Specific ID.

• Flat address space, not hierarchical.

revisionCards.title: MAC Address

revisionCards.explanation: **Ethernet** (IEEE 802.3) is the dominant physical cabling and frame protocol standard for wired LANs.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Uses **CSMA/CD** (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection) to manage access on shared media.

• Ethernet frame contains: Preamble, SFD (Start Frame Delimiter), Destination MAC, Source MAC, EtherType, Data Payload, and FCS (CRC-32 trailer).

• Minimum Ethernet frame size is **64 bytes** (to ensure collision detection works before transmission ends).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Formula for min frame size: `Frame Size >= 2 * Propagation Time * Bandwidth`. If the frame is too short, the sender finishes sending before the collision signal reaches it.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• IEEE 802.3 standard.

• Min frame size: 64 bytes (CSMA/CD constraint).

• FCS trailer contains CRC-32 checksum.

revisionCards.title: Ethernet

revisionCards.explanation: An **IP Address** is a logical identifier used to address and route packets globally across the network layer.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **IPv4**: 32-bit address, dotted-decimal notation (e.g., `192.168.1.1`). Total space: ~4.3 billion IPs.

• **IPv6**: 128-bit address, hexadecimal colon notation (e.g., `2001:db8::ff00:42:8329`). Practically infinite space.

• Hierarchical routing: divided into Network ID (routing) and Host ID (local interface).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Network prefix routing is how routers scale. Routers only route packets based on the network prefix, not individual host addresses, keeping routing tables small.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Logical address (Layer 3).

• IPv4 = 32-bits (4 bytes).

• IPv6 = 128-bits (16 bytes).

revisionCards.title: IP Addressing

revisionCards.explanation: The **IPv4 Header** contains essential fields for logical addressing, path routing, and packet assembly.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **TTL (Time to Live)**: 8-bit hop counter decremented by 1 at each router. Prevents packet loops (dropped if TTL reaches 0).

• **Protocol**: Specifies the Transport Layer protocol (TCP = 6, UDP = 17) to hand the payload to.

• **Flags & Fragment Offset**: Used to fragment and reconstruct packets when crossing interfaces with smaller MTUs.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Interviewers love TTL questions. If a packet gets stuck in a loop, it will rotate forever unless TTL kills it. ICMP TTL Expired is sent back, which is how Traceroute works.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Standard header size: 20 to 60 bytes (Options field).

• TTL prevents infinite routing loops.

• Fragment offset allows reassembly at target host.

revisionCards.title: IPv4

revisionCards.explanation: **IPv6** replaces IPv4 to solve address exhaustion and streamline routing operations.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Massive 128-bit space eliminates the absolute dependency on NAT.

• Simplified fixed-size 40-byte base header (faster hardware processing).

• No header checksum (errors handled at Layers 2 and 4 to boost speed).

• No router fragmentation: source host path-discovery is mandatory.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • By making the base header size fixed (40 bytes), router hardware can process packet fields in parallel pipelines rather than calculating variable offsets.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• 128-bit address space.

• Fixed base header size of 40 bytes.

• Eliminates mid-network fragmentation.

revisionCards.title: IPv6

revisionCards.explanation: Subnetting divides a large network block into smaller, isolated logical subnets to optimize security and broadcast traffic.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Determine the number of subnets needed. Convert this value to bits `2^S >= Subnets`. Borrow S bits from Host ID.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: Write the new Subnet Mask by shifting the boundary to the right. Class C mask `/24` with 2 borrowed bits becomes `/26`.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body: Calculate block size: `2^(Host bits remaining)`. For `/26`, host bits = 32 - 26 = 6. Block size = `2^6 = 64` IPs.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: Subnets start at intervals of 64: Network 1: `.0` to `.63`, Network 2: `.64` to `.127`. Total usable hosts per subnet = `Block Size - 2` (network address and broadcast address reserved).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: Usable hosts formula: `2^H - 2`. Subtract the first IP (network ID) and last IP (directed broadcast IP).

revisionCards.title: Subnetting

revisionCards.explanation: **CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing)** replaces old classful addressing with variable-length subnet masks (VLSM).

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Denoted as `IP/Prefix` (e.g., `192.0.2.0/24`).

• Prefix indicates the number of static bits representing the Network ID.

• Allows precise, custom-sized IP allocations, minimizing wasted address space.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Classful allocation was wasteful: Class A gave 16M hosts, Class B gave 65k, Class C gave 254. If you needed 1000 hosts, you had to take Class B, wasting 64,000 addresses. CIDR allows `/22` (1024 IPs).

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Eliminates Class A/B/C static boundaries.

• Uses slash notation (`/x`) for mask prefix.

• Enables route aggregation (supernetting).

revisionCards.title: CIDR

revisionCards.explanation: **ARP (Address Resolution Protocol)** dynamically maps a logical IP address to a physical MAC address on a local network.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **ARP Request**: Broadcast frame (`FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF`) asking "Who has IP X? Tell MAC Y".

• **ARP Reply**: Unicast frame from the owner containing its MAC address.

• **ARP Cache**: In-memory table on devices to store IP-to-MAC mappings, avoiding broadcast overload.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • IP routing gets the packet to the correct local network interface. But to physically cross the Ethernet cable to the next card, it MUST be wrapped in a frame with the next card's MAC address. ARP finds that MAC.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Bridges Layer 3 (IP) to Layer 2 (MAC).

• ARP Request is Broadcast; ARP Reply is Unicast.

• Operates within the local broadcast domain only.

revisionCards.title: ARP

revisionCards.explanation: **NAT (Network Address Translation)** allows multiple devices on a private network to share a single public IP address.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Translates private IP/ports to public IP/ports at the network gateway.

• Saves public IPv4 addresses and acts as a security firewall.

• **PAT (Port Address Translation / Overloading)**: Maps multiple private IPs to one public IP using unique source port numbers.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • When your home phone requests a page, NAT router translates private `192.168.1.5:5000` to public `203.0.113.1:9000` and records this mapping in its translation table to route the return packets.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Translates private IP ranges (`10.x`, `172.16.x`, `192.168.x`) to Public IPs.

• Conserves IPv4 addresses.

• Relies on NAT Translation Tables.

revisionCards.title: NAT

revisionCards.explanation: **TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)** is a connection-oriented, reliable Transport Layer protocol.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Reliable Delivery**: Re-transmits lost packets and ensures in-order delivery using sequence numbers and ACKs.

• **Connection-Oriented**: Requires setup handshake before data exchange.

• **Byte-Stream**: Views data as an unstructured stream of bytes, not message blocks.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • TCP guarantees that whatever the application sends is exactly what the receiver gets, in the correct order, without duplicates. It manages this reliability over noisy, unpredictable IP routes.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Connection-oriented (handshake).

• Guarantees order and arrival.

• Flow and Congestion control mechanisms.

revisionCards.title: TCP

revisionCards.explanation: **UDP (User Datagram Protocol)** is a connectionless, lightweight, and fast Transport Layer protocol.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Connectionless**: Sends datagrams immediately without setup handshake.

• **Unreliable Delivery**: No guarantees of packet arrival, ordering, or duplicate checks.

• **Message-Oriented**: Keeps application boundary records intact for each write.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • UDP has zero connection overhead or wait state. If a packet is lost, it is ignored. This is perfect for real-time multiplayer gaming, live streams, DNS, and VOIP where speed is preferred over reliability.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Unreliable and Connectionless.

• No flow/congestion control, minimal overhead.

• Preferred for real-time streaming and quick query applications.

revisionCards.title: UDP

revisionCards.explanation: The **TCP Header** contains control flags and window configurations to manage connection reliability and speed.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Sequence & ACK Numbers**: 32-bit tracking fields for byte byte-stream ordering.

• **Flags**: control indicators (`SYN`, `ACK`, `FIN`, `RST`, `PSH`, `URG`).

• **Window Size**: 16-bit field advertising the receiver's buffer size (used for Flow Control).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • If the Window Size is advertised as 0, the sender must stop sending data immediately. This stops the receiver buffer from overflowing (Flow Control).

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Minimum size: 20 bytes.

• Control Flags manage session state.

• Window Size field controls the flow speed.

revisionCards.title: TCP Header

revisionCards.explanation: The **UDP Header** is minimal and designed for low-overhead packet processing.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Source & Destination Ports**: 16-bit fields routing packets to correct processes.

• **Length**: 16-bit field indicating size of header + payload data.

• **Checksum**: 16-bit validation field (optional on IPv4, mandatory on IPv6).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • UDP header is exactly **8 bytes** fixed. This makes UDP processing extremely fast and highly suitable for simple query-response protocols.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Fixed size: exactly 8 bytes.

• Only 4 fields: Ports, Length, Checksum.

• Minimal processing overhead.

revisionCards.title: UDP Header

revisionCards.explanation: Flow control is a speed-matching mechanism in TCP to prevent a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Implemented using a **Sliding Window Protocol**.

• Receiver advertises its available buffer space (`rwnd`) in every ACK.

• Sender must ensure that the total unacknowledged bytes in transit never exceed the advertised `rwnd`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Flow Control is **end-to-end** (Sender vs Receiver). This is different from Congestion Control, which handles traffic limits inside the network routing path.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• End-to-end mechanism.

• Driven by receiver's advertised Window Size (`rwnd`).

• Prevents receiver buffer overflows.

revisionCards.title: Flow Control

revisionCards.explanation: Congestion control throttles the sender to prevent overloading the network routers and links.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• **Slow Start**: Sender starts with small window (`cwnd` = 1 MSS) and doubles it every RTT (exponential growth).

• **Congestion Avoidance**: Increases `cwnd` linearly (+1 MSS per RTT) once it reaches threshold (`ssthresh`).

• **Fast Retransmit & Recovery**: Triggers retransmission immediately upon receiving 3 duplicate ACKs without waiting for timeout.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • If a packet drops, TCP assumes the network is congested. It halves `ssthresh` and drops the `cwnd` down to 1 MSS (or halves it in Fast Recovery) to allow the network routers to recover.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Network-level mechanism (Sender vs Network capacity).

• driven by Congestion Window (`cwnd`).

• Uses AIMD (Additive Increase Multiplicative Decrease) strategy.

revisionCards.title: Congestion Control

revisionCards.explanation: **HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol)** is a stateless application layer protocol used for transferring web resources.

slides.headline: 💡 How It Works
slides.body:
• Runs on top of TCP (Port 80).

• Client-Server model: Client sends requests (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), Server replies with resources.

• Stateless: Each request/response pair is isolated. States are maintained using Cookies or Sessions.

slides.headline: Packet / Request Flow
slides.body: • Client opens TCP connection ➔ Sends request headers ➔ Server processes ➔ Returns status code (e.g., 200 OK, 404 Not Found) + HTML payload ➔ Closes/reuses connection.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • HTTP/1.1 introduced persistent connections (keep-alive) to reuse the same TCP connection. HTTP/2 added multiplexing over a single connection, and HTTP/3 moved from TCP to UDP (QUIC) to eliminate head-of-line blocking.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Port 80, TCP base.

• Stateless by design.

• HTTP/3 uses UDP (QUIC).

revisionCards.title: HTTP

revisionCards.explanation: **HTTPS** is HTTP encapsulated within an encrypted SSL/TLS session to provide security and integrity.

slides.headline: 💡 How It Works
slides.body:
• Runs on top of TCP (Port 443).

• Uses SSL/TLS to provide: **Encryption** (confidentiality), **Authentication** (identity validation), and **Data Integrity** (prevents tampering).

slides.headline: Packet / Request Flow
slides.body: • TCP 3-way handshake ➔ SSL/TLS handshake (Certificates verified, Session keys generated) ➔ Encrypted HTTP data starts flowing.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • HTTPS encrypts the entire HTTP header, path, and data payload. Only the destination IP address and port remain visible to intermediate routers.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Port 443, Secure socket base.

• Uses symmetric encryption for data, asymmetric for key exchange.

• Protects against Man-in-the-Middle attacks.

revisionCards.title: HTTPS

revisionCards.explanation: **DNS (Domain Name System)** translates human-readable domain names to machine-readable IP addresses.

slides.headline: 💡 How It Works
slides.body:
• Acts as the phonebook of the Internet. Typically uses UDP (Port 53) for speed.

• Hierarchical database: Root servers (`.`), TLD servers (`.com`), and Authoritative servers.

slides.headline: Packet / Request Flow
slides.body: • Client requests IP for domain ➔ Local Resolver checks cache ➔ Queries Root (directs to TLD) ➔ Queries TLD (directs to Authoritative) ➔ Queries Authoritative (gets IP) ➔ Returns to client.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Why does DNS use UDP? Speed. Setting up a TCP connection for a single name translation would double web page load times. DNS only falls back to TCP for large zone transfers (exceeding 512 bytes).

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Port 53, primarily UDP.

• Hierarchical lookup flow.

• Resolver queries Root ➔ TLD ➔ Authoritative.

revisionCards.title: DNS

revisionCards.explanation: **DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol)** dynamically assigns IP addresses and network parameters to devices joining a network.

slides.headline: 💡 How It Works
slides.body:
• Uses UDP (Port 67 for server, Port 68 for client).

• Avoids manual IP conflicts and automates network boot parameters.

slides.headline: Packet / Request Flow
slides.body:
• **Discover**: Client broadcasts query.

• **Offer**: Server offers an IP.

• **Request**: Client requests to lease that IP.

• **ACK**: Server commits the IP lease.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Remember the **DORA** sequence in interviews: Discover (Broadcast) ➔ Offer (Unicast/Broadcast) ➔ Request (Broadcast) ➔ ACK (Unicast/Broadcast).

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Automates IP configuration.

• DORA lease handshake.

• Uses UDP ports 67 & 68.

revisionCards.title: DHCP

revisionCards.explanation: **Distance Vector Routing** calculates the shortest path based on direction (vector) and distance to target nodes.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Uses the **Bellman-Ford algorithm**.

• Each router maintains a table containing the distance to all nodes and the next-hop router.

• Routers periodically share their entire routing table with **immediate neighbors** only.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Has a famous vulnerability: the **Count-to-Infinity problem** during link failures. Resolved using **Split Horizon** (do not advertise routes back to the neighbor they were learned from) and **Route Poisoning**.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Based on Bellman-Ford algorithm.

• Shares complete tables to neighbors only.

• Vulnerable to routing loops (count-to-infinity).

revisionCards.title: Distance Vector Routing

revisionCards.explanation: **Link State Routing** allows each router to build a complete topological map of the entire network to calculate routes.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Uses **Dijkstra's algorithm**.

• Routers flood LSP (Link State Packets) containing link states to **all routers** in the network.

• Each node runs Dijkstra independently to find the shortest path tree.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Unlike Distance Vector, Link State routers don't rely on neighbors' routing summaries. They get the raw topology map and calculate routes themselves, which avoids routing loops.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Based on Dijkstra's algorithm.

• Floods link states globally.

• Converges faster than Distance Vector.

revisionCards.title: Link State Routing

revisionCards.explanation: RIP, OSPF, and BGP are routing protocols optimized for different network scales and routing constraints.

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: OSPF (Interior Gateway)
slides.body:
• Link State protocol used inside Autonomous Systems.

• Uses Dijkstra algorithm for fast routing convergence.

• Scale: High capacity, uses metric cost based on link bandwidth.

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: BGP (Exterior Gateway)
slides.body:
• Path-Vector protocol routing between Autonomous Systems.

• Routes packets based on policy and path rules (hop count is ignored).

• The operational routing protocol of the global Internet.

slides.headline: Comparison Table
slides.body:
• **Type**: Distance Vector (RIP) ➔ Link State (OSPF) ➔ Path Vector (BGP)

• **Metric**: Hop count (Max 15) ➔ Cost (Bandwidth) ➔ Path attributes

• **Scope**: Small enterprise ➔ Large enterprise ➔ Global Internet

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Understand that RIP uses simple hop counts (16 is infinity, meaning unreachable). OSPF is for routing inside your company network, and BGP handles routing across different ISPs.

revisionCards.title: RIP, OSPF, BGP Basics

revisionCards.explanation: Stop and Wait ARQ is the simplest flow control protocol: the sender transmits a packet and waits for an ACK before sending the next.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Identify transmission time: `Tx = Packet Size / Bandwidth`. Identify propagation time: `Tp = Distance / Speed`.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: Calculate total cycle time to send a packet and receive its ACK: `Total Time = Tx + 2 * Tp`. (Neglect ACK Tx time).

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body: Calculate link efficiency `η`: the ratio of useful transmission time to total cycle time: `η = Tx / (Tx + 2 * Tp)`.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: Efficiency: `η = 1 / (1 + 2 * a)` where `a = Tp / Tx`.Usable link utilization is extremely low if propagation time `Tp` is high (e.g., satellite links).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: If `Tp >> Tx` (long distance, high speed), efficiency drops to near zero. Sliding window protocols are required to keep the link busy.

revisionCards.title: Stop and Wait

revisionCards.explanation: Go-Back-N (GBN) is a sliding window protocol that allows the sender to transmit multiple packets before receiving an ACK.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Identify sender window size `Ws` and receiver window size `Wr`. In GBN, `Ws = 2^k - 1` (where k is sequence bits) and `Wr = 1`.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: If a packet is lost or corrupted, the receiver discards it and all subsequent packets (out-of-order packets are not buffered).

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body: The sender window slides only upon receiving cumulative ACKs. If a packet timeout occurs, the sender retransmits the entire window.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: Efficiency: `η = Ws / (1 + 2 * a)`. GBN is highly efficient when errors are rare, but retransmitting the entire window wastes bandwidth on noisy links.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: Remember: GBN uses cumulative ACKs. If packet 0, 1, 2 are sent, and ACK 2 is received, it means all packets up to 2 were received.

revisionCards.title: Go Back N

revisionCards.explanation: Selective Repeat ARQ improves GBN by buffering out-of-order packets and retransmitting only the lost packet.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Identify window sizes: in Selective Repeat, sender and receiver windows are equal: `Ws = Wr = 2^(k-1)`.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: The receiver maintains a buffer for out-of-order packets and sends negative ACKs (NAK) for missing frames.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body: Upon receiving a NAK, the sender retransmits only the specified lost frame without sliding the window.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: Efficiency: `η = Ws / (1 + 2 * a)`. Minimizes bandwidth wastage on noisy links at the cost of buffer memory at the receiver.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: Constraint: To avoid window overlap issues, the sum of sender and receiver windows must be less than or equal to the sequence number space: `Ws + Wr <= 2^k`.

revisionCards.title: Selective Repeat

revisionCards.explanation: The **SSL/TLS Handshake** establishes an encrypted session keys exchange before HTTPS application transmission starts.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Client sends `ClientHello` advertising cipher suites and a random number.

• Server replies with `ServerHello` (cipher chosen), random number, and its public Key certificate.

• Client verifies the certificate authority (CA) signature.

• Client generates a `Pre-Master Secret`, encrypts it using the server's public key, and sends it. Both compute the symmetric session key.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Why both asymmetric and symmetric encryption? Asymmetric (RSA/Diffie-Hellman) is heavy and slow; it is used only to securely exchange a session key. Symmetric (AES) is extremely fast and encrypts the actual HTTP data.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Protects against eavesdropping and modification.

• Asymmetric encryption authenticates and exchanges keys.

• Symmetric session keys encrypt the data stream.

revisionCards.title: SSL/TLS

revisionCards.explanation: Symmetric and asymmetric cryptography protect communications using different key structures.

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: Symmetric Encryption
slides.body:
• Uses a single shared key for both encryption and decryption.

• Extremely fast; optimized for bulk data transfers.

• Key distribution problem: key must be shared securely beforehand.

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: Asymmetric Encryption
slides.body:
• Uses a key pair: Public Key (encrypts) and Private Key (decrypts).

• Slow; computationally expensive.

• No distribution problem: public key can be openly shared.

slides.headline: Comparison Table
slides.body:
• **Key Count**: 1 shared key ➔ 2 keys (Public + Private)

• **Processing Speed**: Very fast ➔ Slow

• **Common Algorithms**: AES, DES, Blowfish ➔ RSA, Diffie-Hellman, ECC

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • In interviews, emphasize that modern secure protocols (like TLS) leverage **both**: Asymmetric encryption sets up the session, and Symmetric encryption takes over for data transfer.

revisionCards.title: Symmetric vs Asymmetric Encryption

revisionCards.explanation: Typing a URL (e.g., `https://www.example.com`) triggers an end-to-end network operation spanning all layers.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: **DNS Lookup**: Browser checks caches (Browser, OS, Router). If missed, recursive resolver queries DNS root, TLD, and authoritative servers to fetch the IP address.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: **ARP Resolution**: If the target IP is outside, client uses ARP to get default gateway router MAC. If target is inside, ARP gets host MAC.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body: **TCP Handshake**: Client initiates a TCP connection (Port 443) with the target IP via a 3-way handshake (SYN ➔ SYN-ACK ➔ ACK).

slides.headline: Step 4
slides.body: **TLS Negotiation**: Secure handshake establishes encryption algorithms and exchanges symmetric session keys.

slides.headline: Step 5
slides.body: **HTTP Request/Response**: Browser sends GET request, server processes, and returns HTML/assets. Connection is closed or kept alive.

slides.headline: Final Flow
slides.body: URL Input ➔ DNS Query ➔ ARP Resolution ➔ TCP 3-Way Handshake ➔ TLS Encrypted Session ➔ HTTP Exchange ➔ Render Page.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • This is the most common interview question. Routers handle IP hops (Layer 3), switches manage local frames (Layer 2), and DNS resolves names (Layer 7). Walk through each layer logically.

revisionCards.title: What Happens When You Type a URL

revisionCards.explanation: TCP and UDP are the two primary Transport Layer protocols, offering different reliability and speed trade-offs.

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: TCP
slides.body:
• Reliable: re-transmits lost packets and ensures correct ordering.

• Connection-oriented (requires setup handshake).

• Heavier header overhead (20 to 60 bytes) and slower speeds.

slides.headline: 💡 Concept: UDP
slides.body:
• Unreliable: no delivery or ordering guarantees.

• Connectionless: fires packets immediately without setup.

• Minimal header overhead (exactly 8 bytes) and maximum speed.

slides.headline: Comparison Table
slides.body:
• **Reliability**: Guaranteed ➔ Best-effort

• **Connection**: Handshake required ➔ No handshake

• **Speed**: Slower (congestion windows) ➔ Maximum speed

• **Common Protocols**: HTTP, HTTPS, SSH, FTP ➔ DNS, DHCP, VOIP, Games

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
