slides.body: • Ask yourself: does a packet drop matter? If yes (loading a webpage or file), use TCP. If no (video frame dropped in zoom call, game ping packet lost), use UDP.

revisionCards.title: TCP vs UDP

revisionCards.explanation: TCP uses a three-way handshake to synchronize sequence numbers and establish a connection.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: **SYN**: Client sends segment with `SYN = 1`, and a random sequence number `ISN_C` (e.g., `x`). Status: `SYN_SENT`.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: **SYN-ACK**: Server replies with `SYN = 1`, `ACK = 1`, sequence number `ISN_S` (e.g., `y`), and `ACK number = x + 1`. Status: `SYN_RCVD`.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body: **ACK**: Client sends segment with `ACK = 1`, `sequence number = x + 1`, and `ACK number = y + 1`. Status: `ESTABLISHED`.

slides.headline: Final Flow
slides.body: Client sends SYN (seq=x) ➔ Server replies SYN-ACK (seq=y, ack=x+1) ➔ Client sends ACK (seq=x+1, ack=y+1) ➔ Connection Established.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Why is it a 3-way handshake and not 2? To prevent stale connection requests. If an old delayed SYN packet arrives at the server, the server replies with SYN-ACK, but the client ignores it since it didn't initiate a connection.

revisionCards.title: Three Way Handshake

revisionCards.explanation: TCP connections are terminated using a four-way handshake to allow both sides to gracefully flush data.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: **FIN**: Active side (e.g., client) sends `FIN = 1` indicating it has no more data. Status: `FIN_WAIT_1`.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: **ACK**: Passive side (server) replies with `ACK = 1` acknowledging the close request. Status: `CLOSE_WAIT` (server can still send data).

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body: **FIN**: Server finishes sending data, sends its own `FIN = 1`. Status: `LAST_ACK`.

slides.headline: Step 4
slides.body: **ACK**: Client replies with `ACK = 1`. Status: `TIME_WAIT` (client waits 2 MSL to ensure ACK reached server, then closes).

slides.headline: Final Flow
slides.body: Client sends FIN ➔ Server sends ACK ➔ Server sends FIN ➔ Client sends ACK ➔ TIME_WAIT ➔ Closed.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Why the `TIME_WAIT` state? If the final ACK is lost, the server will retransmit its FIN. The client must stay alive in `TIME_WAIT` (typically 2-4 mins) to retransmit the ACK; else the connection resets.

revisionCards.title: Four Way Termination

revisionCards.explanation: The **Sample Space** (denoted by `S` or `Ω`) is the set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Formulates the baseline of any probability computation by setting boundaries for outcomes.
Must be mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive to avoid overlaps or unrepresented possibilities.

• Determines the denominator in classical probability. If the sample space contains outcomes that are equally likely, then
`P(A) = |A| / |S|`.

• Can be discrete (e.g., throwing a die `S = {1,2,3,4,5,6}`) or continuous (e.g., measuring lifetime of a bulb `S = [0, ∞)`).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • In interviews, always define your sample space first. Missing a single outcome (like a coin landing on its edge or not accounting for birth order in gender puzzles) leads to wrong calculations.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Sample space is the set of **all** possible experiment outcomes.

• Must be mutually exclusive (no overlap) and exhaustive.

• Sizing the sample space provides the math denominator.

revisionCards.title: Sample Space

revisionCards.explanation: A **Favorable Outcome** represents an event subset `E` within the sample space `S` that satisfies a specific condition.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Represents the target events whose probability is being computed. The number of favorable outcomes is denoted by `|E|`.

• Formulates the numerator in the classical probability formula `P(E) = |E| / |S|`. Finding this often requires counting tools like combinations.

• Can be a single outcome (simple event) or a combination of multiple outcomes (compound event).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body:
• Focus on how restrictions filter the sample space. For example, when throwing two dice, if the event is "sum equals 7", the favorable subset is
`{(1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1)}` out of 36.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Favorable outcomes represent the event subset `E`.

• Provides the mathematical numerator in probability ratios.

• Requires systematic enumeration or combinatorics to calculate accurately.

revisionCards.title: Favorable Outcomes

revisionCards.explanation: Two events `A` and `B` are **Independent** if the occurrence of one does not change the probability of the other.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Pathways of influence: Mathematically defined as `P(A ∩ B) = P(A) * P(B)`. This is the multiplication rule for independent events.

• Implies that conditional probability matches absolute probability: `P(A|B) = P(A)` and `P(B|A) = P(B)`. Knowing `B` happened gives zero new info about `A`.

• Different from physical isolation. Independent events can happen in the same time-space, but their underlying systems must share no statistical correlation.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • A common mistake is assuming "independent" means "disjoint". Disjoint events are highly dependent: if `A` happens, `B` cannot happen, meaning `P(B|A) = 0`. Independence requires zero information exchange.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Independence formula:
`P(A ∩ B) = P(A) * P(B)`.

• Conditional probability matches absolute:
`P(A|B) = P(A)`.

• Do not confuse independence with mutually exclusive events.

revisionCards.title: Independent Events

revisionCards.explanation: Two events are **Dependent** if the occurrence of one changes the probability of the occurrence of the other.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Statistical connection: Occurs when the probability of event `B` changes depending on whether `A` happened. Mathematically,
`P(B|A) ≠ P(B)`.

• The joint probability of dependent events requires conditional probability:
`P(A ∩ B) = P(A) * P(B|A)`.

• Common in processes without replacement (e.g., drawing cards from a deck without putting them back alters the deck size and composition).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Identify dependencies by tracking the state of the system. If the sample space changes in size or composition after the first step, subsequent steps are dependent on it.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Dependency formula:
`P(A ∩ B) = P(A) * P(B|A)`.

• Commonly occurs during "drawing without replacement" setups.

• Requires tracking structural shifts in the sample space.

revisionCards.title: Dependent Events

revisionCards.explanation: Events are **Mutually Exclusive** (or disjoint) if they cannot occur at the same time.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Exclusive states: If event `A` occurs, event `B` cannot occur. Their intersection is empty:
`A ∩ B = ∅`.

• Mathematically, their joint probability is zero:
`P(A ∩ B) = 0`.

• The addition rule simplifies for disjoint events: `P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B)`. There is no overlap to subtract.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Think of a coin flip: landing on Heads and landing on Tails are mutually exclusive. In interviews, remember that mutually exclusive events are dependent because knowing one happened tells you the other definitely did not.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Intersection probability is zero:
`P(A ∩ B) = 0`.

• Simplified addition rule:
`P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B)`.

• Disjoint events are inherently dependent.

revisionCards.title: Mutually Exclusive Events

revisionCards.explanation: The **Complement Rule** states that the probability of an event `A` occurring plus the probability of its complement `A'` is exactly `1`.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• System partitioning: Written as `P(A) + P(A') = 1` or `P(A') = 1 - P(A)`. The event and its complement partition the sample space.

• Saves time when calculating "at least one" events. Instead of summing many complex terms, compute the probability of "none" and subtract from 1.

• Extends to multiple events where the complement event is simpler to construct and count.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • If an interviewer asks for "the probability of getting at least one 6 in 4 rolls", do not sum the probabilities of getting 1, 2, 3, or 4 sixes. Compute the probability of getting "no 6" in all rolls (`(5/6)^4`) and subtract it from 1.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Complement formula:
`P(A') = 1 - P(A)`.

• Highly effective for calculating "at least one" probabilities.

• Reduces complex multi-event problems to a single calculation.

revisionCards.title: Complement Rule

revisionCards.explanation: The **Addition Rule** calculates the probability of the union of two events (either event `A` or event `B` occurring).

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Venn mathematics: The general formula is
`P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B)`. We subtract the intersection because it is counted twice.

• If the events are mutually exclusive, the intersection is zero, simplifying the formula to:
`P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B)`.

• Extends to three events:

`P(A ∪ B ∪ C) = P(A) + P(B) + P(C) - P(A ∩ B) - P(B ∩ C) - P(A ∩ C) + P(A ∩ B ∩ C)`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Visualize a Venn diagram. Adding the circles `A` and `B` doubles the weight of the overlapping region. Subtracting the intersection restores the balance.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Union formula:

`P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B)`.

• Subtracting the intersection prevents double counting.

• Simplifies to `P(A) + P(B)` for disjoint events.

revisionCards.title: Addition Rule

revisionCards.explanation: The **Multiplication Rule** calculates the joint probability of two events occurring together (intersection of `A` and `B`).

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Intersection calculations: The general formula is `P(A ∩ B) = P(A) * P(B|A)` or `P(A ∩ B) = P(B) * P(A|B)`. This applies to all events.

• For independent events, since `P(B|A) = P(B)`, the formula simplifies to:
`P(A ∩ B) = P(A) * P(B)`.

• Can be chained for multiple events:

`P(A ∩ B ∩ C) = P(A) * P(B|A) * P(C|A ∩ B)`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Think of the rule as walking down a path of decision trees. You must cross the first gate (`P(A)`) and then cross the second gate given you crossed the first (`P(B|A)`).

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Joint probability:
`P(A ∩ B) = P(A) * P(B|A)`.

• Independent version:
`P(A ∩ B) = P(A) * P(B)`.

• Can be chained sequentially for any number of events.

revisionCards.title: Multiplication Rule

revisionCards.explanation: The **Law of Total Probability** calculates the overall probability of an event by summing its conditional probabilities across a partitioned sample space.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Partition summing: If events `B1, B2, ..., Bn` partition the sample space (disjoint and sum to 1), then
`P(A) = Σ P(A|Bi) * P(Bi)`.

• Allows you to solve a complex probability by dividing it into simpler conditional branches.

• Forms the mathematical denominator for Bayes Theorem calculations.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Think of it as a weighted average. If you are drawing from three bags with different ball ratios, the overall probability of drawing a red ball is the sum of the probabilities of choosing a bag times the probability of drawing red from that bag.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Total probability formula:
`P(A) = Σ P(A|Bi) * P(Bi)`.

• Requires a partition of the sample space.

• Essential for solving multi-stage branch problems.

revisionCards.title: Law of Total Probability

revisionCards.explanation: Probability tricks utilize symmetry, complements, and indicator variables to bypass long calculations in interviews.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Symmetry: If `N` items are arranged randomly in a circle, the probability that item `A` is next to `B` is independent of their exact locations.

• Complement shortcut: Whenever you see "at least", reformulate the problem to `1 - P(None)` to avoid summing multiple terms.

• Geometric probability: For continuous variables, sketch the coordinate system and compute the ratio of the areas representing the favorable condition vs the sample space.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Look for symmetry. If 100 people roll a die, the probability that the 50th person rolls a 6 is exactly `1/6`, the same as the 1st person. Order of execution without replacement maintains uniform probability distribution across positions.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Use symmetry to resolve order-based questions instantly.

• Use complements to avoid sum series.

• Use area ratios for continuous probability.

revisionCards.title: Probability Tricks

revisionCards.explanation: Probability interview patterns group questions into recurring archetypes like coin sequences, random walks, and bag drawings.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Coin sequences: Finding the expected flips to get `HT` vs `HH`. These are solved using recursive conditional equations.

• Bag drawings: Drawing colored balls with/without replacement. These require combinatorics (`nCr`) or conditional chains.

• Grid/Path walks: Moving on a coordinate grid from `(0,0)` to `(X,Y)` with random steps, solved using combinations.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Recognize the archetype early. When an interviewer describes a system that resets or transitions based on states, immediately set up recursive state equations (`E[X] = 1 + ...`).

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Identify coin/dice state-reset patterns.

• Use combinations for bag drawing paths.

• Map state spaces to solve random walks.

revisionCards.title: Probability Interview Patterns

revisionCards.explanation: **Conditional Probability** measures the probability of an event `A` occurring given that another event `B` has already occurred.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Math description: Denoted as `P(A|B)` (read "probability of A given B").

• Formula: `P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B)`, where `P(B) > 0`. We restrict our universe to the outcomes in `B`.

• Shifts the sample space from the entire universe `S` to the subset `B`. Only the outcomes of `A` that fall inside `B` remain favorable.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body:
• Think of it as filtering a spreadsheet. If you look at all candidates, the probability of knowing C++ is `P(C++)`. If you filter to only CS graduates, you compute the conditional probability:
`P(C++ | CS)`.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Formula:
`P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B)`.

• Restricts the sample space denominator to the given event.

• Forms the foundation of Bayes Theorem.

revisionCards.title: Conditional Probability Basics

revisionCards.explanation: **Bayes Theorem** relates conditional probabilities and their inverses, updating event likelihood based on new evidence.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Reverse modeling: Formula is:

`P(A|B) = [P(B|A) * P(A)] / P(B)`.

• Can be expanded using the Law of Total Probability:

`P(A|B) = [P(B|A) * P(A)] / [P(B|A)*P(A) + P(B|A')*P(A')]`.

• Components: `P(A)` is the Prior, `P(B|A)` is the Likelihood, `P(B)` is the Normalizing Constant, and `P(A|B)` is the Posterior.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Bayes Theorem allows you to reverse conditional directions. If you know the probability of having a fever given you have flu, Bayes helps you find the probability of having flu given you have a fever.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Bayes Formula:

`P(A|B) = [P(B|A) * P(A)] / P(B)`.

• Allows reversing conditional directions.

• Updates prior beliefs using new evidence.

revisionCards.title: Bayes Theorem

revisionCards.explanation: Bayes Intuition helps prevent the base rate fallacy by separating the prior likelihood from test accuracy.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Cognitive alignment: Base Rate Fallacy occurs when misinterpreting high test accuracy as a high posterior probability while ignoring the rarity of the condition.

• Likelihood ratio: A highly accurate test for a rare disease still yields mostly false positives because the base rate of healthy people is massive.

• Updates: Prior probability is updated by evidence to produce the posterior. Rarity acts as an anchor.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • If a disease affects 1 in 10,000 people and a test is 99% accurate, a positive test result only means a `~1%` chance of actually having the disease. The pool of false positives from the 9,999 healthy people dominates the pool of true positives.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Always combine base rates with test accuracy.

• Rare priors require extremely strong evidence to shift.

• Avoid the base rate fallacy in diagnostics.

revisionCards.title: Bayes Intuition

revisionCards.explanation: Calculate the probability that a patient has a disease given a positive test result, considering base rate and accuracy.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Identify the parameters: Prior probability `P(D) = 0.001` (1 in 1000 have the disease). Test sensitivity `P(+|D) = 0.99` (true positive rate) and specificity `P(-|D') = 0.98` (true negative rate, which means false positive rate `P(+|D') = 0.02`).

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body:
Apply the Law of Total Probability to find the overall positive test rate
`P(+) = P(+|D)*P(D) + P(+|D')*P(D')`. Substituting values:

`P(+) = (0.99 * 0.001) + (0.02 * 0.999) = 0.00099 + 0.01998 = 0.02097`.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body:
Use Bayes Theorem to calculate the posterior probability:

`P(D|+) = [P(+|D) * P(D)] / P(+) = 0.00099 / 0.02097`.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: Posterior probability `P(D|+) ≈ 0.047` or `4.7%`. Despite a 99% accurate test, there is only a 4.7% chance the patient has the disease due to its rarity.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body:
Out of 100,000 people, 100 have it (99 test positive) and 99,900 do not (1,998 test positive). Total positive tests = 2,097. Probability =
`99 / 2097 ≈ 4.7%`.

revisionCards.title: Medical Testing Problems

revisionCards.explanation: A classic puzzle: You choose a coin from a bag containing one two-headed coin, one regular coin, and one two-tailed coin. You flip it and get Heads. What is the probability that the other side is also Heads?

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body:
Define the events and priors. Three coins: `C1` (double Heads), `C2` (normal), `C3` (double Tails). Priors:
`P(C1) = P(C2) = P(C3) = 1/3`.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body:
Define the condition. We see Heads on the flip. The conditional probabilities of flipping Heads are: `P(H|C1) = 1`, `P(H|C2) = 0.5`,
`P(H|C3) = 0`.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body:
Calculate overall probability of flipping Heads:
`P(H) = P(H|C1)*P(C1) + P(H|C2)*P(C2) = (1 * 1/3) + (0.5 * 1/3) = 1/2`. Now find

`P(C1|H) = [P(H|C1) * P(C1)] / P(H) = (1 * 1/3) / (1/2) = 2/3`.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body:
The probability that the other side is Heads is the probability that you chose the double-headed coin, which is:
`2/3`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body:
There are 6 sides in total. 3 sides are Heads (2 from C1, 1 from C2). If you see a Head, you are looking at one of these 3 sides. In 2 of those cases, the coin is C1. Probability =
`2/3`.

revisionCards.title: Coin Flip Conditional Probability

revisionCards.explanation: Calculate the probability of drawing specific cards sequentially without replacement.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Identify the target: drawing two Aces in a row from a standard 52-card deck.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body:
Find the probability of the first card being an Ace:
`P(A1) = 4 / 52`.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body:
Find the conditional probability of drawing a second Ace given the first was an Ace: `P(A2|A1) = 3 / 51` (one Ace and one card removed). Calculate joint:
`P(A1 ∩ A2) = (4/52) * (3/51)`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body:
Number of ways to draw 2 Aces is `4C2 = 6`. Total ways to draw 2 cards is `52C2 = 1326`. Probability =
`6 / 1326 = 1 / 221`.

revisionCards.title: Card Drawing Conditional Probability

revisionCards.explanation: Introducing new facts about a system filters the sample space and alters the probabilities of remaining outcomes.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Information constraints: Known as the "Boy or Girl" paradox archetype. Knowing a family has at least one boy yields different probabilities than knowing the eldest child is a boy.

• "Eldest is a boy" specifies a position: sample space is `{BG, BB}` (favorable `BB` = 1/2).

• "At least one is a boy" does not specify position: sample space is `{BG, GB, BB}` (favorable `BB` = 1/3).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Pay close attention to how information is revealed. If the information specifies a particular instance (e.g. "I saw the eldest child"), it divides the space symmetrically. If it is global (e.g. "At least one"), it removes options unsymmetrically.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Specific identifiers preserve symmetry.

• Global constraints filter the sample space asymmetrical.

• Always list the filtered sample space when new info is given.

revisionCards.title: Information Changes Probability

revisionCards.explanation: Avoid standard cognitive errors in conditional probability, such as treating dependent events as independent or ignoring base rates.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Prosecutor's Fallacy: Confusing `P(Evidence | Innocent)` with `P(Innocent | Evidence)`. A low match rate of DNA does not mean guilt if the population is massive.

• Monty Hall Trap: Assuming that since two doors remain, the probability is split `50/50`. The host's action was dependent on your choice, which concentrates probability.

• Order effects: Forgetting to scale by arrangements when calculating conditional combinations.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • In interviews, if a question seems too simple (like a 50/50 split after an event), check if the revealing action was dependent on hidden parameters.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Never confuse `P(A|B)` with `P(B|A)`.

• Verify if revealing actions are random or restricted.

• Write out intersections explicitly during doubts.

revisionCards.title: Common Interview Traps

revisionCards.explanation: The **Expected Value (EV)** of a random variable is its long-run arithmetic average value over many repetitions.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Equilibrium point: Reps the center of gravity of the probability distribution. It does not have to be a value the variable can actually take.

• Weighted average: Each possible value is multiplied by its probability of occurrence, and the products are summed.

• Linearity of Expectation: `E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y]` holds true even if `X` and `Y` are dependent. This is a powerful shortcut.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • If you play a game where you win $10 with 50% probability and lose $5 with 50% probability, the expected value is `$2.50`. Over thousands of runs, your average payoff per game converges to this value.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• EV is the long-term average value of a random variable.

• Formula:
`E[X] = Σ x * P(X = x)`.

• Linearity of expectation holds for dependent variables.

revisionCards.title: Expected Value Basics

revisionCards.explanation: The mathematical formulas define expected value for both discrete and continuous random variables.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Mathematical representations: Discrete formula is `E[X] = Σ x_i * P(X = x_i)` for all possible outcomes `i`.

• Continuous formula: `E[X] = ∫ x * f(x) dx` integrated from `-∞` to `+∞`, where `f(x)` is the probability density function.

• Properties: `E[c] = c` (constant), `E[cX] = c * E[X]`, and if `X` and `Y` are independent,
`E[X * Y] = E[X] * E[Y]`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body:
• Remember that `E[X^2]` is not `(E[X])^2`. Their difference is the variance:
`Var(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2`.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Discrete: Sum of value times probability.

• Continuous: Integration of value times density.

• Difference of `E[X^2]` and `E[X]^2` is Variance.

revisionCards.title: EV Formula

revisionCards.explanation: A **Fair Game** is a game of chance where the expected value of the net profit is exactly zero.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Game neutrality: For a game to be fair, the entry cost must equal the expected gross payoff:

`E[Net Profit] = E[Payoff] - Cost = 0`.

• If `E[Net Profit] > 0`, the game favors the player; if `E[Net Profit] < 0`, it favors the house (casino edge).

• In finance, pricing derivatives uses risk-neutral valuation, which forces the expectation of returns to match the risk-free rate (making transactions fair).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • If an interviewer asks "How much would you pay to play a game where you roll a die and get paid the face value?", calculate the EV of the die (`3.5`). A fair price to pay is exactly `$3.50`.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Fair game:
`E[Net Profit] = 0`.

• Entry fee must equal expected payoff.

• Foundation of financial asset pricing.

revisionCards.title: Fair Game Concept

revisionCards.explanation: An **Unfair Game** has a non-zero expected profit, creating an edge for either the player or the house.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Asymmetrical advantages: All casino games are unfair games with negative EV for the player (e.g. Roulette house edge is `~2.7%` to `5.3%`).

• If a game has a positive EV for you, the optimal strategy is to maximize play count to let the Law of Large Numbers secure your profit.

• Helps in risk management: avoiding bets where the probability of winning is high but the payout is too low to cover the loss risk.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body:
• In trading or betting, look for "positive expectancy". Even if your win rate is only 40%, if your average win pays 3x your average loss, the EV is positive:
`(0.4 * 3) + (0.6 * -1) = +0.6`.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Unfair game:
`E[Net Profit] ≠ 0`.

• House edge guarantees long-term player losses.

• Expectancy combines win rate with payout size.

revisionCards.title: Unfair Game Concept

revisionCards.explanation: Calculate the expected value of rolling one or more standard dice under specific conditions.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body:
Identify the outcomes of a standard 6-sided die: `{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}`, each with probability:
`1/6`.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body:
Calculate the expected sum of two independent dice: using Linearity of Expectation,
`E[X1 + X2] = E[X1] + E[X2] = 3.5 + 3.5 = 7` (holds even if they are somehow tied/dependent).

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: Expected value of one die is `3.5`. Expected sum of two dice is `7`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body:
Symmetry rule: The average of the minimum (1) and maximum (6) outcomes of a uniform discrete distribution is:
`(1 + 6) / 2 = 3.5`.

revisionCards.title: Dice EV Problems

revisionCards.explanation: Calculate expected value when flipping coins, such as counting the expected number of Heads in a series of trials.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body:
Set up the experiment: Flip a fair coin `N` times. Let `X` be the number of Heads. We want to find
`E[X]`.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body:
Define indicator variables: Let `Xi = 1` if the `i-th` flip is Heads, and `Xi = 0` otherwise. The probability `P(Xi = 1) = 0.5`. Thus,

`E[Xi] = 1 * 0.5 + 0 * 0.5 = 0.5`.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body:
Sum the expectations: Total Heads `X = X1 + X2 + ... + XN`. Using linearity:

`E[X] = E[X1] + E[X2] + ... + E[XN] = N * 0.5`.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body:
Expected number of Heads in `N` flips is:
`N / 2`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body:
For any binomial distribution with parameters `N` and `p`, the expected value is simply `N * p`. Here,
`N * 0.5 = 0.5N`.

revisionCards.title: Coin EV Problems

revisionCards.explanation: Calculate the expected value of a lottery ticket to determine if buying it is a rational financial decision.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Identify the payoffs and probabilities: Ticket costs $2. Grand prize is $10 million with probability 1 in 10 million. Smaller prizes: $100 with probability 1 in 1,000.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body:
Calculate expected net profit:

`E[Net] = E[Gross] - Cost = $1.10 - $2.00 = -$0.90`.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: Expected net profit is `-$0.90` per ticket. Buying a ticket loses 90 cents on average, making it a negative EV decision.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: Unless the jackpot grows huge (and tax/split-prize options are neglected) such that `E[Gross] > Ticket Cost`, playing lotteries is a losing game.

revisionCards.title: Lottery EV

revisionCards.explanation: Calculate expected payoffs in multi-stage games where actions in early rounds affect options in later rounds.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Understand the game: You roll a die. You can either keep the face value in dollars or reject it and roll a second time (final value). What is your optimal strategy and expected value?

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body:
Work backward from the final round. If you roll a second time, the expected value of that roll is:
`E[R2] = 3.5`.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body:
Determine optimal strategy for Round 1: You should roll again only if the first roll is less than the expected value of the second roll (`< 3.5`). So, keep `{4, 5, 6}` and reject `{1, 2, 3}`. Calculate EV:

`(1/2 * average(4,5,6)) + (1/2 * E[R2]) = (1/2 * 5) + (1/2 * 3.5) = 2.5 + 1.75 = 4.25`.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: Expected value of this game is `$4.25`. Optimal strategy is to keep rolls ≥ 4.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body:
Symmetry of choice: The average payoff from keeping is `5` (half the time). The payoff from rolling again is `3.5` (half the time). Overall EV =
`0.5*5 + 0.5*3.5 = 4.25`.

revisionCards.title: Multiple Round EV

revisionCards.explanation: Solve expected value problems with infinite loops or resetting conditions using recursive equations.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Understand the problem: A game involves flipping a fair coin until you get two consecutive Heads (HH). What is the expected number of flips?

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: Define states: Let `x` be the expected flips from start. Let `y` be the expected remaining flips if we just got a Head (H).

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body:
Set up recursive equations: From start:
`x = 1 + 0.5*x (got T, reset) + 0.5*y (got H)`. From H state:
`y = 1 + 0.5*0 (got H, game ends) + 0.5*x (got T, reset)`. Simplify: `x = 1 + 0.5x + 0.5y` ➔ `0.5x = 1 + 0.5y` ➔ `x = 2 + y`. Substitute into second equation: `y = 1 + 0.5x` ➔ `y = 1 + 0.5(2 + y) = 2 + 0.5y` ➔ `0.5y = 2` ➔ `y = 4`. Find
`x = 2 + 4 = 6`.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: The expected number of flips to get two consecutive Heads (HH) is `6`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: State transition trick: Let `E` be the target flips. `E` satisfies the recursive partition: `E = 6`. (For HT, the answer is 4, showing sequence patterns matter due to overlaps).

revisionCards.title: Recursive EV Problems

revisionCards.explanation: Expected Value Optimization is the process of selecting decisions that maximize expected utility or payoff.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Asymptotic utility: Combines decision trees with probability weights. The optimal decision is:
`D* = argmax E[Utility(D)]`.

• Utility vs Cash: Rational decision makers optimize expected *utility* rather than cash value. This explains risk aversion (utility of $10M is not 10x the utility of $1M).

• Continuous optimization: Solved by setting the derivative of the expected payoff function with respect to the decision variable to zero.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • In trading or bidding, bidding lower increases profit if you win but decreases the probability of winning. Optimization finds the sweet spot where `P(Win) * Profit` is maximized.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Select actions that maximize expected utility.

• Accounts for risk preferences using utility functions.

• Balances payoff size against execution probability.

revisionCards.title: EV Optimization

revisionCards.explanation: Recognize expected value patterns in interviews, such as indicator variables, state-machines, and stop-rules.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Common architectures: Indicator variables are used to calculate expectations of sums (e.g. number of couples sitting together at a table) without computing joint distributions.

• First-step analysis: Setting up conditional expectation based on the first outcome of the process, leading to linear equations.

• Symmetric bets: Finding pricing limits for asymmetric payoffs.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body:
• If the question asks for the expected number of cards you need to turn over to find the first Ace, do not sum a giant series. Use indicator variables for the non-Ace cards, yielding
`E[X] = 10.6`.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Indicator variables simplify complex joint systems.

• First-step analysis resolves infinite chains.

• Symmetry reduces dimensional calculations.

revisionCards.title: Interview EV Patterns

revisionCards.explanation: The **Rule of Sum** is a fundamental counting principle used to calculate the size of the union of disjoint sets.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Set partitions: If an event can occur in `A` ways, and a second disjoint event can occur in `B` ways, then either event can occur in `A + B` ways.

• Disjoint condition: The options must be mutually exclusive. If they overlap, you must apply the Inclusion-Exclusion Principle instead.

• Corresponds to the logical operator **OR** in counting systems.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • If a restaurant offers 5 vegetarian dishes and 4 meat dishes, and you want to choose *one* dish, you have `5 + 4 = 9` options. You cannot choose both.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Rule of Sum = Addition for disjoint choices.

• Corresponds to the logical operator OR.

• Requires zero overlap between sets.

revisionCards.title: Rule of Sum

revisionCards.explanation: The **Rule of Product** is a counting principle used to calculate the total options in a sequence of choices.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Sequential events: If a first choice can be made in `A` ways, and for each of these choices a second choice can be made in `B` ways, the sequence of choices can be made in `A * B` ways.

• Applies to independent sequential operations. The choice made in the first step does not restrict the number of choices in the second step.

• Corresponds to the logical operator **AND** in counting systems.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • If you have 3 shirts and 4 pants, the number of unique outfits you can choose is `3 * 4 = 12`. For each shirt, you can pair it with any of the 4 pants.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Rule of Product = Multiplication for sequential steps.

• Corresponds to the logical operator AND.

• Requires independent options at each stage.

revisionCards.title: Rule of Product

revisionCards.explanation: A **Factorial** (denoted by `n!`) represents the number of ways to arrange `n` distinct objects in a linear sequence.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Arrangements logic: Formula is
`n! = n * (n-1) * (n-2) * ... * 1`, with definition
`0! = 1`.

• Grows extremely fast (faster than exponential functions). Stirling's approximation `n! ≈ √(2πn) * (n/e)^n` is used to estimate large factorials.

• Forms the basis of permutation and combination formulas.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body:
• If you arrange 5 books on a shelf, you have 5 choices for the first slot, 4 for the second, 3 for the third, 2 for the fourth, and 1 for the last. Total arrangements =
`5! = 120`.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Arranging `n` distinct items = `n!` ways.

• Grows faster than exponential functions.

• Defined as `0! = 1` for consistent formula algebra.

revisionCards.title: Factorials

revisionCards.explanation: A **Permutation** calculates the number of ways to select and arrange a subset of objects from a larger set where order matters.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Arranging selections: Formula is `nPr = n! / (n - r)!`, representing the number of ways to arrange `r` items chosen from a pool of `n` items.

• Order-sensitive: Arranging items `A` and `B` as `AB` is counted as a different permutation than `BA`.

• Can be solved using the multiplication rule: `n` options for slot 1, `n-1` for slot 2, down to:
`n-r+1`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body:
• If 10 runners compete in a race, the number of ways the gold, silver, and bronze medals can be awarded is
`10P3 = 10! / 7! = 10 * 9 * 8 = 720`. Ordering matters.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Permutations formula:
`nPr = n! / (n - r)!`.

• Order of selected items is critical.

• Equivalent to selection followed by ordering.

revisionCards.title: Permutations

revisionCards.explanation: A **Combination** calculates the number of ways to select a subset of objects from a larger set where order does not matter.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Unordered selections: Formula is `nCr = n! / [r! * (n - r)!]`, also denoted as `(n choose r)`.

• Order-insensitive: Selecting `A` then `B` is identical to selecting `B` then `A`. We divide by `r!` to strip away arrangement duplicates.

• Symmetry property: `nCr = nC(n-r)`. Choosing `r` items to keep is identical to choosing `n-r` items to discard.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body:
• If you want to choose a committee of 3 people from a group of 10, the order of selection is irrelevant. The number of unique committees is:

`10C3 = (10*9*8) / (3*2*1) = 120`.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Combinations formula:
`nCr = n! / [r!(n-r)!]`.

• Order of selected items is irrelevant.

• Symmetrical property:
`nCr = nC(n-r)`.

revisionCards.title: Combinations

revisionCards.explanation: Circular arrangements count the ways to arrange objects in a loop, where rotations are considered identical.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Rotational loops: Arranging `n` distinct items in a circle has `(n - 1)!` unique ways. We fix one item to break rotational symmetry.

• If the circle can be flipped (like a necklace of beads where clockwise and counterclockwise arrangements are identical), divide by 2:
`(n - 1)! / 2`.

• Relative positions are what matter, rather than absolute coordinate positions.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • If 5 people sit at a round table, placing them as `ABCDE` or `BCDEA` is the same seating arrangement because everyone has the same neighbors. Fixing person `A` leaves 4 slots to fill: `4! = 24` arrangements.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Linear arrangements: `n!`, Circular arrangements:
`(n - 1)!`.

• Divide by 2 if clockwise/counterclockwise matches.

• Fixing one element breaks rotational symmetry.

revisionCards.title: Circular Arrangements

revisionCards.explanation: Arrange items containing identical duplicates by dividing out permutation repetitions.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Multiset partitions: Arranging `n` items where `n1` are identical of type 1, `n2` of type 2, etc., has `n! / (n1! * n2! * ...)` ways.

• Prevents overcounting: swapping identical items does not create a new visual sequence.

• Forms the basis of path counting on grids.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • To arrange the letters of "PEPPER" (6 letters: 3 P's, 2 E's, 1 R): start with `6! = 720`. Divide by `3!` for P repetitions and `2!` for E repetitions: `720 / (6 * 2) = 60` arrangements.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Arrangements formula:
`n! / (n1! * n2! ...)`.

• Divides out internal permutations of identical elements.

• Crucial for word arrangement puzzles.

revisionCards.title: Repeated Elements

revisionCards.explanation: Calculate the number of ways to arrange `n` items such that no item appears in its original starting position.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body:
Identify the derangement formula `D(n) = n! * Σ ((-1)^k / k!)` summed from `k = 0` to `n`. Or use the recurrence relation:

`D(n) = (n - 1) * (D(n - 1) + D(n - 2))`.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body:
Understand probability connection: The probability that a random permutation is a derangement converges to `1/e ≈ 0.3678` very quickly for
`n ≥ 4`.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: Number of derangements for `n=4` is `9`, and for `n=5` is `44`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body:
For any `n`, the number of derangements `D(n)` is the nearest integer to:
`n! / e`.

revisionCards.title: Derangements

revisionCards.explanation: Calculate selection combinations when picking teams under gender or role-based constraints.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Understand the problem: A committee of 5 people must be chosen from a group of 6 men and 4 women. The committee must contain at least 3 women. How many combinations exist?

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: Identify the cases: Case 1: Exactly 3 women and 2 men. Case 2: Exactly 4 women and 1 man. Case 3: Exactly 5 women (not possible since there are only 4 women total).

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body:
Calculate combinations for each case. Case 1: `4C3 * 6C2 = 4 * 15 = 60`. Case 2: `4C4 * 6C1 = 1 * 6 = 6`. Sum the cases:
`60 + 6 = 66`.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: The number of valid committee combinations is `66`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: Complement alternative: If you had many cases, calculate the total combinations `10C5 = 252` and subtract invalid cases (0, 1, or 2 women).

revisionCards.title: Committee Selection

revisionCards.explanation: Calculate arrangements of items where certain objects must sit together or must not sit next to each other.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Understand the problem: Arrange 5 boys and 3 girls in a row such that no two girls sit next to each other.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: Use the **Gap Method**. Arrange the unrestricted items (5 boys) first: `5! = 120` ways. This creates gaps before, between, and after the boys.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body:
Count the gaps: 5 boys create 6 gaps (`_ B _ B _ B _ B _ B _`). Choose 3 gaps for the 3 girls: `6C3 = 20` ways. Arrange the girls in those gaps: `3! = 6` ways. Calculate total:
`120 * 20 * 6 = 14,400`.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: Total arrangements with no girls adjacent is `14,400`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: Tie Method: If items *must* sit together, tie them into a single block, arrange the block with the rest of the items, then multiply by the internal arrangements of the tied block.

revisionCards.title: Arrangement Restrictions

revisionCards.explanation: Utilize combinatorial short-cuts such as the tie method, gap method, and grid projection during coding interviews.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Operational rules: Tie Method groups items that must remain adjacent as one "super item". Arrange the set, then multiply by the internal arrangements.

• Gap Method: Whenever items must remain separated, arrange the other items first, then place the restricted items in the gaps.

• Grid mapping: Transform paths on grids to binary strings of moves (e.g. Right/Down), converting path searches to combinations.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • If the interviewer says "Arrange 6 books such that book A is not next to book B", do not calculate all separations. Calculate total arrangements (`6! = 720`) and subtract the case where they are tied together (`2 * 5! = 240`), yielding `480`.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Tie method: group adjacent items into one.

• Gap method: place separated items in gaps between unrestricted items.

• Saves time by subtracting adjacent cases from the total.

revisionCards.title: Common Interview Counting Tricks

revisionCards.explanation: Counting without enumeration uses mathematical structures to find the size of large sets without listing their elements.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Implicit sizes: Bypasses manual lists, which are prone to errors on large scales.

• Uses algebraic formulas (like sums of sequences or binomial coefficients) to compute set size.

• Requires mapping the objects to a known counted structure (e.g. binary sequences).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • If you want to count the number of subsets of a set of size 10, do not list them. Know that each element has 2 choices (in or out), yielding `2^10 = 1024` subsets instantly.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Avoid manual listing for large sets.

• Map configurations to binary state choices.

• Use combinatorial coefficients for calculations.

revisionCards.title: Counting Without Enumeration

revisionCards.explanation: The **Inclusion-Exclusion Principle (PIE)** calculates the size of the union of multiple overlapping sets by adjusting for intersections.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Set overlapping adjustments: For two sets:
`|A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| - |A ∩ B|`.

• For three sets:

`|A ∪ B ∪ C| = |A| + |B| + |C| - |A ∩ B| - |B ∩ C| - |A ∩ C| + |A ∩ B ∩ C|`.

• Alternates signs: Include single sets, exclude pairwise intersections, include triple intersections, and so on.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body:
• If you count numbers divisible by 2 (50) and divisible by 3 (33) up to 100, adding them counts numbers divisible by 6 (16) twice. Subtracting the intersection gives
`50 + 33 - 16 = 67`.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• PIE adjusts for double counting in overlapping sets.

• Alternates addition and subtraction for intersections.

• Essential for counting numbers with multiple properties.

revisionCards.title: Inclusion Exclusion Principle

revisionCards.explanation: Calculate the number of ways to distribute `n` identical objects into `k` distinct bins.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Identify the objects as stars (`*`) and the dividers between bins as bars (`|`). To partition into `k` bins, we need `k - 1` bars.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: The total slots to arrange stars and bars is `n + k - 1`. Choose `k - 1` slots to place the bars: `(n + k - 1) choose (k - 1)`. This allows empty bins.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body:
If bins must be non-empty (at least 1 object per bin), distribute 1 object to each bin beforehand, leaving `n - k` objects. The formula becomes
`(n - 1) choose (k - 1)`.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body:
Number of ways to distribute 10 identical apples to 3 children:
`(10 + 3 - 1)C(3 - 1) = 12C2 = 66` ways (allowing empty allocations).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body:
Bins can be empty: `(n+k-1)C(k-1)`. Bins must have at least 1:
`(n-1)C(k-1)`.

revisionCards.title: Stars and Bars

revisionCards.explanation: **Complement Counting** calculates the size of a target set by subtracting the size of its complement from the total universal set.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Subtraction models: Formula is `|A| = |Universe| - |A'|`. Useful when the complement `A'` has fewer cases or is easier to define.

• Prevents breaking the target condition into many complex sub-cases.

• Commonly used with keywords like "at least", "at most", or "contains no".

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • If you want to count 4-digit numbers that contain at least one digit 7, do not count numbers with 1, 2, 3, or 4 sevens. Subtract the count of numbers with *no* sevens (`8 * 9 * 9 * 9 = 5832`) from total 4-digit numbers (`9000`), yielding `3168`.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Formula:
`|A| = |Total| - |Complement|`.

• Simplifies "at least" counting constraints.

• Reduces calculations by targeting the opposite state.

revisionCards.title: Complement Counting

revisionCards.explanation: **Bijection Thinking** counts a set by establishing a one-to-one mapping to another set that is easier to count.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Isomorphic mappings: Bijection is a mapping where every element in set `X` matches exactly one element in set `Y`, meaning
`|X| = |Y|`.

• Transforms hard-to-visualize problems into standard counting setups (e.g. paths on a grid matching strings of characters).

• Useful for proving identities or proving that two different-looking problems are mathematically identical.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Think of the "handshakes at a party" problem. Instead of summing connections, notice a bijection: every handshake corresponds to a unique choice of 2 people. Counting handshakes is simply choosing `N` choose 2.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Map complex sets to simple sets via one-to-one correspondence.

• Proves equality of size: if bijection exists,
`|X| = |Y|`.

• Standard technique for advanced interview puzzles.

revisionCards.title: Bijection Thinking

revisionCards.explanation: **Double Counting** is a proof and counting technique that calculates the size of a set in two different ways to establish an algebraic identity.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Dual angles: By counting the elements of a set or relationships in a bipartite graph from two different perspectives, the two resulting formulas must be equal.

• Useful for proving combinatorial identities without algebraic expansion.

• Helps find averages or verify structural constraints in networks.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • In a grid of people, summing the row counts must equal summing the column counts. If you count the total edges in a graph by summing degrees, you get `2 * Edges` because every edge has two endpoints. This is double counting.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Count from two perspectives (e.g. rows vs columns).

• Establishes identities:
`Result A = Result B`.

• Prevents missing elements in complex matrices.

revisionCards.title: Double Counting

revisionCards.explanation: The **Pigeonhole Principle (PHP)** states that if `n` items are put into `m` containers and `n > m`, at least one container must hold more than one item.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Collision proofs: Generalized PHP states that if `n` items are put into `m` containers, at least one container must contain at least `ceil(n/m)` items.

• Non-constructive: It proves an item exists with a certain property without telling you which one it is or how to find it.

• Used to guarantee worst-case thresholds in data structures, hashing collisions, and logical puzzles.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • In a room of 367 people, at least two people must share a birthday because there are only 366 possible birth dates. The birth dates are the pigeonholes, the people are the pigeons.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• If pigeons > holes, at least one hole has multiple pigeons.

• Generalized form: at least one hole contains `ceil(n/m)` items.

• Used to guarantee collisions or matching properties.

revisionCards.title: Pigeonhole Principle

revisionCards.explanation: Calculate the number of paths between two points on a grid, moving only in restricted directions (e.g. right and up).

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Identify the grid dimensions. To move from `(0,0)` to `(X,Y)`, you must take exactly `X` right steps (`R`) and `Y` up steps (`U`).

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: The total number of steps is `X + Y`. Any path is a sequence of `X` R's and `Y` U's.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body:
Calculate the arrangements of these steps (selection of slots for R): `(X + Y) choose X` or
`(X + Y) choose Y`.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: The number of paths from `(0,0)` to `(4,3)` is `(4 + 3) choose 4 = 7C4 = 35` paths.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body:
If you must pass through an intermediate point `(A,B)`, the total paths is:

`[Paths(0,0 ➔ A,B)] * [Paths(A,B ➔ X,Y)]`.

revisionCards.title: Counting Paths

revisionCards.explanation: Calculate the total number of rectangles or squares contained within a grid of size `M x N`.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Identify the grid lines: An `M x N` grid of squares has `M + 1` horizontal lines and `N + 1` vertical lines.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: To form any rectangle, you must choose 2 horizontal lines and 2 vertical lines.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body:
Calculate the combinations of choosing these lines: `(M + 1) choose 2` times
`(N + 1) choose 2`.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: A standard `8x8` chessboard contains `9C2 * 9C2 = 36 * 36 = 1296` rectangles.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: To find only *squares* in an `N x N` grid, sum the squares of the dimensions: `Σ k^2` from `k = 1` to `N` (for 8x8 chessboard, this is `1^2 + 2^2 + ... + 8^2 = 204` squares).

revisionCards.title: Counting Grids

revisionCards.explanation: Counting probability outcomes scales combinatorics to calculate probability numerator and denominator terms.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Scaling events: Combines combinations with multiplication rules. The probability of getting a specific hand in Poker is:
`Favorable Hands / Total Hands`.

• Denominator: Total possible outcomes (e.g. choosing 5 cards from 52 is `52C5 = 2,598,960`).

• Numerator: Favorable ways to choose the target pattern (e.g. Full House: choose card rank for triplet, choose 3 cards of that rank, choose rank for pair, choose 2 cards of that rank).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Break down the selection into sequential stages. For a Full House: select triplet rank (`13C1`), select 3 suits (`4C3`), select pair rank (`12C1`), select 2 suits (`4C2`). Multiply all terms to get the numerator.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Calculate total sample space as the denominator.

• Break down numerator selection into sequential combinatorics.

• Verify that no cards are counted in multiple roles.

revisionCards.title: Counting Probability Outcomes

revisionCards.explanation: **Optimal Play** is a strategy in game theory where a player selects moves that guarantee the best possible outcome regardless of the opponent's choices.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Rational choices: Assumes both players are rational and seek to maximize their payoffs.

• In zero-sum games, one player's gain is the other's loss. Optimal play matches the Nash Equilibrium where neither player wants to change strategy.

• Often solved using backward induction: working backward from the end states of the game.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • If you play a game where you can take 1 or 2 coins, and the person who takes the last coin wins, if there are 3 coins left, your optimal move is to take 2 because it leaves the opponent with 1 coin (forcing their loss).

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Optimal play assumes perfect opponent rationality.

• Matches the Nash Equilibrium in zero-sum games.

• Solved by working backward from end-game states.

revisionCards.title: Optimal Play Concept

revisionCards.explanation: A state in a game is a **Winning State** (P-position) or a **Losing State** (N-position) based on who can force a win from that position.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• State classifications: Losing State (L) is a position where every valid move leads to a winning state for the opponent.

• Winning State (W): A position from which there exists at least one valid move leading to a losing state for the opponent.

• Terminal states (where no moves are left) are classified as losing states under normal play rules (the player who cannot move loses).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • To solve coin/matchstick games, start at state 0 (Losing state because you cannot move). State 1 is a Winning state (move to 0). State 2 is a Winning state (move to 0). State 3 is a Losing state because all moves (taking 1 or 2) lead to Winning states (2 or 1).

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Losing state: All moves lead to winning states.

• Winning state: At least one move leads to a losing state.

• Analyze states from the terminal state 0 backwards.

revisionCards.title: Winning and Losing States

revisionCards.explanation: Calculate winning moves and states for a game with a single pile of items where you can remove a restricted number of items.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Identify game rules: A pile has `N` items. You can remove between 1 and `M` items per turn. The player who cannot move loses.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: Map the losing states. If `N` is a multiple of `M + 1`, it is a losing state (P-position). If it is not, it is a winning state (N-position).

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body: Determine strategy: If you are at a winning state (not a multiple of `M + 1`), remove `N mod (M + 1)` items to force the pile size to a multiple of `M + 1` (a losing state for the opponent).

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: For `N = 10` and `M = 3`, the losing states are multiples of 4: `{0, 4, 8}`. Since 10 is not a multiple, it is a winning state; your optimal move is to take `10 mod 4 = 2` items.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: Always reduce the pile size to the nearest multiple of `M + 1` on your turn.

revisionCards.title: Single Pile Nim

revisionCards.explanation: Determine if a multi-pile Nim game is a winning or losing state, and find the optimal move using the Nim Sum.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body:
Identify pile sizes: e.g. three piles of size `3, 4, 5`. Convert these sizes to binary: `3 = 011_2`, `4 = 100_2`,
`5 = 101_2`.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body:
Calculate the **Nim Sum** (XOR sum of pile sizes):
`011 XOR 100 XOR 101 = 010_2 = 2`. Since the Nim Sum is not zero, this is a winning state.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body: Find the optimal move to reduce the Nim Sum to zero. Find a pile where `Pile XOR NimSum < Pile`. Pile 3 (`3 XOR 2 = 1 < 3`), or Pile 5 (`5 XOR 2 = 7 > 5`), or Pile 4 (`4 XOR 2 = 6 > 4`). Reduce Pile 1 (size 3) to 1 (remove 2 items). New sizes: `1, 4, 5`.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: Optimal move: Remove 2 items from the pile of size 3. New sizes `1, 4, 5` have Nim Sum `001 XOR 100 XOR 101 = 0` (losing state for opponent).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: If the XOR sum is non-zero, you can always make a single move to set the XOR sum to zero, securing your win.

revisionCards.title: Multi Pile Nim

revisionCards.explanation: Solve games where players take turns removing coins from a line under adjacency constraints.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Identify the rules: There are `N` coins in a line. A player can remove any 1 coin or any 2 adjacent coins. The player who takes the last coin wins.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: Use **Symmetry Strategy**. If the opponent removes coins, mirror their actions relative to the center of the board.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body: Set up the win: In round 1, if `N` is even, remove the 2 central coins (splitting the line into two equal segments of size `(N-2)/2`). If `N` is odd, remove the 1 central coin. Now, whatever the opponent does to one side, mirror it on the other side.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: Player 1 wins by taking the central coin(s) in the first turn and mirroring the opponent's moves thereafter.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: Symmetry guarantees that if you copy the opponent's moves on an identical independent half of the game, you will always get the final move.

revisionCards.title: Coin Removal Games

revisionCards.explanation: Solve matchstick removal puzzles, finding the winning strategy for the first player.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Identify the rules: There are 21 matchsticks. You can remove 1, 2, 3, or 4 matchsticks per turn. The player who takes the last matchstick loses (Misere play).

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: Work backward from the end. You want to force the opponent to take the last matchstick, which means you want to leave them with exactly 1 matchstick (losing state).

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body: Establish target sizes: To leave 1, you want to leave `1`, `6`, `11`, `16` matchsticks on your turns (intervals of `M + 1 = 5`).

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: If the game starts with 21: since `21 = 5*4 + 1`, the starting state is a losing state if you go first. If the opponent goes first, whatever they take `k`, you take `5 - k` to force the count to 16, 11, 6, and finally 1.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: Complimentary taking: If the step size constraint is `M`, group turns into units of `M + 1` items.

revisionCards.title: Matchstick Games

revisionCards.explanation: **Backward Induction** is a reasoning process that works backward from the end of a decision tree to determine optimal sequential choices.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Retrograde reasoning: Starts at terminal nodes (the final moves of the game) where outcomes are known.

• Determines what the last player would do, then moves up one level to determine what the second-to-last player would do, assuming rational play.

• Prunes suboptimal branches, resolving subgame perfect equilibria.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • In the "100 Pirates" coin splitting game, look at what happens if only 2 pirates remain. Pirate 2 will take everything and vote yes. Knowing this, work backward to see what offers Pirate 3, 4, and 5 must make to secure votes.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Work backward from final terminal states.

• Assumes perfect future rationality of all players.

• Essential for solving finite sequential games.

revisionCards.title: Backward Induction

revisionCards.explanation: **Minimax** is a decision rule that minimizes the maximum possible loss, commonly used in zero-sum two-player games.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Adversarial evaluations: Max Player seeks to maximize their payoff. Min Player seeks to minimize the Max player's payoff.

• Minimax value: The optimal score reached when both players play perfectly. Max chooses the move that yields the maximum of the minimums.

• Implemented in game AI (like chess engines) using alpha-beta pruning to speed up node searches.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • When looking at your choices, assume that whatever move you make, the opponent will make the worst possible reply for you. Thus, choose the move whose worst-case reply is the most tolerable.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Minimize your maximum possible loss.

• Assumes opponent always makes their best move.

• Forms the basis of zero-sum game algorithms.

revisionCards.title: Minimax Thinking

revisionCards.explanation: Identify game theory patterns in interviews, such as symmetry, modular invariants, and subtraction sets.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Interviewer strategies: Symmetry splits the game board into identical mirrored halves, allowing the second player to win by duplicating moves.

• Modular invariants: Winning states tied to `N mod (M + 1)`. The player forces this remainder to zero at each step.

• SG (Sprague-Grundy) Theorem: Assigning Grundy values (mex of next states) to states, converting any impartial game into an equivalent pile of Nim.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • If a game involves removing items, check if the moves allow you to maintain a modular invariant. If they do, your strategy is to keep the state at `0 mod k`.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Look for board symmetries to copy opponent moves.

• Modular invariants resolve taking games.

• Sprague-Grundy theorem converts impartial games to Nim.

revisionCards.title: Game Theory Interview Patterns

revisionCards.explanation: A classic game show puzzle: You choose one of three doors. Behind one is a car, and behind the others are goats. The host opens a goat door and asks if you want to switch. Should you?

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body:
Identify prior probabilities: The probability that your initial choice has the car is `1/3`. The probability that the car is behind one of the other two doors is:
`2/3`.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: Analyze the host's action: The host *must* open a door containing a goat. This action is not random; it is dependent on your initial choice and the location of the car.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body:
Evaluate switching: The host's action concentrates the entire `2/3` probability of the other two doors into the single remaining unopened door. The probability of your initial door remains
`1/3`.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body:
You should switch. Switching gives you a `2/3` probability of winning the car, while keeping your initial door gives only
`1/3`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: If you switch, you only lose if your initial choice was correct (which happens `1/3` of the time). So switching wins `2/3` of the time.

revisionCards.title: Monty Hall Problem

revisionCards.explanation: 100 prisoners must find their own numbers in 100 closed boxes. Each can open 50 boxes. If one fails, all die. Find the optimal strategy.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Identify the problem: If prisoners choose randomly, the probability of survival is `(1/2)^100 ≈ 0` (effectively zero).

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: Define the **Loop Strategy**: Every prisoner starts by opening the box labeled with their own number. If they find their number, they succeed. If not, the box contains another number `K`; they proceed to open box `K`, and repeat this cycle.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body: Analyze the cycles: This strategy links boxes into closed loops. A prisoner succeeds if their number is in a loop of size ≤ 50. Since all prisoners in a loop share the same loop size, the entire team succeeds if the longest loop in the box arrangement is ≤ 50.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: Using the loop strategy, the probability that the longest loop is ≤ 50 is `1 - ln(2) ≈ 31.18%`. This increases survival rate from near-zero to 31.18%.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body:
Sum of loop sizes: The probability of a random permutation having no cycle of length > 50 is `1 - Σ (1/k)` from `k = 51` to:
`100 ≈ 31.18%`.

revisionCards.title: 100 Prisoners Problem

revisionCards.explanation: A group of people with blue eyes and brown eyes live on an island. If they discover they have blue eyes, they must leave at midnight. A visitor announces: "At least one of you has blue eyes." If there are N blue-eyed people, what happens?

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Apply mathematical induction. Case `N = 1`: The single blue-eyed person looks around, sees no one else with blue eyes, realizes they must be the one, and leaves on night 1.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: Case `N = 2`: Person A and B have blue eyes. On day 1, A sees B has blue eyes and expects B to leave on night 1. But B does not leave (because B sees A). On day 2, A realizes B didn't leave because B saw someone else with blue eyes. Since B only sees A, A realizes they have blue eyes. Both A and B leave on night 2.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body: Generalize: If there are `N` blue-eyed people, nothing happens for `N - 1` days. On the `N-th` day, all `N` blue-eyed people realize their color and leave together at midnight.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: All `N` blue-eyed people leave on the `N-th` night after the announcement.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: Common knowledge creation: The announcement made the existence of blue eyes common knowledge, allowing the synchronization of days as indicators of eye counts.

revisionCards.title: Blue Eyes Puzzle

revisionCards.explanation: You have 1000 bottles of wine, and exactly one is poisoned. A poisoned bottle kills a rat in 24 hours. What is the minimum number of rats needed to find the poisoned bottle in 24 hours?

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Identify the binary nature of test results: A rat either dies (1) or lives (0). Thus, `R` rats can represent `2^R` unique states.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: Map states to bottles: We need `2^R ≥ 1000` to uniquely identify each bottle. The smallest integer is `R = 10` (since `2^10 = 1024`).

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body: Design the testing matrix: Number the bottles 1 to 1000 in binary (10 digits). Rat `i` drinks from all bottles that have a `1` in the `i-th` digit of their binary code. After 24 hours, if rat `i` dies, write a `1` in the `i-th` digit of the secret code; else write `0`.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: The minimum number of rats needed is `10`. The binary code of the dead rats points directly to the poisoned bottle.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: Binary search projection: Every rat acts as a bit in the binary representation of the target bottle number.

revisionCards.title: Poisoned Bottle Puzzle

revisionCards.explanation: Four people must cross a bridge at night. A max of two can cross at a time, carrying a torch. Crossing times are: A (1 min), B (2 min), C (5 min), D (10 min). What is the minimum time needed for all to cross?

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Avoid the greedy choice trap: Crossing the two fastest (A + B = 2 min) and returning the fastest (A = 1 min) to bring the slow ones (C + D) back results in `2 + 1 + 10 + 1 + 2 = 16` min. We can do better.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: Group the slow crossers: We want C and D to cross together so their crossing times overlap: `C + D = 10` min. But we need a fast person already on the other side to bring the torch back.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body: Design optimal steps: Step 1: A and B cross (2 min). Step 2: A returns with torch (1 min). Step 3: C and D cross (10 min). Step 4: B returns with torch (2 min). Step 5: A and B cross (2 min). Sum: `2 + 1 + 10 + 2 + 2 = 17` min.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: The minimum time needed for all four to cross the bridge is `17` minutes.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: Slower overlap rule: To send two slow items `S1` and `S2` together, use two fast items `F1` and `F2` to manage the torch returns.

revisionCards.title: Bridge and Torch Puzzle

revisionCards.explanation: Three players stand in a circle with a red or blue hat. They see others' hats but not their own. They must simultaneously guess or pass. Team wins if at least one guesses right and no one guesses wrong. What is the optimal strategy?

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Identify target: We want to maximize the probability of winning. If they guess randomly, win rate is low. We want to coordinate guesses.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: Look for asymmetry: If a player sees two hats of the *same* color, they guess the *opposite* color. If they see different colors, they pass.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body: Analyze outcomes: Case 1: Hats are all same color (RRR, BBB), happens `2/8` of the time. Everyone sees same colors and guesses opposite, so all three guess wrong (Loss). Case 2: Hats are mixed (e.g. RRB), happens `6/8` of the time. The player with B sees two R's and guesses B (correct!). The two players with R see R and B, so they pass. Team wins!

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: Optimal strategy: Guess the opposite color if you see two identical hat colors, else pass. This yields a `6/8 = 75%` win rate.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: Hamming code geometry: The strategy partitions the 8 states into 2 losing centers and 6 winning neighbors.

revisionCards.title: Hat Color Puzzle

revisionCards.explanation: You stand before two doors. One leads to freedom, the other to execution. Guarding the doors are twin guards: one tells the truth, the other lies. You can ask only one question to one guard. What question do you ask?

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Understand the goal: We want to ask a question that yields the same answer regardless of whether we ask the truth-teller or the liar.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: Combine the operations: A truth (T) combined with a lie (L) always results in a lie (`T * L = L`). We must ask about the other guard's answer.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body: Formulate the question: Ask guard 1: "Which door would your twin say leads to freedom?"

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: Whichever door they point to, choose the **other** door. The truth-teller will tell you the liar's lie (pointing to the bad door); the liar will lie about the truth-teller's truth (pointing to the bad door). Both point to the bad door.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: Double operation negation: Asking guard A what guard B would say always applies a negation step, guaranteeing a false answer.

revisionCards.title: Two Doors Puzzle

revisionCards.explanation: Solve puzzles where characters represent truth-tellers, liars, or random answerers, using logical deduction.

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Identify statements: You meet three people, A, B, and C. One is a truth-teller, one is a liar, and one answers randomly. A says: "B is the liar." B says: "C is the liar."

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: Map logical consistency: If A is the truth-teller, then B is indeed the liar. If B is the liar, then C is not the liar (C is the random one). This state is consistent.

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body: Verify other cases: If B is the truth-teller, A must be the liar. If A is the liar, A's statement is false, meaning B is not the liar (consistent). C is the random one.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: Deduce identity by tracking contradiction loops. A truth-teller's statement must match reality; a liar's must negate it.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: Look for claims of "I am a liar". A truth-teller cannot say this (contradiction), and a liar cannot say this (contradiction). Thus, only a random answerer can claim to be a liar.

revisionCards.title: Truth Teller and Liar

revisionCards.explanation: A farmer must cross a river with a wolf, a goat, and a cabbage. His boat can hold only him and one other item. wolf eats goat, or goat eats cabbage if left unattended. How does he cross?

slides.headline: Step 1
slides.body: Identify the constraint: The farmer must keep goat-wolf and goat-cabbage separated. The goat is the common link; it must be moved first.

slides.headline: Step 2
slides.body: Step 1: Take goat across. Return alone. Step 2: Take wolf across. Return with goat (to prevent wolf eating goat).

slides.headline: Step 3
slides.body: Step 3: Leave goat, take cabbage across. Return alone. Step 4: Take goat across.

slides.headline: Final Answer
slides.body: Move goat ➔ Return empty ➔ Move wolf ➔ Return goat ➔ Move cabbage ➔ Return empty ➔ Move goat.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Shortcut
slides.body: Never leave the goat with either the wolf or the cabbage. Use the goat as a return weight to break conflicts.

revisionCards.title: River Crossing Puzzle

revisionCards.explanation: Systematize puzzle-solving in interviews by mapping constraints, assumptions, and contradiction states.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Reasoning platforms: Constraint mapping writes down the rules of the system as logical formulas.

• Assumption testing: Assume a node state (e.g. "A is the liar") and propagate results. If a contradiction occurs, the assumption is false.

• Symmetry reduction: Reduce the number of cases by grouping symmetric configurations.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Interviewers assess your *thinking process*. Do not guess. State your assumptions, trace their implications step-by-step, and explain how you eliminate invalid branches.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Write out constraints explicitly.

• Use proof by contradiction for assumptions.

• Group symmetric options to save time.

revisionCards.title: Logical Deduction Framework

revisionCards.explanation: The **Mean** (arithmetic average) is the sum of a set of values divided by the number of values.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Formula distributions: Formula is `μ = (Σ x_i) / N` for a population, and `x̄ = (Σ x_i) / n` for a sample.

• Highly sensitive to outliers. A single extreme value can shift the mean significantly, misrepresenting the center of the distribution.

• Represents the physical center of mass of the data distribution.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • If 9 people earn $50,000 and 1 person earns $1,000,000, the mean salary is `$145,000`. This average does not represent what most people earn due to the outlier.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Mean = Sum / Count.

• Highly sensitive to outlier values.

• Matches the expected value of a uniform sample.

revisionCards.title: Mean

revisionCards.explanation: The **Median** is the middle value of a data set sorted in ascending or descending order.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Sorted center: If the number of data points `N` is odd, the median is the value at position `(N + 1) / 2`. If `N` is even, it is the average of values at `N/2` and
`N/2 + 1`.

• Outlier resistant: Extreme values at the ends of the sorted list do not affect the median.

• Splits the data distribution into two equal halves (50th percentile).

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Intuition
slides.body: • Using the salary example: sorted salaries has $50k at the center. The median is `$50,000`, which represents the typical salary of the group much better than the mean of `$145,000`.

slides.headline: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
• Median is the sorted middle value.

• Outlier resistant (robust metric).

• Splits the distribution into two 50% halves.

revisionCards.title: Median

revisionCards.explanation: The **Mode** is the value that appears most frequently in a data set.

slides.headline: 💡 Explanation
slides.body:
• Frequency distributions: A data set can have one mode (unimodal), multiple modes (bimodal/multimodal), or no mode at all if all values are unique.
