• Notation: Written using the curly delta symbol: `(\partial f) / (\partial x)`.

• **Student Shorthand**: Measures rates of change along a single coordinate axis.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Formula:
`(\partial f(x, y)) / (\partial x) = \lim_{h -> 0} (f(x+h, y) - f(x, y)) / (h)`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: Slicing a multi-dimensional surface with a plane parallel to the target coordinate axis, measuring the slope of the resulting curve.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body:
• Find partial derivatives of `f(x, y) = x^2 y + 3y^2`:

• `(\partial f) / (\partial x) = 2xy`,
`(\partial f) / (\partial y) = x^2 + 6y`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How are partial derivatives used in backpropagation?"

• **A**: They calculate how the total loss changes with respect to individual weights, treating all other parameter values in the network as constants.

revisionCards.title: Gradients
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Vector of partial derivatives of a multi-variable function.

Direction: Points in the direction of steepest ascent of the function.

Magnitude: Measures the rate of change in that direction.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Vector of partial derivatives of a multi-variable function.

• Direction: Points in the direction of steepest ascent of the function.

• Magnitude: Measures the rate of change in that direction.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Formula:
`∇ f(x, y) = [ (\partial f) / (\partial x), (\partial f) / (\partial y) ]`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: The gradient is the steepest uphill vector pointing from a coordinate position on a 3D landscape.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How does gradient descent use the gradient?"

• **A**: To minimize loss, parameters are updated in the *negative* direction of the gradient (direction of steepest descent): `w arrow w - \eta ∇ L`.

revisionCards.title: Chain Rule
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Formula to calculate derivatives of nested composite functions.

Composition: If `z = f(y)` and `y = g(x)`, then `z = f(g(x))`.

**Student Shorthand**: Multiplies rate-of-change fractions along the function chain.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Formula to calculate derivatives of nested composite functions.

• Composition: If `z = f(y)` and `y = g(x)`, then `z = f(g(x))`.

• **Student Shorthand**: Multiplies rate-of-change fractions along the function chain.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body: • Formula: `dz / dx = dz / dy * dy / dx`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: Think of nested functions as linked gears: the rate of change of the last gear is the product of gear ratio changes along the chain.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why is the Chain Rule crucial for Deep Learning?"

• **A**: Backpropagation is the chain rule applied iteratively from the output layer back to the input layer to compute parameter gradients across hidden layers.

revisionCards.title: Gradient Descent
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Optimization algorithm that iteratively updates parameter values in the negative gradient direction to find loss function minimums.

Learning Rate (`\eta`): Scalar controlling the step size of parameter updates.

Shorthand: Updates weights iteratively using `w arrow w - \eta ∇ L(w)`.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Optimization algorithm that iteratively updates parameter values in the negative gradient direction to find loss function minimums.

• Learning Rate (`\eta`): Scalar controlling the step size of parameter updates.

• Shorthand: Updates weights iteratively using `w arrow w - \eta ∇ L(w)`.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Update Rule:
`w^{(t+1)} = w^{(t)} - \eta ∇ L(w^{(t)})`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: Walking down a foggy hill by feeling the slope under your feet and taking steps downhill.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How does learning rate selection impact convergence?"

• **A**: An overly large learning rate causes updates to overshoot the minimum, leading to divergence. An overly small learning rate makes convergence extremely slow.

revisionCards.title: Missing Values
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Absent values in variables, classified as MCAR (completely at random), MAR (at random), or MNAR (not at random).

Impact: Most ML algorithms fail if inputs contain missing values (NaN/None).

**Student Shorthand**: MNAR is the most dangerous because the missingness itself contains information (e.g. high-income users refusing to report salary).

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Absent values in variables, classified as MCAR (completely at random), MAR (at random), or MNAR (not at random).

• Impact: Most ML algorithms fail if inputs contain missing values (NaN/None).

• **Student Shorthand**: MNAR is the most dangerous because the missingness itself contains information (e.g. high-income users refusing to report salary).

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Locate missing fields using mask checks.

• Apply removal strategies (dropping rows/columns) or imputation strategies (replacing with mean, median, mode, or model-based estimates).

• Verify if imputation shifts variance or introduces skew.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Missing values are like holes in a water pipe. You can block them by cutting out the pipe section (dropping data) or filling them with putty (imputation).

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "When is mean imputation bad?"

• **A**: Mean imputation is bad if the column contains outliers or is highly skewed, because it changes the distribution shape and reduces variance artificially. Use median or mode imputation instead.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • MCAR vs MNAR: MCAR means missingness is independent of any values. MNAR means missingness depends on the unobserved value itself, requiring domain-specific handling.

revisionCards.title: Outliers
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Data points that lie far away from the overall pattern of the rest of the dataset.

Detection: Common statistical methods include Z-score thresholding (>3 or <-3) and IQR scaling (`1.5 * IQR`).

Sensitivity: Distance-based models (KNN, K-Means) and linear regressions are highly sensitive to outliers.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Data points that lie far away from the overall pattern of the rest of the dataset.

• Detection: Common statistical methods include Z-score thresholding (>3 or <-3) and IQR scaling (`1.5 * IQR`).

• Sensitivity: Distance-based models (KNN, K-Means) and linear regressions are highly sensitive to outliers.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Z-score check: Flag points where `Z = (x - μ) / (σ) > 3`.

• IQR check: Flag points outside range
`[Q1 - 1.5 * IQR, Q3 + 1.5 * IQR]`.

• Handle by trimming (dropping), capping (winsorization), or applying mathematical transformations (log transform).

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: An outlier is like a giant entering a room of average-height people. The average height shifts dramatically, but the median height remains unchanged.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How do you handle outliers in linear regression?"

• **A**: 1. Remove them if they are measurement errors. 2. Cap them using winsorization. 3. Use robust cost functions like Huber Loss instead of Mean Squared Error.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Anomaly detection vs Outliers: Outliers are noise/anomalies in existing datasets. Anomaly detection is the task of identifying novel, unexpected patterns in streaming data.

revisionCards.title: Encoding
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Converting categorical text labels into numerical values so ML algorithms can process them.

**Types**: Label Encoding (integer maps for ordinal data) and One-Hot Encoding (binary columns for nominal data).

**Student Shorthand**: One-hot encoding nominal variables with high cardinality creates massive, sparse columns, which slows down models.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Converting categorical text labels into numerical values so ML algorithms can process them.

• **Types**: Label Encoding (integer maps for ordinal data) and One-Hot Encoding (binary columns for nominal data).

• **Student Shorthand**: One-hot encoding nominal variables with high cardinality creates massive, sparse columns, which slows down models.

slides.headline: Python Code
slides.body: Review the clean, highly optimized implementation below:
slides.code:
import pandas as pd
# Nominal categorical data
df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["NY", "LA", "NY"]})
# One-Hot Encoding
ohe_df = pd.get_dummies(df, columns=["city"], drop_first=True)
# Output has: city_NY (binary column, LA dropped to prevent collinearity)

slides.headline: 💡 Code Breakdown
slides.body: • Line 4: Converts nominal strings into binary columns. Setting `drop_first=True` drops the first class column, preventing multicollinearity (dummy variable trap).

slides.headline: 🧠 Performance Footprint
slides.body:
• Time Complexity: O(R * C) where R is rows and C is unique labels.

• Space Complexity: O(R * C) memory expansion for one-hot matrices.

slides.headline: 🧠 Common Interview Questions
slides.body:
• Gotcha: Label encoding nominal data (e.g. mapping "LA" to 0, "NY" to 1) tricks models into assuming mathematical order (NY > LA), which degrades linear/distance model performance.

• Gotcha: High cardinality nominal features (e.g. Zip codes) should be encoded using target encoding or frequency encoding instead of one-hot encoding.

revisionCards.title: Scaling
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Transforming feature ranges so they have similar scales.

Why it matters: Bypasses scaling dominance where large-scale features (e.g. salary) dominate small-scale features (e.g. age) in distance calculations.

Standardization: Scaling features to have a mean of 0 and variance of 1.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Transforming feature ranges so they have similar scales.

• Why it matters: Bypasses scaling dominance where large-scale features (e.g. salary) dominate small-scale features (e.g. age) in distance calculations.

• Standardization: Scaling features to have a mean of 0 and variance of 1.

slides.headline: Python Code
slides.body: Review the clean, highly optimized implementation below:
slides.code:
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
scaler = StandardScaler()
# Fit on train, transform both train and test
scaled_train = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
scaled_test = scaler.transform(X_test)

slides.headline: 💡 Code Breakdown
slides.body: • Line 3-4: `fit_transform` calculates training mean and variance, then scales training data. Test data is scaled using the *same* training statistics to prevent data leakage.

slides.headline: 🧠 Performance Footprint
slides.body:
• Time Complexity: Fit: O(R * C) | Transform: O(R * C).

• Space Complexity: O(R * C) for scaled output arrays.

slides.headline: 🧠 Common Interview Questions
slides.body:
• Gotcha: Standard scaling assumes data is normally distributed. If data contains extreme outliers, use `RobustScaler` (which scales using median and IQR) instead.

• Gotcha: Scaling target variable `Y` is rarely required, but scaling inputs is vital for gradient descent speed and distance model correctness.

revisionCards.title: Normalization
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Scaling features to a fixed range, typically between 0 and 1.

Formula: Min-Max scaling:

`x_{scaled} = (x - x_{\min}) / (x_{\max) - x_{\min}}`.

**Student Shorthand**: Ideal for algorithms that do not assume normal distributions (e.g. neural networks or KNN).

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Scaling features to a fixed range, typically between 0 and 1.

• Formula: Min-Max scaling:
`x_{scaled} = (x - x_{\min}) / (x_{\max) - x_{\min}}`.

• **Student Shorthand**: Ideal for algorithms that do not assume normal distributions (e.g. neural networks or KNN).

slides.headline: Python Code
slides.body: Review the clean, highly optimized implementation below:
slides.code:
from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler
scaler = MinMaxScaler(feature_range=(0, 1))
# Apply Min-Max scaling
X_train_norm = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_norm = scaler.transform(X_test)

slides.headline: 💡 Code Breakdown
slides.body: • Line 3-4: Fits parameters (`X_{min}` and `X_{max}`) on the training set, then scales both datasets.

slides.headline: 🧠 Performance Footprint
slides.body:
• Time Complexity: O(R * C) operations.

• Space Complexity: O(R * C) array allocations.

slides.headline: 🧠 Common Interview Questions
slides.body:
• Gotcha: Outliers ruin min-max scaling because they stretch `X_{max}` artificially, compressing normal values into a tiny range (e.g. 0.01 to 0.05).

• Gotcha: Min-Max normalization does not handle values outside the training range during test time gracefully. They will map outside the [0, 1] range.

revisionCards.title: Train Test Split
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Splitting a dataset into distinct sets: training (to fit models) and testing (to evaluate performance).

Stratification: Ensuring split sets contain the same proportion of target classes as the original dataset.

Data Leakage: Preprocessing (scaling, imputation) must occur *after* splitting, using statistics calculated solely from the training set.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Splitting a dataset into distinct sets: training (to fit models) and testing (to evaluate performance).

• Stratification: Ensuring split sets contain the same proportion of target classes as the original dataset.

• Data Leakage: Preprocessing (scaling, imputation) must occur *after* splitting, using statistics calculated solely from the training set.

slides.headline: Python Code
slides.body: Review the clean, highly optimized implementation below:
slides.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
# Stratified split for class balance
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42
)

slides.headline: 💡 Code Breakdown
slides.body: • Line 3-4: Splits data with 20% allocated for testing. Setting `stratify=y` guarantees that both train and test sets have the same ratio of class outcomes.

slides.headline: 🧠 Performance Footprint
slides.body:
• Time Complexity: O(R) row copying.

• Space Complexity: O(R * C) memory allocation.

slides.headline: 🧠 Common Interview Questions
slides.body:
• Gotcha: Forgetting to set a static `random_state` causes the split to change on every execution, making model evaluation results inconsistent and hard to reproduce.

• Gotcha: For time-series data, never use random splitting. It leaks future information into past predictions. Use sequential splits (`TimeSeriesSplit`) instead.

revisionCards.title: EDA Workflow
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Systematically analyzing datasets to summarize their main characteristics, identify patterns, and find anomalies.

Steps: 1. Shape and type inspection. 2. Summary stats. 3. Missing/Outlier detection. 4. Univariate & Multivariate visualization.

**Student Shorthand**: Never build models without performing EDA. It determines your feature engineering and algorithm selection strategies.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Systematically analyzing datasets to summarize their main characteristics, identify patterns, and find anomalies.

• Steps: 1. Shape and type inspection. 2. Summary stats. 3. Missing/Outlier detection. 4. Univariate & Multivariate visualization.

• **Student Shorthand**: Never build models without performing EDA. It determines your feature engineering and algorithm selection strategies.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Run `.info()`, `.describe()`, and `.isna().sum()` to get a quick summary of the data.

• Visualize distributions using histograms and box plots.

• Analyze variables using scatter plots and correlation heatmaps.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: EDA is like inspecting a second-hand car before buying it: checking for rust, checking oil levels, and taking it for a test drive.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "What are the core metrics checked in numerical columns during EDA?"

• **A**: Check the range (min/max), skewness, standard deviation, and count of missing values.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Data Profiling: Automating EDA workflows using libraries like `ydata-profiling` to generate HTML reports. Great for quick checks, but manual deep dives are still needed.

revisionCards.title: Univariate Analysis
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Analyzing the distribution, central tendency, and spread of a single variable in isolation.

Numerical: Analyzed using histograms, density plots (KDE), box plots, and summary statistics.

Categorical: Analyzed using bar charts, pie charts, and frequency tables.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Analyzing the distribution, central tendency, and spread of a single variable in isolation.

• Numerical: Analyzed using histograms, density plots (KDE), box plots, and summary statistics.

• Categorical: Analyzed using bar charts, pie charts, and frequency tables.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Extract a single target column.

• Compute descriptive statistics (mean, median, standard deviation, skewness).

• Plot the distribution (histogram for continuous data, bar chart for categorical data).

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Univariate analysis is like examining each candidate's resume individually before comparing them.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How do you identify skewness in univariate analysis?"

• **A**: Compare the mean and median: if Mean > Median, it is right-skewed; if Mean < Median, it is left-skewed. Check visual symmetry on a histogram.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Constant Features: Columns with zero variance (every row has the same value). Identify and drop them during univariate analysis since they add no predictive power.

revisionCards.title: Bivariate Analysis
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Analyzing the relationship or correlation between two variables.

Num-Num: Analyzed using scatter plots, line plots, and correlation coefficients.

Cat-Num: Analyzed using box plots, violin plots, and grouped bar charts.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Analyzing the relationship or correlation between two variables.

• Num-Num: Analyzed using scatter plots, line plots, and correlation coefficients.

• Cat-Num: Analyzed using box plots, violin plots, and grouped bar charts.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Select two variables of interest (e.g. age vs. salary).

• Choose the appropriate visualization based on their data types (scatter plot for numeric-numeric).

• Calculate statistical measures of association (e.g. Pearson correlation or t-test).

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Bivariate analysis is like studying the dynamics between two dance partners: how their movements change relative to each other.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How do you analyze the relationship between a categorical variable and a numerical variable?"

• **A**: Use grouped box plots or violin plots to show the distribution of the numerical variable across each category.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Simpson's Paradox: A trend appearing in different groups of data can reverse when the groups are combined. Always segment your bivariate analysis to check for hidden confounding variables.

revisionCards.title: Correlation Analysis
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Measuring the statistical relationship between variables.

**Types**: Pearson (linear relationships), Spearman (rank-based monotonic relationships), Kendall (ordinal association).

Correlation Range: Scaled from -1 to +1.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Measuring the statistical relationship between variables.

• **Types**: Pearson (linear relationships), Spearman (rank-based monotonic relationships), Kendall (ordinal association).

• Correlation Range: Scaled from -1 to +1.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Compute the correlation matrix for all numerical variables.

• Visualize coefficients using a correlation heatmap.

• Flag features with high mutual correlation (>0.8) to address multicollinearity.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: High correlation is like two clocks ticking in sync: they move together, but one clock does not cause the other to tick.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "When is Spearman rank correlation preferred over Pearson?"

• **A**: When the relationship between variables is monotonic but non-linear (e.g. exponential growth), or when the dataset contains significant outliers that distort linear calculations.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Spurious Correlation: Variables showing high correlation due to pure coincidence or a shared hidden factor (e.g., ice cream sales and shark attacks both increase during summer).

revisionCards.title: Machine Learning Overview
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Algorithmic systems that learn patterns directly from data to make predictions, rather than relying on hardcoded rules.

**Types**: Supervised (labeled outputs), Unsupervised (unlabeled structure), Reinforcement (feedback loop).

**Student Shorthand**: Replaces standard programming (`data + rules = answers`) with learning (`data + answers = rules`).

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Algorithmic systems that learn patterns directly from data to make predictions, rather than relying on hardcoded rules.

• **Types**: Supervised (labeled outputs), Unsupervised (unlabeled structure), Reinforcement (feedback loop).

• **Student Shorthand**: Replaces standard programming (`data + rules = answers`) with learning (`data + answers = rules`).

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Collect and clean training data.

• Select a model architecture and define a cost/loss function.

• Optimize parameter weights using algorithms like gradient descent to minimize loss.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Standard programming is like baking with a detailed recipe. Machine learning is like trial-and-error baking, adjusting ingredients based on taste tests.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "What is the difference between parametric and non-parametric models?"

• **A**: Parametric models assume a fixed shape for the mapping function (e.g. Linear Regression, defined by weights). Non-parametric models grow in complexity with the size of the training data (e.g. Decision Trees, KNN).

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • No Free Lunch Theorem: No single machine learning algorithm works best for every problem. The optimal model depends on the dataset size, dimensionality, and noise.

revisionCards.title: Bias
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Error introduced by approximating a complex real-world problem with a simple model.

High Bias: Leads to underfitting. The model is too simple to capture patterns in the training data.

**Student Shorthand**: The difference between the expected prediction of our model and the true value.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Error introduced by approximating a complex real-world problem with a simple model.

• High Bias: Leads to underfitting. The model is too simple to capture patterns in the training data.

• **Student Shorthand**: The difference between the expected prediction of our model and the true value.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Formula:
`Bias[f_hat(x)] = E[f_hat(x)] - f(x)`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: In a dartboard model, high bias is throwing a cluster of darts that lands far away from the bullseye.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body:
• Using a straight line (linear model) to fit a highly quadratic dataset.

• The model has high bias, resulting in large errors on both the training and test sets.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How do you reduce model bias?"

• **A**: 1. Use more complex model architectures. 2. Engineer more features. 3. Decrease regularization penalties.

revisionCards.title: Variance
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: The sensitivity of a model to small fluctuations in the training set.

High Variance: Leads to overfitting. The model learns random noise in the training set rather than the underlying pattern.

**Student Shorthand**: Measures how much the predictions would change if the model was trained on a different sample of the same data.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: The sensitivity of a model to small fluctuations in the training set.

• High Variance: Leads to overfitting. The model learns random noise in the training set rather than the underlying pattern.

• **Student Shorthand**: Measures how much the predictions would change if the model was trained on a different sample of the same data.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Formula:
`Variance[f_hat(x)] = E[(f_hat(x) - E[f_hat(x)])^2]`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: In a dartboard model, high variance is darts scattered randomly all over the board, showing high sensitivity to throwing conditions.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body:
• Fitting a 20-degree polynomial curve to a linear dataset with 10 points.

• The curve passes through every training point (zero error) but fluctuates wildly between points, resulting in poor generalization.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How do you reduce model variance?"

• **A**: 1. Gather more training data. 2. Simplify the model architecture. 3. Increase regularization penalties. 4. Use bagging ensemble methods.

revisionCards.title: Underfitting
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: When a model is too simple to learn the underlying structure of the training data.

Symptoms: High training error and high testing error.

Root Cause: High bias. The model makes strong, incorrect assumptions about the data.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: When a model is too simple to learn the underlying structure of the training data.

• Symptoms: High training error and high testing error.

• Root Cause: High bias. The model makes strong, incorrect assumptions about the data.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Increase model complexity (e.g. add layers to a neural network, or use polynomial features).

• Train for more epochs or reduce regularization penalties.

• Engineer better features and inputs.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Underfitting is like a student memorizing only one page of a textbook. They perform poorly on both practice quizzes and the final exam.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "What are the common indicators of underfitting?"

• **A**: Training performance is poor, and test performance is also poor, indicating the model failed to capture the training patterns.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Underfitting vs Noise: Sometimes high error is due to pure noise in the labels (irreducible error), which no model can resolve. Verify data quality before increasing model complexity.

revisionCards.title: Overfitting
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: When a model learns the noise and details of the training data to the extent that it negatively impacts generalization.

Symptoms: Low training error but high testing error.

Root Cause: High variance. The model is too flexible and memorizes individual training points.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: When a model learns the noise and details of the training data to the extent that it negatively impacts generalization.

• Symptoms: Low training error but high testing error.

• Root Cause: High variance. The model is too flexible and memorizes individual training points.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Introduce regularization penalties (L1/L2 weights decay).

• Apply early stopping during training, or use dropout in neural networks.

• Reduce model complexity and collect more training data.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Overfitting is like a student memorizing the exact answers to a specific practice test. They get a perfect score on the practice test, but fail the final exam because they cannot apply the concepts to new questions.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How do you identify overfitting from a training curve?"

• **A**: Overfitting is occurring if the training loss continues to decrease while the validation loss stops decreasing and starts to rise.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Overfitting to the validation set: If you tune model hyperparameters repeatedly based on validation performance, the model can overfit the validation set. Always reserve a final test set for independent evaluation.

revisionCards.title: Regularization
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Adding penalty terms to the loss function to constrain model weights and prevent overfitting.

**Types**: L1 Regularization (Lasso, pushes weights to exactly 0) and L2 Regularization (Ridge, shrinks weights towards 0).

**Student Shorthand**: Controls the trade-off between model simplicity and training performance.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Adding penalty terms to the loss function to constrain model weights and prevent overfitting.

• **Types**: L1 Regularization (Lasso, pushes weights to exactly 0) and L2 Regularization (Ridge, shrinks weights towards 0).

• **Student Shorthand**: Controls the trade-off between model simplicity and training performance.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Lasso Loss (L1): `L = Loss + λ ∑ |w_i|`, promoting feature sparsity.

• Ridge Loss (L2): `L = Loss + λ ∑ w_i^2`, penalizing extreme weights.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Regularization acts like a speed limit: it prevents the model from moving too fast and over-reacting to noise in the data.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why does L1 regularization lead to feature sparsity?"

• **A**: L1 regularization uses absolute values, creating sharp corners in the constraint boundary. Optimization paths tend to hit these corners along coordinate axes, setting weights to exactly zero.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body:
• Elastic Net: Combines L1 and L2 penalties:
`L = Loss + r λ ∑ |w_i| + 1-r / 2 λ ∑ w_i^2`. Ideal when features are highly correlated.

revisionCards.title: Cross Validation
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Partitioning datasets into multiple folds to evaluate model generalization and prevent validation bias.

K-Fold: Data is split into K equal folds; the model is trained on K-1 folds and tested on the remaining fold, repeating the process K times.

Stratified K-Fold: Ensures each fold preserves class proportions (highly recommended for imbalanced datasets).

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Partitioning datasets into multiple folds to evaluate model generalization and prevent validation bias.

• K-Fold: Data is split into K equal folds; the model is trained on K-1 folds and tested on the remaining fold, repeating the process K times.

• Stratified K-Fold: Ensures each fold preserves class proportions (highly recommended for imbalanced datasets).

slides.headline: Python Code
slides.body: Review the clean, highly optimized implementation below:
slides.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, KFold
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
# 5-fold cross validation setup
kf = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
scores = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(), X, y, cv=kf)
# scores: array of 5 validation metrics

slides.headline: 💡 Code Breakdown
slides.body: • Line 4-5: Automatically splits the data into 5 folds, trains the model on 4 folds, tests it on the 5th fold, and repeats the process 5 times, returning an array of scores.

slides.headline: 🧠 Performance Footprint
slides.body:
• Time Complexity: O(K * T) where T is the training time of a single model.

• Space Complexity: O(R * C) to store split datasets.

slides.headline: 🧠 Common Interview Questions
slides.body:
• Gotcha: Performing preprocessing (e.g. scaling, PCA) globally before cross-validation leaks information from validation folds into training folds. Wrap steps in a scikit-learn `Pipeline` to prevent this.

• Gotcha: For time-series data, K-Fold cross-validation leaks future data into the past. Use `TimeSeriesSplit` (expanding training windows) instead.

revisionCards.title: Linear Regression
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Parametric model that predicts continuous target values using linear combinations of inputs.

Cost Function: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) minimizes Mean Squared Error (MSE).

Assumptions: Linearity, homoscedasticity (constant variance of residuals), independence, and normality of residuals.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Parametric model that predicts continuous target values using linear combinations of inputs.

• Cost Function: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) minimizes Mean Squared Error (MSE).

• Assumptions: Linearity, homoscedasticity (constant variance of residuals), independence, and normality of residuals.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Model Equation: `y_hat = w^T x + b`

• OLS Cost:
`J(w, b) = 1 / 2N ∑_{i=1}^N (y_i - y_hat_i)^2`

• Normal Equation (Closed-form): `w = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: Linear regression fits a flat hyperplane through data coordinates, minimizing the sum of squared vertical distances from points to the hyperplane.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body:
• Computing closed-form solution: `w = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y`.

• If features are collinear, `X^T X` is singular (not invertible), causing the closed-form calculation to fail.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How do you detect multicollinearity in linear regression?"

• **A**: Calculate Variance Inflation Factors (VIF). A VIF > 5 or 10 indicates high multicollinearity, meaning you should drop or merge correlated features.

revisionCards.title: Logistic Regression
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Linear model for binary classification that outputs probabilities using the sigmoid function.

Decision Boundary: The boundary is linear: the model outputs 1 if probability `≥ 0.5`, which occurs when `w^T x + b ≥ 0`.

Cost Function: Log Loss (Binary Cross-Entropy) because MSE is non-convex for logistic outputs.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Linear model for binary classification that outputs probabilities using the sigmoid function.

• Decision Boundary: The boundary is linear: the model outputs 1 if probability `≥ 0.5`, which occurs when `w^T x + b ≥ 0`.

• Cost Function: Log Loss (Binary Cross-Entropy) because MSE is non-convex for logistic outputs.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Sigmoid Function: `σ(z) = (1) / (1 + e^{-z)}`

• Probability: `P(y=1 | x) = σ(w^T x + b)`

• Log Loss Cost:
`J(w, b) = -1 / N ∑ [y_i log(y_hat_i) + (1-y_i) log(1-y_hat_i)]`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: Logistic regression projects data onto a linear line, then squashes the output through an S-shaped curve (sigmoid) to map it to a [0, 1] range.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body:
• If `z = w^T x + b = 0`, probability is `σ(0) = 0.5` (exactly on the decision boundary).

• If `z = 2`, probability is
`σ(2) = (1) / (1 + e^{-2)} ≈ 0.88`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why can't we use Mean Squared Error as the cost function for Logistic Regression?"

• **A**: Combining MSE with the non-linear sigmoid function results in a non-convex cost surface with many local minima. Gradient descent can get trapped in these local minima. Log Loss ensures a convex cost surface.

revisionCards.title: KNN
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Lazy, non-parametric instance-based algorithm that classifies a query point based on the majority vote of its `K` nearest neighbors.

Distance Metrics: Typically uses Euclidean distance (L2 norm) or Manhattan distance (L1 norm).

Curse of Dimensionality: Performance degrades in high dimensions because distances between points compress and become uniform.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Lazy, non-parametric instance-based algorithm that classifies a query point based on the majority vote of its `K` nearest neighbors.

• Distance Metrics: Typically uses Euclidean distance (L2 norm) or Manhattan distance (L1 norm).

• Curse of Dimensionality: Performance degrades in high dimensions because distances between points compress and become uniform.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Calculate the distance between the query point and all training points.

• Sort points by distance and select the top `K` nearest neighbors.

• Return the majority class (classification) or average target value (regression) of these `K` points.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Birds of a feather flock together: the class of a point is determined by the classes of the points closest to it.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How does selecting `K` impact the model?"

• **A**: Small `K` values (e.g. `K=1`) lead to low bias but high variance (overfitting, sensitive to noise). Large `K` values smooth out boundaries, leading to low variance but high bias (underfitting).

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Lazy Learner: KNN has zero training phase cost. However, testing is computationally expensive (`O(N)`) because it must calculate distances to all training points for every query.

revisionCards.title: Decision Trees
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Non-parametric supervised model that recursively splits datasets based on feature thresholds.

Splitting Criteria: Classification: Gini Impurity or Entropy (Information Gain). Regression: Variance reduction (MSE).

High Variance: Prone to overfitting if allowed to grow to maximum depth without constraints.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Non-parametric supervised model that recursively splits datasets based on feature thresholds.

• Splitting Criteria: Classification: Gini Impurity or Entropy (Information Gain). Regression: Variance reduction (MSE).

• High Variance: Prone to overfitting if allowed to grow to maximum depth without constraints.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Gini Impurity: `I_G(p) = 1 - ∑ p_i^2`

• Entropy: `H(p) = -∑ p_i log_2(p_i)`

• Information Gain: `IG(T, a) = H(T) - H(T | a)`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: Decision trees divide the input feature space into orthogonal rectangular regions (axis-aligned splits).

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body:
• A dataset contains 4 positive and 4 negative classes. Total entropy is
`H(T) = -0.5 log_2(0.5) - 0.5 log_2(0.5) = 1`.

• A split separates the data into a pure positive group (4 points, entropy 0) and a pure negative group (4 points, entropy 0). Information Gain is `1 - 0 = 1` (perfect split).

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How do you control overfitting in decision trees?"

• **A**: 1. Set maximum depth (`max_depth`). 2. Require a minimum number of samples per split (`min_samples_split`). 3. Apply post-pruning techniques like Cost Complexity Pruning.

revisionCards.title: SVM
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Supervised classifier that finds the optimal separating hyperplane maximizing the margin between classes.

Kernel Trick: Projects non-linearly separable data into higher dimensions where it becomes linearly separable.

Support Vectors: The data points that lie closest to the decision boundary and define the separating hyperplane.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Supervised classifier that finds the optimal separating hyperplane maximizing the margin between classes.

• Kernel Trick: Projects non-linearly separable data into higher dimensions where it becomes linearly separable.

• Support Vectors: The data points that lie closest to the decision boundary and define the separating hyperplane.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Primal Optimization: `\min_{w, b} 1 / 2 \|w\|^2` subject to `y_i(w^T x_i + b) ≥ 1`

• RBF Kernel Function:
`K(x, x') = exp(-γ \|x - x'\|^2)`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: SVM places a separating wall between two classes, pushing the wall as far as possible from the nearest data points of both classes.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body:
• Linear SVM finds decision boundary weights. Points on the margin boundaries satisfy `w^T x_i + b = ± 1`.

• The margin width is given by `2 / \|w\|`, so minimizing `\|w\|^2` maximizes the margin.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "What are the C and gamma parameters in an RBF SVM?"

• **A**: C controls the tradeoff between margin width and classification errors: large C penalizes errors heavily (narrower margin, risk of overfitting). Gamma controls the radius of influence of support vectors: large gamma creates localized decision boundaries (overfitting).

revisionCards.title: Naive Bayes
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Classifier based on Bayes Theorem that assumes conditional independence between features given the class label.

Naive Assumption: Assumes the presence of one feature does not affect the presence of another, given the target class.

Shorthand: Fast to train, highly effective for high-dimensional text classification (e.g. spam detection).

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Classifier based on Bayes Theorem that assumes conditional independence between features given the class label.

• Naive Assumption: Assumes the presence of one feature does not affect the presence of another, given the target class.

• Shorthand: Fast to train, highly effective for high-dimensional text classification (e.g. spam detection).

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Classification Rule:
`y_hat = \arg\max_c P(y=c) ∏_{i=1}^D P(x_i | y=c)`

• Laplace Smoothing:
`P(x_i | y=c) = (count(x_i, c) + α) / (count(c) + α D)`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: Multiplies probability scores along the features dimension to determine which class is more likely.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body:
• Predicting spam: A new email contains the word "Winner" (which appeared in 5/10 spam emails and 0/10 non-spam emails).

• Without smoothing, `P("Winner" | Non-Spam) = 0`, causing the entire joint probability to collapse to 0. Laplace smoothing (adding `α=1` to counts) prevents this.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why is the Naive Bayes assumption called naive?"

• **A**: Because real-world features are rarely independent (e.g. in text, the word "machine" is highly likely to be followed by "learning"). Despite this incorrect assumption, the model performs surprisingly well in practice.

revisionCards.title: Clustering
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Grouping unlabeled data points so that points in the same group are similar, and points in different groups are distinct.

**Types**: Partitioning (K-Means), Hierarchical (Agglomerative), Density-Based (DBSCAN).

Validation: Internal validation metrics (Silhouette score) and external validation metrics (Adjusted Rand Index).

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Grouping unlabeled data points so that points in the same group are similar, and points in different groups are distinct.

• **Types**: Partitioning (K-Means), Hierarchical (Agglomerative), Density-Based (DBSCAN).

• Validation: Internal validation metrics (Silhouette score) and external validation metrics (Adjusted Rand Index).

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Choose a similarity/distance metric (e.g. Euclidean distance).

• Group data points iteratively to optimize cluster tightness (compactness).

• Evaluate cluster quality and cohesion.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Clustering is like sorting a pile of unsorted clothes into separate piles: shirts, pants, and socks.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How do you evaluate clustering quality without labels?"

• **A**: Use the Silhouette Coefficient: `s = (b - a) / (\max(a, b))` where `a` is intra-cluster distance and `b` is nearest-cluster distance. Scores close to 1 indicate well-separated, compact clusters.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Sensitive to scaling: Feature scale impacts distance calculations. Always scale features prior to clustering.

revisionCards.title: K Means
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Centroid-based partitioning algorithm that splits data into `K` non-overlapping clusters.

Initialization: Choosing initial centroids. Standard K-Means is sensitive to initialization; `K-Means++` resolves this by placing initial centroids far apart.

Limitations: Struggles with non-spherical shapes, outliers, and varying densities.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Centroid-based partitioning algorithm that splits data into `K` non-overlapping clusters.

• Initialization: Choosing initial centroids. Standard K-Means is sensitive to initialization; `K-Means++` resolves this by placing initial centroids far apart.

• Limitations: Struggles with non-spherical shapes, outliers, and varying densities.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Objective Function: Minimize Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS):
`J = ∑_{j=1}^K ∑_{x ∈ C_j} \|x - μ_j\|^2`.

• **Step 1**: Assign each point to the closest centroid (Voronoi iteration).

• **Step 2**: Update centroids by calculating the mean of all assigned points. Repeat until convergence.

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: K-Means partitions space into Voronoi cells where each cell boundaries are equidistant from the centroid.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body: • Selecting optimal K: Plot WCSS values for different K values. Identify the "elbow" point where the rate of decrease in WCSS slows down.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why does standard K-Means converge to local minima?"

• **A**: Because the assignment-update optimization step is coordinate descent, which is greedy. Running multiple initializations (`n_init`) decreases the risk of getting trapped in a poor local minimum.

revisionCards.title: Hierarchical Clustering
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Clustering algorithm that builds a tree of clusters (dendrogram) using bottom-up (agglomerative) or top-down (divisive) splits.

Linkage Criteria: Single linkage (minimum distance between points), Complete linkage (maximum distance), Average linkage, or Ward linkage (minimizes variance increase).

**Student Shorthand**: The dendrogram allows you to choose the number of clusters after running the algorithm.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Clustering algorithm that builds a tree of clusters (dendrogram) using bottom-up (agglomerative) or top-down (divisive) splits.

• Linkage Criteria: Single linkage (minimum distance between points), Complete linkage (maximum distance), Average linkage, or Ward linkage (minimizes variance increase).

• **Student Shorthand**: The dendrogram allows you to choose the number of clusters after running the algorithm.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Treat every data point as an individual cluster.

• Find the two closest clusters and merge them.

• Repeat until all points are merged into a single cluster. Cut the dendrogram at the desired height to extract clusters.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Hierarchical clustering is like building a family tree: individuals form couples, couples form families, families form clans, and clans form the entire population.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "What are the computational limits of hierarchical clustering?"

• **A**: High computational complexity: Time complexity is `O(N^3)` (or `O(N^2)` optimized) and space complexity is `O(N^2)` to store the distance matrix. This makes it unsuitable for large datasets.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Chaining Effect: A drawback of single linkage where clusters get pulled together into a long chain because of intermediate noise points between them.

revisionCards.title: DBSCAN
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise. Groups points in dense regions and flags sparse points as outliers.

Hyperparameters: `eps` (search radius) and `minSamples` (minimum points required within the radius).

Point Types: Core points (sufficient neighbors), Border points (reachable from core), Noise points (outliers).

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise. Groups points in dense regions and flags sparse points as outliers.

• Hyperparameters: `eps` (search radius) and `minSamples` (minimum points required within the radius).

• Point Types: Core points (sufficient neighbors), Border points (reachable from core), Noise points (outliers).

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• For each point, count neighbors within radius `eps`. If counts `≥` `minSamples`, flag as a Core point.

• Connect core points within `eps` distance to form density-reachable clusters.

• Assign border points to clusters, and flag remaining points as Noise.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: DBSCAN is like locating crowded party groups: core members are in the center, friends on the edge are border members, and isolated individuals in empty space are noise.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "What are the main advantages of DBSCAN over K-Means?"

• **A**: 1. You do not need to specify the number of clusters (K) in advance. 2. It can identify arbitrary, non-spherical cluster shapes. 3. It natively filters out noise and outliers.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Struggles with varying densities: If the dataset contains clusters of different densities, a single `eps` value cannot capture them all. Use OPTICS instead.

revisionCards.title: PCA
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Unsupervised dimensionality reduction technique that projects high-dimensional data onto orthogonal axes of maximum variance.

Principal Components: The eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, ordered by their corresponding eigenvalues.

Multicollinearity: PCA eliminates multicollinearity because the principal components are orthogonal (uncorrelated).

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Unsupervised dimensionality reduction technique that projects high-dimensional data onto orthogonal axes of maximum variance.

• Principal Components: The eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, ordered by their corresponding eigenvalues.

• Multicollinearity: PCA eliminates multicollinearity because the principal components are orthogonal (uncorrelated).

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Mean-center the data: `X_c = X - μ`.

• Calculate the covariance matrix: `C = 1 / N X_c^T X_c`.

• Compute eigenvectors and eigenvalues of `C`. Select the top `k` eigenvectors to form the projection matrix `W`. Project data: `Z = X_c W`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: PCA projects data points onto the line/plane that minimizes the sum of squared reconstruction errors.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body:
• If covariance matrix `C` has eigenvalues `λ_1 = 80` and `λ_2 = 20`:

• The first principal component captures `80 / 80+20 = 80%` of total dataset variance.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why is mean-centering mandatory before running PCA?"

• **A**: If data is not mean-centered, the first principal component will point in the direction of the dataset mean vector instead of the direction of maximum variance.

revisionCards.title: Confusion Matrix
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: A tabular layout displaying classifier predictions against true outcomes.

Terms: True Positive (TP), True Negative (TN), False Positive (FP, Type I error), False Negative (FN, Type II error).

**Student Shorthand**: The diagonal represents correct predictions; off-diagonal elements are prediction errors.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: A tabular layout displaying classifier predictions against true outcomes.

• Terms: True Positive (TP), True Negative (TN), False Positive (FP, Type I error), False Negative (FN, Type II error).

• **Student Shorthand**: The diagonal represents correct predictions; off-diagonal elements are prediction errors.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Row indices represent true classes (Actual 1, Actual 0).

• Column indices represent predicted classes (Predicted 1, Predicted 0).

• Populate cells by matching actual vs. predicted values for all data points.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: A scoreboard that separates correct calls from incorrect calls, showing exactly where mistakes were made.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How does confusion matrix change with class imbalance?"

• **A**: With class imbalance (e.g. fraud detection), the TN count is massive, masking high rates of FN errors. Focus on precision and recall instead of raw accuracy.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body:
• Accuracy: Total correct predictions divided by all predictions:
`ACC = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)`. Can be highly misleading in imbalanced datasets.

revisionCards.title: Precision
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: The ratio of correctly predicted positive observations to the total predicted positive observations.

Use Case: Critical when the cost of a False Positive is high (e.g. spam filters where flag-as-spam must not catch important emails).

**Student Shorthand**: Out of all instances predicted as positive, how many were actually positive?

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: The ratio of correctly predicted positive observations to the total predicted positive observations.

• Use Case: Critical when the cost of a False Positive is high (e.g. spam filters where flag-as-spam must not catch important emails).

• **Student Shorthand**: Out of all instances predicted as positive, how many were actually positive?

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body: • Formula: `Precision = (TP) / (TP + FP)`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: The fraction of the predicted positive region that overlaps with actual positive points.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body:
• A model predicts 10 emails as spam. 8 are actually spam, 2 are legitimate (False Positives).

• `Precision = 8 / 8+2 = 0.80`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How do you increase precision?"

• **A**: Increase the decision threshold (e.g. from 0.5 to 0.8). The model becomes more conservative, making fewer positive predictions but with higher confidence.

revisionCards.title: Recall
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: The ratio of correctly predicted positive observations to all actual positive observations.

Use Case: Critical when the cost of a False Negative is high (e.g. cancer detection, where missing a positive case is catastrophic).

**Student Shorthand**: Out of all actual positive instances, how many did the model identify?

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: The ratio of correctly predicted positive observations to all actual positive observations.

• Use Case: Critical when the cost of a False Negative is high (e.g. cancer detection, where missing a positive case is catastrophic).

• **Student Shorthand**: Out of all actual positive instances, how many did the model identify?

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body: • Formula: `Recall = (TP) / (TP + FN)`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: The fraction of the actual positive points that overlap with predicted positive regions.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body:
• A patient cohort has 10 actual cancer cases. The model identifies 7 cases, missing 3 (False Negatives).

• `Recall = 7 / 7+3 = 0.70`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How do you increase recall?"

• **A**: Lower the decision threshold (e.g. from 0.5 to 0.2). The model becomes more sensitive, making more positive predictions and reducing False Negatives.

revisionCards.title: F1 Score
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, providing a single evaluation metric.

Why Harmonic Mean: Penalizes extreme differences between precision and recall, unlike the arithmetic mean.

**Student Shorthand**: A robust metric for imbalanced classification tasks.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, providing a single evaluation metric.

• Why Harmonic Mean: Penalizes extreme differences between precision and recall, unlike the arithmetic mean.

• **Student Shorthand**: A robust metric for imbalanced classification tasks.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Formula:
`F_1 = 2 * (Precision * Recall) / (Precision + Recall) = (2TP) / (2TP + FP + FN)`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: F1-score falls to 0 if either precision or recall is 0, requiring both metrics to be high to get a high score.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body:
• If a classifier has Precision = 0.9 and Recall = 0.1:

• Arithmetic mean is `0.9+0.1 / 2 = 0.5`.

• Harmonic mean (F1) is `2 * 0.09 / 1.0 = 0.18` (reflecting poor performance).

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• F-beta Score: Generalizes F1 to weigh precision or recall higher:
`F_β = (1+β^2) (Precision * Recall) / (β^2 Precision + Recall)`. `β=2` weighs recall twice as high; `β=0.5` weighs precision twice as high.

revisionCards.title: ROC Curve
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Receiver Operating Characteristic curve. A graphical plot of True Positive Rate (TPR, Recall) vs False Positive Rate (FPR) across all classification thresholds.

FPR: The fraction of actual negative instances that are incorrectly predicted as positive: `FPR = (FP) / (TN + FP)`.

**Student Shorthand**: Evaluates classifier performance across all threshold settings.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Receiver Operating Characteristic curve. A graphical plot of True Positive Rate (TPR, Recall) vs False Positive Rate (FPR) across all classification thresholds.

• FPR: The fraction of actual negative instances that are incorrectly predicted as positive: `FPR = (FP) / (TN + FP)`.

• **Student Shorthand**: Evaluates classifier performance across all threshold settings.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Calculate predictions for the dataset.

• Sort predictions by probability and step through threshold values from 1.0 down to 0.0.

• Calculate and plot TPR and FPR coordinates at each step.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: A diagnostic dial: turning the dial makes the test more sensitive (higher TPR) but increases false alarms (higher FPR).

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "What does the diagonal line represent on an ROC curve?"

• **A**: The diagonal line represents a random classifier (no predictive power). The closer the curve is to the top-left corner, the better the model.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Threshold independence: ROC curves evaluate ranking quality, meaning they remain unchanged even if the dataset class balance shifts.

revisionCards.title: AUC
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Area Under the ROC Curve. Measures the probability that a classifier will rank a randomly chosen positive instance higher than a randomly chosen negative instance.

Range: Bound between 0.5 (random guess) and 1.0 (perfect classifier).

Interpretation: Higher AUC scores indicate better model separation capability.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Area Under the ROC Curve. Measures the probability that a classifier will rank a randomly chosen positive instance higher than a randomly chosen negative instance.

• Range: Bound between 0.5 (random guess) and 1.0 (perfect classifier).

• Interpretation: Higher AUC scores indicate better model separation capability.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body: • Formula: `AUC = ∫_0^1 TPR(FPR) d(FPR)`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: AUC measures the area under the ROC curve on the [0,1] grid.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body: • An AUC score of 0.85 indicates there is an 85% chance the model will assign a higher probability score to a true positive instance than a true negative instance.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "When does AUC fail as an evaluation metric?"

• **A**: With extreme class imbalance (e.g. 1 positive in 10,000 negatives), the FPR denominator (`TN+FP`) is dominated by TN. A model can make many false positive errors while maintaining a low FPR and high AUC. Use Precision-Recall AUC (PR-AUC) instead.

revisionCards.title: Feature Selection
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Selecting a subset of relevant features for model construction.

Methods: Filter methods (statistical checks: ANOVA, Chi-square), Wrapper methods (recursive elimination), Embedded methods (L1 regularization).

**Student Shorthand**: Bypasses model noise and speeds up training times.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Selecting a subset of relevant features for model construction.

• Methods: Filter methods (statistical checks: ANOVA, Chi-square), Wrapper methods (recursive elimination), Embedded methods (L1 regularization).

• **Student Shorthand**: Bypasses model noise and speeds up training times.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Filter: Evaluate statistical relationship of each input feature against the target.

• Wrapper: Train models on subsets and add/remove features sequentially (e.g. forward selection).

• Embedded: Fit models that constrain weights (e.g. Lasso) and drop zero-weight features.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Feature selection is like picking the best ingredients for a recipe, rather than putting everything in the pantry into the pot.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How do wrapper methods compare to filter methods?"

• **A**: Wrapper methods evaluate feature subsets using actual model performance. They are more accurate but computationally expensive. Filter methods are model-agnostic and fast.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Variance Thresholding: A simple filter method that drops features with variance below a set threshold (e.g. columns where 99% of values are identical).

revisionCards.title: Feature Extraction
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Transforming raw data into new, lower-dimensional numerical features that contain the original information.

Shorthand: Differs from feature selection (which drops columns); extraction projects data onto new feature dimensions.

**Examples**: Extracting text embeddings, image edge features, or using dimensionality reduction algorithms.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Transforming raw data into new, lower-dimensional numerical features that contain the original information.

• Shorthand: Differs from feature selection (which drops columns); extraction projects data onto new feature dimensions.

• **Examples**: Extracting text embeddings, image edge features, or using dimensionality reduction algorithms.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Map raw features through mathematical functions.

• Project coordinates onto lower-dimensional spaces.

• Combine multiple correlated columns into single composite indicators.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Summarizing a 500-page book into a 5-page outline: you capture the core themes without keeping all the original sentences.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How does feature extraction help image classification?"

• **A**: Raw pixel arrays are high-dimensional and noisy. Extracting features (e.g. using HOG or CNN layers) captures edges and textures, improving classification performance.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Information loss: Feature extraction techniques (like PCA) reduce dimensions but can lose non-linear patterns. Use t-SNE or UMAP if preserving non-linear structure is vital.

revisionCards.title: PCA Feature Transformation
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Using Principal Component Analysis as a preprocessing step to generate uncorrelated, lower-dimensional inputs.

Multicollinearity: Ideal for linear models because the principal components are orthogonal.

Variance retention: Select components that capture a target percentage (e.g. 95%) of cumulative explained variance.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Using Principal Component Analysis as a preprocessing step to generate uncorrelated, lower-dimensional inputs.

• Multicollinearity: Ideal for linear models because the principal components are orthogonal.

• Variance retention: Select components that capture a target percentage (e.g. 95%) of cumulative explained variance.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Fit PCA on the training set to find principal component axes.

• Transform both the training and test sets using these axes.

• Feed the transformed features into downstream classification or regression models.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Taking a 2D photograph of a 3D sculpture from the angle that captures the most detail.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "What are the drawbacks of using PCA in feature engineering?"

• **A**: It ruins model interpretability. The principal components are linear combinations of all original features, making it hard to explain which input variables drive predictions.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Scaling dependency: Features with larger scales will dominate PCA axes. Always standardize features (mean=0, variance=1) before fitting PCA.

revisionCards.title: Dimensionality Reduction
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Reducing the number of input variables in a dataset.

Why it matters: Bypasses the Curse of Dimensionality: in high dimensions, data points become sparse and distance metrics lose separation power.

Common methods: Linear (PCA, LDA) and Non-linear (t-SNE, UMAP, Autoencoders).

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Reducing the number of input variables in a dataset.

• Why it matters: Bypasses the Curse of Dimensionality: in high dimensions, data points become sparse and distance metrics lose separation power.

• Common methods: Linear (PCA, LDA) and Non-linear (t-SNE, UMAP, Autoencoders).

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Analyze dataset shape and feature correlations.

• Select a reduction technique based on linearity (PCA for linear structures, t-SNE for localized clusters).

• Project features onto the selected low-dimensional space.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Flattening a 3D globe onto a 2D map: you lose some accuracy, but the map is much easier to store and analyze.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "What is t-SNE used for?"

• **A**: t-SNE (t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) is a non-linear dimensionality reduction technique used for high-dimensional data visualization, as it preserves local neighborhoods.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • t-SNE is strictly for visualization. It is computationally expensive (`O(N^2)`) and does not output a projection function that can be applied to new test data.

revisionCards.title: Bagging
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Bootstrap Aggregating. Training multiple base estimators in parallel on random subsets of the data with replacement, and averaging their predictions.

**Goal**: Reduces model variance (overfitting) without increasing bias.

Out-Of-Bag (OOB): Evaluating models on left-out bootstrap samples, bypassing the need for a separate validation set.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Bootstrap Aggregating. Training multiple base estimators in parallel on random subsets of the data with replacement, and averaging their predictions.

• **Goal**: Reduces model variance (overfitting) without increasing bias.

• Out-Of-Bag (OOB): Evaluating models on left-out bootstrap samples, bypassing the need for a separate validation set.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Generate `B` bootstrap samples from the training set by sampling with replacement.

• Train a separate base model (typically deep decision trees) on each sample in parallel.

• Combine predictions: majority vote for classification, average for regression.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Asking a jury of 50 people to vote on a verdict. Individual biases cancel out, resulting in a more robust final decision.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why does bagging reduce variance?"

• **A**: Averaging predictions from multiple independent, high-variance models reduces the variance of the average by a factor of `B` (if models are uncorrelated).

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Base Estimator Choice: Bagging works best with high-variance, unstable base estimators (e.g. unpruned decision trees). It adds no value to low-variance models like linear regression.

revisionCards.title: Boosting
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Training base estimators sequentially, where each new estimator focuses on correcting the errors made by previous estimators.

**Goal**: Reduces model bias (underfitting) and can decrease variance.

Base Estimators: Uses weak learners (e.g. shallow decision trees/decision stumps).

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Training base estimators sequentially, where each new estimator focuses on correcting the errors made by previous estimators.

• **Goal**: Reduces model bias (underfitting) and can decrease variance.

• Base Estimators: Uses weak learners (e.g. shallow decision trees/decision stumps).

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Train a weak learner on the training set.

• Calculate prediction errors and adjust sample weights (or fit the next model to the residuals).

• Repeat sequentially, combining models using weighted voting.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: A student studying for an exam: they take a practice test, identify their mistakes, study those specific topics, and repeat the process.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How does boosting compare to bagging?"

• **A**: Bagging trains models in parallel to reduce variance. Boosting trains models sequentially to reduce bias. Boosting is more accurate but is prone to overfitting if noise is high.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Sensitivity to noise: Since boosting focuses on misclassified points, it can overfit outliers and noise in the labels. Clean datasets before boosting.

revisionCards.title: Random Forest
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Ensemble model that combines bagging with random feature selection to decorrelate base decision trees.

Feature Randomness: Each split in a tree is chosen from a random subset of features (typically `√(D)` features).

**Student Shorthand**: Decorrelating the trees reduces the variance of the average prediction compared to standard bagging.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Ensemble model that combines bagging with random feature selection to decorrelate base decision trees.

• Feature Randomness: Each split in a tree is chosen from a random subset of features (typically `√(D)` features).

• **Student Shorthand**: Decorrelating the trees reduces the variance of the average prediction compared to standard bagging.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Create a bootstrap sample of the training set.

• Grow a decision tree on the sample. At each split, select a random subset of features to find the best split.

• Repeat `B` times and average predictions.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Instead of one expert analyzing a problem, you ask a forest of experts who each look at different features of the problem.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why does Random Forest select random features at each split?"

• **A**: If a few features are highly predictive, standard bagging trees will all split on those same features, making the trees highly correlated. Selecting random features at each split decorrelates the trees, reducing average variance.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Feature Importance: Calculated by measuring the average decrease in impurity (Gini or entropy) caused by splits on a given feature across all trees.

revisionCards.title: XGBoost
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Extreme Gradient Boosting. An optimized implementation of gradient boosted decision trees that uses second-order Taylor expansion and regularization.

Regularization: Adds L1/L2 regularization to the loss function to constrain tree complexity.

Speed: Uses parallel split finding, block compression, and cache-aware structures.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Extreme Gradient Boosting. An optimized implementation of gradient boosted decision trees that uses second-order Taylor expansion and regularization.

• Regularization: Adds L1/L2 regularization to the loss function to constrain tree complexity.

• Speed: Uses parallel split finding, block compression, and cache-aware structures.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Objective Function: Optimize regularized loss:
`L^{(t)} ≈ ∑ [g_i f_t(x_i) + 1 / 2 h_i f_t^2(x_i)] + Ω(f_t)`.

• Calculate first-order gradient (`g_i`) and second-order gradient (`h_i`, Hessian) of the loss.

• Build trees sequentially to fit these gradients, and apply learning rate shrinkage.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Standard gradient boosting takes steps downhill. XGBoost calculated the curvature of the hill (second derivative) to take faster, more accurate steps.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why is XGBoost faster than standard Gradient Boosting?"

• **A**: 1. Parallel tree construction. 2. Cache-aware data access. 3. Built-in handling of missing values. 4. Column block splitting.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Missing Value Handling: XGBoost automatically learns a default direction (left or right split) for missing values based on which direction reduces training loss.

revisionCards.title: AdaBoost
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Adaptive Boosting. Sequential ensemble method that adjusts sample weights, increasing weights for misclassified samples.

Weak Learners: Typically uses decision stumps (1-split decision trees).

Final Predictor: A weighted combination of all weak learners.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Adaptive Boosting. Sequential ensemble method that adjusts sample weights, increasing weights for misclassified samples.

• Weak Learners: Typically uses decision stumps (1-split decision trees).

• Final Predictor: A weighted combination of all weak learners.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Initialize sample weights: `D_1(i) = 1 / N`.

• Train weak learner, calculate error `ε_t`, and compute estimator weight: `α_t = 1 / 2 \ln1-ε_t / ε_t`.

• Update sample weights:
`D_{t+1}(i) = (D_t(i) e^{-α_t y_i h_t(x_i)}) / (Z_t)` (where `Z_t` is a normalization factor).

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: AdaBoost builds a strong classifier by sequentially adding weak classifiers that focus on the mistakes of their predecessors.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body: • If a weak learner has an error rate of 0.5 (random guess), its weight is `α_t = \ln(1) = 0`, meaning it has no influence on the final model.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why is AdaBoost sensitive to outliers?"

• **A**: Because it increases sample weights exponentially for misclassified points. Outliers are hard to classify, so the model focuses heavily on them, which can degrade generalization.

revisionCards.title: Deep Learning Overview
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Subfield of ML based on artificial neural networks with multiple layers, designed to learn representations from data.

Representation Learning: Bypasses manual feature engineering by learning features directly from raw inputs.

Universal Approximation: A feedforward neural network with a single hidden layer can approximate any continuous function, given non-linear activations.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Subfield of ML based on artificial neural networks with multiple layers, designed to learn representations from data.
