• Representation Learning: Bypasses manual feature engineering by learning features directly from raw inputs.

• Universal Approximation: A feedforward neural network with a single hidden layer can approximate any continuous function, given non-linear activations.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Pass inputs forward through hidden layers (forward propagation).

• Calculate cost by comparing outputs against target labels.

• Pass gradients back through the network (backpropagation) and update weights.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Deep learning is like processing raw clay through multiple sculpting hands: early layers shape basic structures (edges), and deep layers carve intricate details (faces).

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why has Deep Learning exploded recently?"

• **A**: 1. **Availability** of massive labeled datasets. 2. GPU acceleration for parallel matrix math. 3. Algorithmic advances (e.g. ReLU, dropout).

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Data dependency: Deep learning models are data-hungry. If training data is small, standard ML models (e.g. Random Forest) often generalize better.

revisionCards.title: Perceptron
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: The fundamental building block of artificial neural networks, representing a single neuron.

Linear Classifier: Classifies inputs by calculating a weighted sum and applying a step function.

XOR Limit: A single perceptron can only learn linear decision boundaries, making it unable to solve the XOR problem.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: The fundamental building block of artificial neural networks, representing a single neuron.

• Linear Classifier: Classifies inputs by calculating a weighted sum and applying a step function.

• XOR Limit: A single perceptron can only learn linear decision boundaries, making it unable to solve the XOR problem.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Activation Formula: `z = w^T x + b`

• Step Output:
`y_hat = \begin{cases} 1 & if z ≥ 0 \\ 0 & if z < 0 \end{cases}`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: A perceptron divides space into two halves using a linear decision boundary.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body:
• Calculate output for inputs `x = [1, 0]` with weights `w = [2, -1]` and bias `b = -1`:

• `z = (1 * 2) + (0 * -1) - 1 = 1 ≥ 0 \implies y_hat = 1`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why did the XOR problem cause a winter in AI history?"

• **A**: Minsky and Papert proved that a single-layer perceptron cannot learn non-linear boundaries like XOR. The AI community abandoned neural networks until multi-layer networks and backpropagation were introduced.

revisionCards.title: Activation Functions
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Mathematical functions applied to neuron outputs to introduce non-linearity.

Why it matters: Without non-linear activation functions, a multi-layer neural network collapses into a single-layer linear model.

Common functions: Sigmoid (probability), Tanh (centered), ReLU (rectified linear, fast, solves vanishing gradients).

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Mathematical functions applied to neuron outputs to introduce non-linearity.

• Why it matters: Without non-linear activation functions, a multi-layer neural network collapses into a single-layer linear model.

• Common functions: Sigmoid (probability), Tanh (centered), ReLU (rectified linear, fast, solves vanishing gradients).

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Sigmoid: `σ(z) = (1) / (1 + e^{-z)}`, outputs range [0, 1].

• Tanh: `g(z) = tanh(z)`, outputs range [-1, 1].

• ReLU: `g(z) = \max(0, z)`, outputs range [0, \infty).

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Activation functions are like light switches with dimmers: they control how much signal is passed to the next layer.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why is ReLU preferred over Sigmoid in hidden layers?"

• **A**: Sigmoid saturates at extreme inputs, meaning its derivative approaches 0. This causes vanishing gradients during training. ReLU has a constant derivative of 1 for positive inputs, which speeds up training.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Dying ReLU Problem: Neurons can get trapped in the inactive state (output 0) if weights receive large negative updates. Solve this by using Leaky ReLU: `g(z) = \max(0.01z, z)`.

revisionCards.title: Backpropagation
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Algorithmic process to calculate the gradients of the loss function with respect to neural network weights.

**Mechanism**: The chain rule of calculus applied recursively from the output layer back to the input layer.

Computational: Computes gradients efficiently by **caching** intermediate derivatives.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Algorithmic process to calculate the gradients of the loss function with respect to neural network weights.

• **Mechanism**: The chain rule of calculus applied recursively from the output layer back to the input layer.

• Computational: Computes gradients efficiently by **caching** intermediate derivatives.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Forward pass: Compute activations at each layer and calculate output loss.

• Backward pass: Compute error gradients at the output layer: `δ^{[L]} = ∇_a L ⊙ g'(z^{[L]})`.

• Propagate errors back:
`δ^{[l]} = (W^{[l+1]T} δ^{[l+1]}) ⊙ g'(z^{[l]})`, and compute weights gradients:
`(\partial L) / (\partial W^{[l])} = δ^{[l]} a^{[l-1]T}`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: Backpropagation flows error signals backward through the network, assigning credit or blame to weights for the output error.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body:
• Gradient path for single weight:
`(\partial L) / (\partial w_i) = (\partial L) / (\partial a) * (\partial a) / (\partial z) * (\partial z) / (\partial w_i)`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "What is the difference between backpropagation and gradient descent?"

• **A**: Backpropagation *calculates* the gradients of the loss function with respect to weights. Gradient descent *uses* these gradients to update the weight values.

revisionCards.title: Loss Functions
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Functions that measure the difference between model predictions and true target values.

Regression: Mean Squared Error (MSE, penalizes outliers), Mean Absolute Error (MAE, robust to outliers).

Classification: Binary Cross-Entropy (two classes), Categorical Cross-Entropy (multi-class).

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Functions that measure the difference between model predictions and true target values.

• Regression: Mean Squared Error (MSE, penalizes outliers), Mean Absolute Error (MAE, robust to outliers).

• Classification: Binary Cross-Entropy (two classes), Categorical Cross-Entropy (multi-class).

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• MSE: `L = 1 / N ∑ (y_i - y_hat_i)^2`

• Cross-Entropy:
`L = -1 / N ∑ ∑ y_{ij} log(y_hat_{ij})`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: A loss function defines the optimization landscape: the goal is to navigate to the lowest point of this landscape.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body:
• Computing Binary Cross-Entropy: For actual label 1 and prediction 0.9: `L = -[1 log(0.9) + 0] ≈ 0.105`.

• If prediction is 0.1: `L = -[1 log(0.1) + 0] ≈ 2.30` (high penalty for incorrect predictions).

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why is Categorical Cross-Entropy paired with the Softmax activation function?"

• **A**: Softmax normalizes output scores into a probability distribution that sums to 1. Categorical Cross-Entropy then calculates the log loss of this probability distribution.

revisionCards.title: Feed Forward Networks
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) where connections between nodes do not form cycles.

Information Flow: Information moves strictly forward: from input layer, through hidden layers, to the output layer.

Fully Connected: Each neuron in a layer is connected to all neurons in the next layer.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) where connections between nodes do not form cycles.

• Information Flow: Information moves strictly forward: from input layer, through hidden layers, to the output layer.

• Fully Connected: Each neuron in a layer is connected to all neurons in the next layer.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Input layer receives feature values.

• Hidden layers apply linear transformations followed by non-linear activations.

• Output layer generates final predictions (Softmax for classification, Linear for regression).

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: An assembly line where each station processes inputs and passes them to the next station, without any feedback loops.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "What are the limitations of Feed Forward Networks?"

• **A**: 1. They do not handle spatial structures (images) well, as flattening inputs loses pixel relationships. 2. They do not process sequential data (text/time-series) well, as they lack temporal memory.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Weight Initialization: Critical to prevent vanishing/exploding gradients on startup. Use Xavier initialization for Sigmoid/Tanh activations, and He initialization for ReLU.

revisionCards.title: Hidden Layers
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Intermediate neuron layers positioned between the input and output layers.

Feature Hierarchy: Early hidden layers extract low-level features (e.g. edges); deep hidden layers extract high-level semantic features (e.g. shapes, objects).

Width vs Depth: Width is the number of neurons per layer. Depth is the number of hidden layers.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Intermediate neuron layers positioned between the input and output layers.

• Feature Hierarchy: Early hidden layers extract low-level features (e.g. edges); deep hidden layers extract high-level semantic features (e.g. shapes, objects).

• Width vs Depth: Width is the number of neurons per layer. Depth is the number of hidden layers.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Receive activations from the previous layer.

• Multiply by weights, add bias, and apply activation functions.

• Pass the resulting activation vectors to the next layer.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Hidden layers act like processing filters in a photo editor: each layer applies a new filter to refine the image features.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How does hidden layer depth affect model performance?"

• **A**: Deeper networks can learn more complex feature hierarchies with fewer parameters than shallow, wide networks. However, they are harder to train and prone to vanishing gradients.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • **Sparsity**: Using regularization (like L1) or activations (like ReLU) to keep many hidden layer outputs at exactly 0, which reduces memory footprints and acts as feature selection.

revisionCards.title: Vanishing Gradients
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: When gradients shrink exponentially as they propagate backward through deep layers during backpropagation.

Impact: Early layers receive tiny gradient updates, preventing them from learning and causing training to stall.

Causes: Saturated activation functions (Sigmoid, Tanh) whose derivatives are less than 1.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: When gradients shrink exponentially as they propagate backward through deep layers during backpropagation.

• Impact: Early layers receive tiny gradient updates, preventing them from learning and causing training to stall.

• Causes: Saturated activation functions (Sigmoid, Tanh) whose derivatives are less than 1.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• During backpropagation, weight gradients are computed by multiplying derivatives across layers (Chain Rule).

• If activation derivatives are consistently `< 0.25`, multiplying them repeatedly causes the gradient to decay exponentially towards 0.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: A whisper game: as the message is passed down a long line of people, it gets quieter and quieter until the first person cannot hear anything at all.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How do you solve the vanishing gradient problem?"

• **A**: 1. Use ReLU activation functions instead of Sigmoid. 2. Use residual connections (skip connections). 3. Apply Batch Normalization. 4. Use proper weight initialization (He/Xavier).

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Exploding Gradients: The opposite problem: when gradients grow exponentially because weights are initialized too large, causing training to diverge. Solve using Gradient Clipping.

revisionCards.title: Batch Normalization
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Normalizing neuron activations within a mini-batch during training to stabilize and speed up training.

Internal Covariate Shift: Reduces shift by stabilizing the distribution of activations across layers.

Shorthand: Placed typically between linear layers and activation functions.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Normalizing neuron activations within a mini-batch during training to stabilize and speed up training.

• Internal Covariate Shift: Reduces shift by stabilizing the distribution of activations across layers.

• Shorthand: Placed typically between linear layers and activation functions.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• **Step 1**: Compute batch mean `μ_B = 1 / m ∑ x_i` and variance `σ_B^2 = 1 / m ∑ (x_i - μ_B)^2`.

• **Step 2**: Normalize:
`x_hat_i = (x_i - μ_B) / (√(σ_B^2 + ε))`.

• **Step 3**: Scale and shift: `y_i = γ x_hat_i + β` (where `γ` and `β` are learnable parameters).

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: Batch Norm stabilizes the input range of each layer, keeping activations from drifting too large or small.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body: • During testing, batch mean and variance are not calculated. Instead, the model uses running averages computed during training.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why does Batch Normalization act as a regularizer?"

• **A**: Because the mean and variance are calculated over mini-batches, they introduce slight noise into activations, which helps regularize the model and reduces the need for dropout.

revisionCards.title: Dropout
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Regularization technique where random neurons are deactivated during training with a probability `p`.

Co-adaptation: Prevents neurons from co-adapting (relying on specific neighboring neurons), forcing them to learn robust features independently.

Test Behavior: Deactivated only during training. During testing, all neurons are active, but weights are scaled by `1-p` to match activation expectations.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Regularization technique where random neurons are deactivated during training with a probability `p`.

• Co-adaptation: Prevents neurons from co-adapting (relying on specific neighboring neurons), forcing them to learn robust features independently.

• Test Behavior: Deactivated only during training. During testing, all neurons are active, but weights are scaled by `1-p` to match activation expectations.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Set dropout probability `p` (e.g. 0.5).

• During a training step, randomly set the activations of a fraction `p` of hidden neurons to 0.

• Scale remaining activations by `1 / 1-p` (inverted dropout) to keep expectations consistent.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: A sports team training: randomly benching key players forces other players to step up and learn to collaborate, creating a more robust team.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How does dropout change between training and testing?"

• **A**: Dropout is active only during training to regularize the model. During testing, all neurons are active to generate deterministic predictions, with no dropout masking applied.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Ensemble Effect: Dropout can be viewed as training an ensemble of `2^H` sub-networks (where `H` is the number of hidden units) with shared weights.

revisionCards.title: Convolution
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Mathematical operation where a sliding filter (kernel) is applied to an input matrix to create a feature map.

Feature extraction: Captures local spatial patterns (edges, textures) in images.

Parameter Sharing: The same filter is applied across the entire image, reducing parameter counts.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Mathematical operation where a sliding filter (kernel) is applied to an input matrix to create a feature map.

• Feature extraction: Captures local spatial patterns (edges, textures) in images.

• Parameter Sharing: The same filter is applied across the entire image, reducing parameter counts.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Formula:
`S(i, j) = (I * K)(i, j) = ∑_m ∑_n I(i-m, j-n) K(m, n)`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: A **sliding window** multiplying element-wise and summing values to detect feature matches.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body:
• Applying a 3x3 Sobel kernel to detect vertical edges in an input image matrix.

• The kernel values are negative on the left, positive on the right. Sliding it over a vertical edge yields high output values, flagging the edge position.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why is convolution preferred over fully connected layers for images?"

• **A**: 1. Preserves spatial structure. 2. Translation invariance (detects features regardless of location). 3. Significantly fewer parameters.

revisionCards.title: Filters
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Kernel matrices representing feature detectors in convolutional layers.

Channels: Filters have a depth dimension matching the input channel count (e.g. 3 for RGB images).

Learning: Unlike manual filters (e.g. Sobel, Gabor), CNN filter weights are learned during training.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Kernel matrices representing feature detectors in convolutional layers.

• Channels: Filters have a depth dimension matching the input channel count (e.g. 3 for RGB images).

• Learning: Unlike manual filters (e.g. Sobel, Gabor), CNN filter weights are learned during training.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Initialize filter weights randomly.

• Slide the filter over the input channels, calculating element-wise products and summing values across channels.

• Update weights using backpropagation to optimize feature extraction.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Filters are like specialized lenses: one lens highlights horizontal lines, another highlights vertical lines, and others detect specific colors.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How does filter depth affect CNNs?"

• **A**: The number of filters in a layer determines the number of output channels (feature maps). Early layers use few filters (e.g. 32); deep layers use many filters (e.g. 512) to detect complex shapes.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Receptive Field: The region in the input space that a specific CNN feature is looking at. Deeper layers have larger receptive fields.

revisionCards.title: Padding
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Adding border pixels around an input matrix before applying convolution.

Why it matters: Prevents spatial dimensions from shrinking after every convolution, and preserves edge information.

**Types**: Valid padding (no padding, shrinks size) and Same padding (adds padding to preserve input dimensions).

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Adding border pixels around an input matrix before applying convolution.

• Why it matters: Prevents spatial dimensions from shrinking after every convolution, and preserves edge information.

• **Types**: Valid padding (no padding, shrinks size) and Same padding (adds padding to preserve input dimensions).

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body: • Same Padding Formula: `P = (F - 1) / (2)` (where `F` is filter size, assuming stride of 1)

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: Adding a border of zeros around the image to allow filters to slide over border pixels without falling off the edge.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body:
• For a 32x32 input with a 5x5 filter and stride 1:

• Without padding (Valid): Output shape is `32 - 5 + 1 = 28 * 28`.

• With Same padding: `P = 5-1 / 2 = 2`. Output shape remains 32x32.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "What is zero-padding vs reflection-padding?"

• **A**: Zero-padding fills borders with 0s, which can introduce border artifacts. Reflection-padding copies edge pixel values outward, reducing border artifacts in generative tasks.

revisionCards.title: Stride
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: The step size (in pixels) by which a filter slides across the input matrix.

Impact: Larger strides reduce output spatial dimensions and decrease computational costs.

Shorthand: A stride of 1 moves the filter by 1 pixel at a time; a stride of 2 moves it by 2 pixels, skipping columns/rows.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: The step size (in pixels) by which a filter slides across the input matrix.

• Impact: Larger strides reduce output spatial dimensions and decrease computational costs.

• Shorthand: A stride of 1 moves the filter by 1 pixel at a time; a stride of 2 moves it by 2 pixels, skipping columns/rows.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Output Dimension Formula:
`O = floor( (I - F + 2P) / (S) ) + 1` (where `I` is input, `F` is filter, `P` is padding, `S` is stride)

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: Stride controls the spacing of filter application points across the image.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body:
• For a 7x7 input, 3x3 filter, padding 0, stride 2:

• `O = (7 - 3 + 0) / (2) + 1 = 2 + 1 = 3 * 3`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "When is strided convolution used instead of pooling?"

• **A**: In modern architectures (e.g. ResNet), strided convolutions (with stride=2) are preferred over max pooling to reduce spatial dimensions, as they allow the model to learn its own downsampling parameters.

revisionCards.title: Pooling
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Downsampling operation that reduces the spatial dimensions of feature maps.

**Types**: Max Pooling (extracts maximum value in window, preserves features) and Average Pooling (calculates average value).

Invariance: Introduces translation invariance, helping the model recognize features even if they shift slightly.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Downsampling operation that reduces the spatial dimensions of feature maps.

• **Types**: Max Pooling (extracts maximum value in window, preserves features) and Average Pooling (calculates average value).

• Invariance: Introduces translation invariance, helping the model recognize features even if they shift slightly.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Define pooling window size (typically 2x2) and stride (typically 2).

• Slide the window over the feature map.

• Select the maximum value (Max Pooling) or compute the average (Average Pooling) within the window.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Looking at a map from a distance: you lose minor details but preserve the locations of major cities.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why is Max Pooling preferred over Average Pooling for classification?"

• **A**: Because Max Pooling acts as a feature detector: it preserves the strongest activation signal in the region (e.g. presence of an edge), while Average Pooling dilutes it.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Information Loss: Pooling is non-reversible and discards spatial details (like exact coordinates), which can be problematic for tasks like image segmentation. Use stride convolutions instead.

revisionCards.title: CNN Architecture
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: End-to-end deep learning model containing alternating convolutional and pooling layers, followed by fully connected layers.

Feature vs Classifier: Convolution/Pooling layers act as the feature extractor; fully connected layers act as the classifier.

**Examples**: Classic architectures include LeNet, VGG, ResNet, and Inception.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: End-to-end deep learning model containing alternating convolutional and pooling layers, followed by fully connected layers.

• Feature vs Classifier: Convolution/Pooling layers act as the feature extractor; fully connected layers act as the classifier.

• **Examples**: Classic architectures include LeNet, VGG, ResNet, and Inception.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Input image passes through convolutional layers to extract feature maps.

• Pooling layers downsample feature maps, reducing spatial resolution while expanding channel depth.

• Flatten the final feature map into a 1D vector and pass it through fully connected layers to generate class probabilities.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Processing a document: first you scan for keywords (convolutions), summarize key points (pooling), and finally write the conclusion (fully connected layers).

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why are skip connections used in ResNet?"

• **A**: Skip connections pass activations directly across layers: `y = F(x) + x`. This allows gradients to flow directly through the skip pathway, solving the vanishing gradient problem in very deep networks (e.g. 152 layers).

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Receptive field expansion: As you go deeper in a CNN, spatial dimensions shrink, but each remaining pixel represents a larger region of the original input image.

revisionCards.title: RNN Basics
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Recurrent Neural Network. A class of neural networks designed for sequential data where connections form feedback loops.

Hidden State (`h_t`): Acts as memory, capturing information from previous time steps:

`h_t = f(W_{hh} h_{t-1} + W_{xh} x_t + b)`.

**Student Shorthand**: Processes sequences step-by-step, sharing weights across time steps.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Recurrent Neural Network. A class of neural networks designed for sequential data where connections form feedback loops.

• Hidden State (`h_t`): Acts as memory, capturing information from previous time steps:
`h_t = f(W_{hh} h_{t-1} + W_{xh} x_t + b)`.

• **Student Shorthand**: Processes sequences step-by-step, sharing weights across time steps.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Hidden State:
`h_t = tanh(W_{hh} h_{t-1} + W_{xh} x_t + b_h)`

• Output Equation: `y_t = W_{hy} h_t + b_y`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: An RNN can be unfolded into a sequence of identical network cells, sharing the same parameters across time.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body: • Processing a sentence: At step `t`, the input is the current word `x_t` and the hidden state `h_{t-1}` representing the context of previous words.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why do standard RNNs struggle with long sequences?"

• **A**: Because they process data step-by-step using recursive multiplication. Over long steps, gradients decay exponentially (vanishing gradients), making the network forget early inputs.

revisionCards.title: Vanishing Gradient Problem
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: The decay of gradients over time steps during Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) in RNNs.

BPTT: Unrolling the network over time steps and calculating gradients using the chain rule.

Effect: Weights in early time steps receive tiny updates, causing the model to lose track of long-term dependencies.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: The decay of gradients over time steps during Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) in RNNs.

• BPTT: Unrolling the network over time steps and calculating gradients using the chain rule.

• Effect: Weights in early time steps receive tiny updates, causing the model to lose track of long-term dependencies.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Unroll the RNN over `T` time steps.

• Calculate output loss at the end of the sequence.

• Propagate gradients back through time steps. Recursive multiplication of weight matrices (`W_{hh}`) causes gradients to shrink if eigenvalues of `W_{hh} < 1`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Trying to read a very long paragraph: by the time you reach the end, you have forgotten what was written in the first sentence.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How do you solve vanishing gradients in RNNs?"

• **A**: 1. Use gated architectures like LSTMs or GRUs. 2. Apply gradient clipping (for exploding gradients). 3. Initialize recurrent weights to the identity matrix.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Exploding Gradients in RNNs: Occurs when eigenvalues of recurrent weights `> 1`, causing gradients to grow exponentially and training to crash. Solve using Gradient Clipping.

revisionCards.title: LSTM
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Long Short-Term Memory network. A gated RNN architecture designed to learn long-term dependencies by resolving vanishing gradients.

Cell State (`C_t`): The internal memory pipeline that runs straight down the chain, modified only by linear interactions.

Gating Mechanism: Regulates information flow using three gates: Forget gate, Input gate, and Output gate.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Long Short-Term Memory network. A gated RNN architecture designed to learn long-term dependencies by resolving vanishing gradients.

• Cell State (`C_t`): The internal memory pipeline that runs straight down the chain, modified only by linear interactions.

• Gating Mechanism: Regulates information flow using three gates: Forget gate, Input gate, and Output gate.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Forget Gate:
`f_t = σ(W_f [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_f)` (drops information).

• Input Gate:
`i_t = σ(W_i [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_i)` and candidate cell state:
`C_tilde_t = tanh(W_c [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_c)`.

• Update Cell State:
`C_t = f_t ⊙ C_{t-1} + i_t ⊙ C_tilde_t`.

• Output Gate:
`o_t = σ(W_o [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_o)` and hidden state update: `h_t = o_t ⊙ tanh(C_t)`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: The cell state acts like a conveyor belt, with gates acting as valves adding or removing information along the belt.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body: • If forget gate `f_t = 1` and input gate `i_t = 0`, the cell state passes through unchanged: `C_t = C_{t-1}`. This linear connection allows gradients to flow back without exponential decay.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "What are the three gates of an LSTM and their roles?"

• **A**: 1. Forget Gate: decides what information to discard from the cell state. 2. Input Gate: decides what new information to store in the cell state. 3. Output Gate: decides what information from the cell state to output as the hidden state.

revisionCards.title: GRU
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Gated Recurrent Unit. A simplified variant of the LSTM that merges the cell state and hidden state, and uses two gates.

Gates: Reset gate (determines how to combine new input with past memory) and Update gate (determines how much past memory to keep).

Efficiency: Fewer parameters than LSTM, making it faster to train and less prone to overfitting on small datasets.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Gated Recurrent Unit. A simplified variant of the LSTM that merges the cell state and hidden state, and uses two gates.

• Gates: Reset gate (determines how to combine new input with past memory) and Update gate (determines how much past memory to keep).

• Efficiency: Fewer parameters than LSTM, making it faster to train and less prone to overfitting on small datasets.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Update Gate:
`z_t = σ(W_z [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_z)`

• Reset Gate:
`r_t = σ(W_r [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_r)`

• Candidate Hidden State:
`h_tilde_t = tanh(W [r_t ⊙ h_{t-1}, x_t] + b)`

• Hidden State Update:
`h_t = (1 - z_t) ⊙ h_{t-1} + z_t ⊙ h_tilde_t`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: GRU merges the gating pipelines, using a single update gate to balance old and new activations.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body: • If update gate `z_t ≈ 0`, the hidden state remains unchanged: `h_t ≈ h_{t-1}`. If `z_t ≈ 1`, the hidden state is overwritten by the new candidate state.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How does a GRU differ from an LSTM?"

• **A**: 1. GRU has 2 gates (Reset, Update); LSTM has 3 gates (Forget, Input, Output). 2. GRU merges cell state and hidden state. 3. GRU is computationally faster and has fewer parameters.

revisionCards.title: Attention Mechanism
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Dynamic scoring mechanism that allows models to focus on specific parts of the input sequence when generating output tokens.

Shorthand: Originally developed for seq2seq translation to replace the fixed-size bottleneck vector with dynamically weighted source vectors.

Alignment Score: Measures the relevance of source word `i` to target word `j`.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Dynamic scoring mechanism that allows models to focus on specific parts of the input sequence when generating output tokens.

• Shorthand: Originally developed for seq2seq translation to replace the fixed-size bottleneck vector with dynamically weighted source vectors.

• Alignment Score: Measures the relevance of source word `i` to target word `j`.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Calculate alignment scores matching decoder hidden states against all encoder hidden states.

• Normalize scores using the Softmax function to generate attention weights.

• Compute a weighted sum of encoder hidden states to form the context vector, and pass it to the decoder.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Looking at a photo and focusing your eyes on the main subject while ignoring the background.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How does Bahdanau (Additive) attention differ from Luong (Multiplicative) attention?"

• **A**: Bahdanau attention calculates scores using a single-layer MLP: `v_a^T tanh(W_a [s, h])`. Luong attention uses matrix dot products: `s^T W_a h`, which is computationally faster.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Bottleneck elimination: Standard encoders compress sequences into a single vector, losing early information. Attention allows the decoder to look at all source states directly.

revisionCards.title: Self Attention
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Attention mechanism matching words within the same sequence to compute representations of that sequence.

Vectors: Queries (`Q`), Keys (`K`), and Values (`V`). Projecting token embeddings into query, key, and value spaces.

Scaled Dot-Product: Dividing dot products by `√(d_k)` to prevent gradients from vanishing in Softmax.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Attention mechanism matching words within the same sequence to compute representations of that sequence.

• Vectors: Queries (`Q`), Keys (`K`), and Values (`V`). Projecting token embeddings into query, key, and value spaces.

• Scaled Dot-Product: Dividing dot products by `√(d_k)` to prevent gradients from vanishing in Softmax.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Formula:
`Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K^T) / (√(d_k)) V`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: Self-attention calculates a lookup table matching each word against all other words in the sentence to build context.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body: • For the sentence "The bank of the river": self-attention links "bank" with "river", resolving semantic ambiguity (water bank vs financial bank).

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why do we scale the dot product by `1 / √(d_k)`?"

• **A**: For large dimension sizes (`d_k`), dot products grow large, pushing the Softmax function into regions with tiny gradients. Scaling by `√(d_k)` keeps variance stable and prevents vanishing gradients during training.

revisionCards.title: Multi Head Attention
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Running multiple self-attention operations (heads) in parallel, allowing the model to attend to information from different representation subspaces.

Parallelism: Queries, keys, and values are split and projected into smaller dimensions.

Aggregation: Outputs from all heads are concatenated and projected back to the original dimension.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Running multiple self-attention operations (heads) in parallel, allowing the model to attend to information from different representation subspaces.

• Parallelism: Queries, keys, and values are split and projected into smaller dimensions.

• Aggregation: Outputs from all heads are concatenated and projected back to the original dimension.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Formula:
`MultiHead(Q, K, V) = Concat(head_1, ..., head_h) W^O`

• Head Equation:
`head_i = Attention(Q W_i^Q, K W_i^K, V W_i^V)`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: Multiple heads act like different observers: one head tracks subject-verb relations, another tracks adjectives, and another tracks coreferences.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body: • If dimension `d_{model} = 512` and heads `h = 8`, each head operates on a projected dimension size of `512 / 8 = 64`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why is Multi-Head Attention better than Single-Head Attention?"

• **A**: A single head averages attention across all words, which can dilute important signals. Multi-head attention allows the model to attend to multiple relationships simultaneously.

revisionCards.title: Positional Encoding
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Adding vector representations to input embeddings to convey word order information.

Order: Unlike RNNs (which process sequentially), Transformers process all tokens in parallel, making them permutation-invariant without positional information.

Sine/Cosine: Sinusoidal functions used to generate positional coordinates.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Adding vector representations to input embeddings to convey word order information.

• Order: Unlike RNNs (which process sequentially), Transformers process all tokens in parallel, making them permutation-invariant without positional information.

• Sine/Cosine: Sinusoidal functions used to generate positional coordinates.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Formula (Even):
`PE_{(pos, 2i)} = sin(pos / 10000^{2i/d})`

• Formula (Odd):
`PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = cos(pos / 10000^{2i/d})`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: Adding wave patterns to embeddings so the model can determine relative distances between words.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body: • Positional encoding values are added directly to token embeddings: `x_{input} = x_{token} + PE`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why are sinusoidal functions used for positional encoding?"

• **A**: Because they allow the model to learn relative position relationships easily: for any fixed offset `k`, `PE_{pos+k}` can be represented as a linear function of `PE_{pos}`, allowing the model to generalize to longer sequences.

revisionCards.title: Transformer Architecture
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Encoder-decoder model architecture based entirely on self-attention mechanisms, bypassing recurrent and convolutional layers.

Encoder: Processes input sequences, generating context vectors.

Decoder: Autoregressively generates output tokens, using masked self-attention and cross-attention.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Encoder-decoder model architecture based entirely on self-attention mechanisms, bypassing recurrent and convolutional layers.

• Encoder: Processes input sequences, generating context vectors.

• Decoder: Autoregressively generates output tokens, using masked self-attention and cross-attention.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Input passes through self-attention, layer normalization, residual skip connections, and feed-forward blocks.

• Decoder uses masked self-attention to prevent looking at future tokens during training.

• Cross-attention maps decoder queries against encoder keys and values.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Translating a book: the encoder reads and indexes the entire book, and the decoder writes the translation page-by-page, referring to the index.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why is layer normalization preferred over batch normalization in Transformers?"

• **A**: Batch normalization normalizes across the batch dimension, which fails with variable sequence lengths. Layer normalization normalizes across features within each token individually, making it sequence-length independent.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Complexity limit: Self-attention has quadratic complexity: `O(N^2)` where `N` is the sequence length. This makes it computationally expensive for long contexts.

revisionCards.title: BERT
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers. Encoder-only model trained to learn contextual representations.

Pre-training tasks: Masked Language Modeling (MLM, predicts masked tokens) and Next Sentence Prediction (NSP).

Bidirectional: Attends to both left and right context in all layers simultaneously.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers. Encoder-only model trained to learn contextual representations.

• Pre-training tasks: Masked Language Modeling (MLM, predicts masked tokens) and Next Sentence Prediction (NSP).

• Bidirectional: Attends to both left and right context in all layers simultaneously.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Mask 15% of input tokens randomly.

• Predict these masked tokens based on context vectors generated by self-attention.

• Fine-tune the model on downstream tasks (classification, Q&A) by adding a task-specific head.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Reading a fill-in-the-blank sentence: you look at words both before and after the blank to guess the missing word.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How does BERT differ from GPT?"

• **A**: BERT is an encoder-only model that uses bidirectional self-attention to build representation context (ideal for analysis). GPT is a decoder-only model that uses masked, causal self-attention to predict the next token (ideal for text generation).

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • NSP limitations: Recent architectures (e.g. RoBERTa) proved that the Next Sentence Prediction task was unnecessary and dropping it improved performance.

revisionCards.title: GPT
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Generative Pre-trained Transformer. Decoder-only model architecture trained to generate text.

Autoregressive: Generates text token-by-token: the output at step `t` becomes the input at step `t+1`.

Causal Masking: Restricts self-attention so tokens can only attend to past tokens in the sequence.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Generative Pre-trained Transformer. Decoder-only model architecture trained to generate text.

• Autoregressive: Generates text token-by-token: the output at step `t` becomes the input at step `t+1`.

• Causal Masking: Restricts self-attention so tokens can only attend to past tokens in the sequence.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Input text sequence is tokenized and embedded.

• Passes through decoder blocks using causal self-attention (masking out future tokens).

• Predicts the probability distribution of the next token using a Softmax output layer.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Writing a story word-by-word: each word you write depends on what you have already written, without knowing what you will write next.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why does GPT use masked self-attention?"

• **A**: To prevent data leakage. During training, the model must learn to predict the next word without seeing future words. Causal masking enforces this constraint.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • In-context learning: Large language models (like GPT-3) can perform tasks with zero or few examples in the prompt, without modifying model weights.

revisionCards.title: Text Preprocessing
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Cleaning and preparing raw text data for NLP pipelines.

Steps: Lowercasing, removing punctuation/special characters, stopword removal, and stemming/lemmatization.

Lemmatization vs Stemming: Stemming cuts off suffixes using rules; lemmatization maps words back to their dictionary root (lemma).

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Cleaning and preparing raw text data for NLP pipelines.

• Steps: Lowercasing, removing punctuation/special characters, stopword removal, and stemming/lemmatization.

• Lemmatization vs Stemming: Stemming cuts off suffixes using rules; lemmatization maps words back to their dictionary root (lemma).

slides.headline: Python Code
slides.body: Review the clean, highly optimized implementation below:
slides.code:
import nltk
from nltk.stem import WordNetLemmatizer
lemmatizer = WordNetLemmatizer()
# Lemmatizing maps word back to root
root_word = lemmatizer.lemmatize("running", pos="v") # "run"
stop_words = set(nltk.corpus.stopwords.words("english"))

slides.headline: 💡 Code Breakdown
slides.body: • Line 4: Maps "running" to its verb root "run" using semantic dictionary lookups.

slides.headline: 🧠 Performance Footprint
slides.body:
• Time Complexity: Stemming: O(N) (fast, rule-based) | Lemmatization: O(N * log M) (slower, dictionary lookup).

• Space Complexity: O(N) memory allocation.

slides.headline: 🧠 Common Interview Questions
slides.body:
• **Common Interview Question**: Stopword removal can lose critical context in tasks like sentiment analysis (e.g. removing "not" in "not good" changes the meaning entirely).

• **Common Interview Question**: Stemming can create non-dictionary words (e.g. "universe" becomes "univers"), which hurts semantic representation.

revisionCards.title: Tokenization
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Splitting text sequences into smaller units, called tokens (words, subwords, or characters).

Subword Tokenization: Modern standard for LLMs, balancing vocabulary size and out-of-vocabulary (OOV) errors.

Algorithms: Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), WordPiece, SentencePiece.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Splitting text sequences into smaller units, called tokens (words, subwords, or characters).

• Subword Tokenization: Modern standard for LLMs, balancing vocabulary size and out-of-vocabulary (OOV) errors.

• Algorithms: Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), WordPiece, SentencePiece.

slides.headline: Python Code
slides.body: Review the clean, highly optimized implementation below:
slides.code:
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")
tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Tokenization is awesome!")
# Output: ['token', '##ization', 'is', 'awesome', '!']

slides.headline: 💡 Code Breakdown
slides.body: • Line 3: Splits unknown or rare words ("Tokenization") into common subwords ("token" and "##ization") to prevent OOV errors.

slides.headline: 🧠 Performance Footprint
slides.body:
• Time Complexity: O(L) where L is the character length of the string.

• Space Complexity: O(T) where T is the number of tokens generated.

slides.headline: 🧠 Common Interview Questions
slides.body:
• **Common Interview Question**: Different pre-trained models use different tokenization schemes. Always use the specific tokenizer paired with your model.

• **Common Interview Question**: Whitespace tokenization fails with languages that do not use spaces (e.g. Chinese, Japanese).

revisionCards.title: Embeddings
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Low-dimensional, continuous vector representations of words or tokens that capture semantic meaning.

Semantic Proximity: Words with similar meanings or contexts map close together in vector space.

Static vs Contextual: Static embeddings (Word2Vec) assign a fixed vector to each word; contextual embeddings (BERT) generate vectors dynamically based on surrounding words.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Low-dimensional, continuous vector representations of words or tokens that capture semantic meaning.

• Semantic Proximity: Words with similar meanings or contexts map close together in vector space.

• Static vs Contextual: Static embeddings (Word2Vec) assign a fixed vector to each word; contextual embeddings (BERT) generate vectors dynamically based on surrounding words.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Map words to unique vocabulary indices.

• Lookup high-dimensional vectors in the model embedding weight matrix.

• Perform downstream calculations or pass vectors to model layers.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Mapping words onto a semantic globe: synonyms (e.g., "huge" and "giant") are placed in the same city, while unrelated words are on different continents.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How does cosine similarity measure semantic proximity?"

• **A**: Cosine similarity measures the directional alignment of two embedding vectors. Values close to 1 indicate highly similar semantic meaning.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Out of Vocabulary (OOV): Static embedding lookup tables fail if a word is missing from the vocabulary. Subword tokenization solves this.

revisionCards.title: Word2Vec
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Prediction-based framework to learn static word embeddings using shallow neural networks.

Architectures: Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW, predicts target from context) and Skip-gram (predicts context from target).

Semantic Math: Captures linear relationships: e.g.

`v_{King} - v_{Man} + v_{Woman} ≈ v_{Queen}`.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Prediction-based framework to learn static word embeddings using shallow neural networks.

• Architectures: Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW, predicts target from context) and Skip-gram (predicts context from target).

• Semantic Math: Captures linear relationships: e.g.
`v_{King} - v_{Man} + v_{Woman} ≈ v_{Queen}`.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Skip-Gram Objective: Maximize average log probability:
`J = 1 / T ∑_{t=1}^T ∑_{-c ≤ j ≤ c, j != 0} log P(w_{t+j} | w_t)`.

• Softmax Probability:
`P(w_O | w_I) = (expv'_{w_O / ^T v_{w_I})}{∑_{w} exp(v'_w{}^T v_{w_I})}`.

• Negative Sampling: Speeds up training by replacing the expensive vocabulary sum with a few negative noise samples.

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: Word2Vec maps words into a dense vector space where spatial directions represent semantic relationships.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body: • Computing softmax over a 100,000-word vocabulary is slow. Negative sampling replaces it with binary logistic regression updates on 5-20 random noise words.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "When is Skip-gram preferred over CBOW?"

• **A**: Skip-gram works better with small datasets and represents rare words more effectively. CBOW is faster to train and shows slightly better accuracy for high-frequency words.

revisionCards.title: TF-IDF
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency. Statistical measure evaluating a word's relevance to a document in a collection.

TF: Measures word frequency within a document:

`TF(t, d) = (count(t, d)) / (total words in d)`.

IDF: Downweights words that appear frequently across all documents (e.g. "the", "is"):

`IDF(t, D) = log((N) / (1 + |\{d ∈ D : t ∈ d\)|})`.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency. Statistical measure evaluating a word's relevance to a document in a collection.

• TF: Measures word frequency within a document:
`TF(t, d) = (count(t, d)) / (total words in d)`.

• IDF: Downweights words that appear frequently across all documents (e.g. "the", "is"):
`IDF(t, D) = log((N) / (1 + |\{d ∈ D : t ∈ d\)|})`.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Formula:
`TF-IDF(t, d, D) = TF(t, d) * IDF(t, D)`

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: TF-IDF scores highlight words that are unique and descriptive of a specific document, helping filter out common noise words.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body:
• If a word appears 10 times in a 100-word document, TF = 0.1.

• If the word appears in all 1,000 documents in the collection, IDF = `log(1000/1000) = 0`, resulting in a TF-IDF score of 0.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "What are the limitations of TF-IDF?"

• **A**: 1. It lacks semantic understanding (treats synonyms as completely different words). 2. It ignores word order and context. 3. Prone to out-of-vocabulary errors on test data.

revisionCards.title: Attention in NLP
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Scoring mechanisms that calculate relevance weights between words to capture contextual relationships.

Seq2Seq: Solved the fixed-length memory bottleneck in encoder-decoder translation pipelines.

Transformers: Replaced recurrence completely, allowing parallel sequence processing.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Scoring mechanisms that calculate relevance weights between words to capture contextual relationships.

• Seq2Seq: Solved the fixed-length memory bottleneck in encoder-decoder translation pipelines.

• Transformers: Replaced recurrence completely, allowing parallel sequence processing.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Map words to Query, Key, and Value vectors.

• Compute dot products of Queries and Keys to generate attention weights.

• Multiply weights by Value vectors to compute context-aware embeddings.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Highlight marker: the model highlights relevant context words while reading, ignoring surrounding filler text.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How does attention resolve word ambiguity?"

• **A**: By weighting neighboring context words. For example, in "The bank of the river", attention weights the word "river" highly when representing "bank", capturing the correct meaning.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Self-Attention Complexity: Calculating attention weights takes `O(N^2)` computations, which limits sequence lengths in Transformer models.

revisionCards.title: Content Based Filtering
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Recommender system that suggests items similar to those a user liked in the past, based on item features.

Features: Uses metadata attributes (e.g. genre, director, actors) or TF-IDF text features.

Cosine Similarity: Standard metric used to compare item feature vectors.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Recommender system that suggests items similar to those a user liked in the past, based on item features.

• Features: Uses metadata attributes (e.g. genre, director, actors) or TF-IDF text features.

• Cosine Similarity: Standard metric used to compare item feature vectors.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Construct a profile vector for the user based on their past ratings.

• Calculate feature vectors for all candidate items.

• Recommend items with the highest cosine similarity to the user profile vector.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: A waiter recommending a dish: "Since you liked our spicy chicken, you will enjoy our spicy beef."

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "What is the main limitation of content-based filtering?"

• **A**: Overspecialization: the model only recommends items similar to what the user has already consumed, failing to suggest novel or diverse items.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • No Collaborative Data: Does not use ratings or actions from other users, meaning it cannot leverage collective patterns.

revisionCards.title: Collaborative Filtering
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Recommender system that makes predictions based on the preferences of similar users.

**Types**: User-User (finds similar users) and Item-Item (finds items rated similarly by the same users).

Shorthand: Bypasses the need for item metadata by relying entirely on user rating matrices.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Recommender system that makes predictions based on the preferences of similar users.

• **Types**: User-User (finds similar users) and Item-Item (finds items rated similarly by the same users).

• Shorthand: Bypasses the need for item metadata by relying entirely on user rating matrices.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Build a User-Item rating matrix.

• Calculate similarity scores between users (or items) using Pearson correlation or cosine similarity.

• Predict ratings for unrated items by computing a weighted average of ratings from similar users.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Asking friends for recommendations: "Your friends liked this movie, so you might like it too."

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why is Item-Item collaborative filtering preferred over User-User in production?"

• **A**: 1. Stability: Item ratings change slowly compared to dynamic user preferences. 2. Scalability: The number of items is typically much smaller than the number of users, making similarity calculations cheaper.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • **Sparsity**: Rating matrices are sparse (most users rate `< 1%` of items), which can degrade similarity calculations.

revisionCards.title: Matrix Factorization
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Model-based collaborative filtering that decomposes the sparse user-item rating matrix into low-dimensional latent feature matrices.

Latent Factors: Unobserved attributes (e.g. movie genres) learned directly from user ratings.

Optimization: Alternating Least Squares (ALS) or Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD).

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Model-based collaborative filtering that decomposes the sparse user-item rating matrix into low-dimensional latent feature matrices.

• Latent Factors: Unobserved attributes (e.g. movie genres) learned directly from user ratings.

• Optimization: Alternating Least Squares (ALS) or Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD).

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• Model Equation: `R_hat_{u, i} = q_i^T p_u` (where `q_i` is item embedding, `p_u` is user embedding).

• Regularized Objective:
`\min ∑ (R_{u, i} - q_i^T p_u)^2 + λ (\|q_i\|^2 + \|p_u\|^2)`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: Matrix factorization projects both users and items into a shared latent space where ratings are dot products.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body: • Decomposing a 10,000 x 1,000 matrix into a 10,000 x K user matrix and a K x 1,000 item matrix (where `K=50` latent features) significantly reduces memory and generalizes predictions.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How do you handle missing ratings during matrix factorization?"

• **A**: Standard matrix factorization only computes loss on observed ratings, ignoring missing cells in the calculation.

revisionCards.title: Cold Start Problem
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: The challenge of making recommendations when new users or items join the system with zero historical rating data.

**Types**: User Cold Start (no user profile) and Item Cold Start (no item ratings).

Solutions: Using metadata, popular defaults, or active learning questionnaires.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: The challenge of making recommendations when new users or items join the system with zero historical rating data.

• **Types**: User Cold Start (no user profile) and Item Cold Start (no item ratings).

• Solutions: Using metadata, popular defaults, or active learning questionnaires.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• For new users, prompt them to select preferred categories or search queries on signup.

• For new items, leverage content-based filtering using item metadata (features) to match them to users.

• Use hybrid architectures that combine collaborative and content-based models.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Starting a new job: you don't know anyone's preferences yet, so you start by offering standard defaults.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How does content-based filtering resolve the item cold start problem?"

• **A**: Because content-based models rely on item metadata features rather than user ratings, they can recommend a new item immediately after it is created.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Exploration vs Exploitation: Using multi-armed bandits to recommend new items to a subset of users to gather initial ratings quickly.

revisionCards.title: Trend
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: The long-term upward or downward movement in time-series data.

Identification: Measured using rolling averages or linear regression trends.

Decomposition: Separated from seasonal and residual noise components during time-series decomposition.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: The long-term upward or downward movement in time-series data.

• Identification: Measured using rolling averages or linear regression trends.

• Decomposition: Separated from seasonal and residual noise components during time-series decomposition.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Apply time-series decomposition to split components:
`Y_t = Trend_t + Seasonality_t + Residuals_t`.

• Calculate moving averages to smooth out short-term fluctuations and highlight the trend.

• Fit linear regressions against the time variable.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: The tide of the ocean: it rises or falls steadily over hours, regardless of individual wave ripples.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How do you detrend a time series?"

• **A**: 1. Subtract the calculated rolling mean. 2. Apply differencing (subtracting previous values: `Y_t - Y_{t-1}`).

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Non-linear trends: Trends can be exponential or quadratic. Apply log transformations to linearize exponential trends before modeling.

revisionCards.title: Seasonality
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Periodic fluctuations that repeat at regular intervals (e.g. daily, weekly, yearly).

Causes: Driven by calendar cycles or weather patterns (e.g. ice cream sales peaking in summer).

Multiplicative vs Additive: Additive seasonality has constant amplitude; multiplicative seasonality amplitude grows with the trend.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Periodic fluctuations that repeat at regular intervals (e.g. daily, weekly, yearly).

• Causes: Driven by calendar cycles or weather patterns (e.g. ice cream sales peaking in summer).

• Multiplicative vs Additive: Additive seasonality has constant amplitude; multiplicative seasonality amplitude grows with the trend.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Calculate autocorrelation to identify repeating lag intervals.

• Split data by seasonal periods (e.g. monthly averages).

• Subtract seasonal averages to deseasonalize the series.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Holiday shopping spikes: retail sales peak every December, repeating the same pattern year after year.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How do you detect seasonality in time-series data?"

• **A**: Use Autocorrelation Function (ACF) plots. Repeating peaks at specific lag intervals (e.g. lag 12 for monthly data) indicate seasonality.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Cyclical vs Seasonal: Seasonal patterns have a fixed, known period (e.g. weekly). Cyclical patterns have variable, unpredictable lengths (e.g. economic recessions).

revisionCards.title: Stationarity
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: A time series is stationary if its statistical properties (mean, variance, autocorrelation) do not change over time.

Why it matters: Most time-series models (ARIMA) require data to be stationary to make reliable predictions.

Testing: Verified using the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: A time series is stationary if its statistical properties (mean, variance, autocorrelation) do not change over time.

• Why it matters: Most time-series models (ARIMA) require data to be stationary to make reliable predictions.

• Testing: Verified using the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body: • Stationary conditions: Mean is constant over time, variance is constant over time, and covariance depends only on lag interval, not time.

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: A stationary time series looks like a flat sequence with constant variance, fluctuating around a fixed mean line.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body:
• ADF test: Null hypothesis (`H_0`) states the series has a unit root (non-stationary).

• If the calculated p-value is `< 0.05`, reject `H_0` and confirm stationarity.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How do you make a non-stationary time series stationary?"

• **A**: 1. Differencing (subtracting the previous value: `Y_t - Y_{t-1}`) to remove trends. 2. Log transformation to stabilize variance.

revisionCards.title: Moving Average
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Calculating averages of rolling windows to smooth out short-term noise and highlight trends.

Simple Moving Average (SMA): Equal weight to all points in the window.

Exponential Moving Average (EMA): Assigns higher weight to recent data points, reacting faster to changes.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Calculating averages of rolling windows to smooth out short-term noise and highlight trends.

• Simple Moving Average (SMA): Equal weight to all points in the window.

• Exponential Moving Average (EMA): Assigns higher weight to recent data points, reacting faster to changes.

slides.headline: Python Code
slides.body: Review the clean, highly optimized implementation below:
slides.code:
import pandas as pd
# Simple Moving Average with window 7
sma = df["sales"].rolling(window=7).mean()
# Exponential Moving Average
ema = df["sales"].ewm(span=7, adjust=False).mean()

slides.headline: 💡 Code Breakdown
slides.body:
• Line 3: Computes the rolling mean over a 7-day window. The first 6 rows return `NaN`.

• Line 5: Computes the EMA using exponential decay parameters.

slides.headline: 🧠 Performance Footprint
slides.body:
• Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of data points.

• Space Complexity: O(N) memory allocation for the output Series.

slides.headline: 🧠 Common Interview Questions
slides.body:
• **Common Interview Question**: Moving averages introduce lag. A 30-day moving average reacts slowly to recent market drops, making it lag behind current price actions.

• **Common Interview Question**: The first `W-1` values (where `W` is window size) are null, requiring imputation or drop handling before training models.

revisionCards.title: ARIMA Basics
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average. Classical time-series forecasting model for stationary data.

Hyperparameters: `p` (autoregressive lags), `d` (order of differencing), `q` (moving average lags of error).

Autoregressive (AR): Predicts future values based on past values:

`Y_t = c + φ_1 Y_{t-1} + ... + ε_t`.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Theorem
slides.body:
• **Definition**: AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average. Classical time-series forecasting model for stationary data.

• Hyperparameters: `p` (autoregressive lags), `d` (order of differencing), `q` (moving average lags of error).

• Autoregressive (AR): Predicts future values based on past values:
`Y_t = c + φ_1 Y_{t-1} + ... + ε_t`.

slides.headline: 💡 Mathematical Formula
slides.body:
• ARIMA Equation:
`Y'_t = c + ∑_{i=1}^p φ_i Y'_{t-i} + ε_t + ∑_{j=1}^q θ_j ε_{t-j}` (where `Y'` is the differenced series)

slides.headline: 🧠 Geometric Model
slides.body: • Model: ARIMA combines past values and past prediction errors to predict the next step in the series.

slides.headline: 🧠 Numerical Walkthrough
slides.body: • Identifying `p` and `q`: Analyze ACF (Autocorrelation) and PACF (Partial Autocorrelation) plots. PACF cutoff at lag `p` suggests AR(`p`); ACF cutoff at lag `q` suggests MA(`q`).

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How does SARIMA differ from ARIMA?"

• **A**: SARIMA adds seasonal terms: SARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)S, allowing the model to handle both standard trends and seasonal cycles with period S.

revisionCards.title: Model Deployment
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Integrating a trained model into a production environment where it can receive inputs and serve predictions.

Deployment Modes: Batch inference (offline predictions) and Real-time inference (online APIs).

APIs: Typically served using frameworks like FastAPI or Flask wrapped in Docker containers.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Integrating a trained model into a production environment where it can receive inputs and serve predictions.

• Deployment Modes: Batch inference (offline predictions) and Real-time inference (online APIs).

• APIs: Typically served using frameworks like FastAPI or Flask wrapped in Docker containers.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Serialize the trained model (e.g. serialize to pickle or ONNX format).

• Wrap the model inside an API endpoint (e.g. using FastAPI).

• Package dependencies inside a Docker container, and deploy to cloud instances (AWS ECS, Kubernetes).

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Moving a prototype engine from the design lab into a functional car on the road.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "When is batch inference preferred over real-time inference?"

• **A**: When predictions do not need to be instant (e.g. daily churn updates or weekly recommendations). Batch inference runs offline on schedule, saving API server hosting costs.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Model serialization risks: Loading untrusted pickle files can execute arbitrary malicious code. Use safer alternatives like ONNX or Joblib in production.

revisionCards.title: Model Monitoring
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Tracking model performance, inputs, and predictions in production to detect degradation.

Performance metrics: Monitoring **latency**, **throughput**, error rates, and predictive accuracy drift.

Logging: Capturing API request payloads and model outputs for downstream analysis.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Tracking model performance, inputs, and predictions in production to detect degradation.

• Performance metrics: Monitoring **latency**, **throughput**, error rates, and predictive accuracy drift.

• Logging: Capturing API request payloads and model outputs for downstream analysis.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Log incoming prediction requests and output predictions.

• Join predictions with actual labels when they become available (e.g. after a purchase occurs).

• Compute and display accuracy metrics on dashboards.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: Monitoring a patient's heart rate: you track key signals in real-time to detect issues before a crash occurs.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How do you detect model performance degradation if ground truth labels are delayed?"

• **A**: Monitor feature distributions and prediction distributions instead. If inputs shift, the model performance has likely degraded.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Feedback loops: Automated alerts that trigger retraining jobs if accuracy drops below a set threshold.

revisionCards.title: Data Drift
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: When the statistical distribution of input data changes over time, causing model performance to degrade.

Concept Drift: The relationship between inputs and targets changes (e.g. user shopping habits change after a macro-economic shift).

Detection: Statistical tests like Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test or Population Stability Index (PSI).

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: When the statistical distribution of input data changes over time, causing model performance to degrade.

• Concept Drift: The relationship between inputs and targets changes (e.g. user shopping habits change after a macro-economic shift).

• Detection: Statistical tests like Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test or Population Stability Index (PSI).

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Store training data distributions as a reference baseline.

• Calculate incoming feature statistics periodically in production.

• Run statistical tests (e.g. KS test) to compare baseline and production distributions. Flag drift if p-value `< 0.05`.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: A navigation app map becoming outdated as new roads are built and old roads are closed.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "How do you resolve data drift?"

• **A**: 1. Retrain the model using the latest production data. 2. Update feature preprocessing transformations. 3. Re-evaluate feature selection.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Covariate Shift: A sub-type of data drift where the input distribution `P(X)` changes but the conditional probability `P(Y mid X)` remains constant.

revisionCards.title: ML Pipelines
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Orchestrating the end-to-end steps of the ML lifecycle: data extraction, preprocessing, training, validation, and deployment.

Orchestrators: Tools like Apache Airflow, Kubeflow, or Prefect.

Reproducibility: Ensures the exact same data splits and preprocessing steps are applied to training and production inputs.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Orchestrating the end-to-end steps of the ML lifecycle: data extraction, preprocessing, training, validation, and deployment.

• Orchestrators: Tools like Apache Airflow, Kubeflow, or Prefect.

• Reproducibility: Ensures the exact same data splits and preprocessing steps are applied to training and production inputs.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Define steps as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).

• Configure dependencies (step B only runs if step A completes successfully).

• Schedule and monitor pipeline executions.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: A clean manufacturing assembly line: raw metal goes in, passes through structured welding stations, and a finished car rolls off the line.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
slides.body:
• **Q**: "Why are ML pipelines preferred over manual scripts?"

• **A**: Pipelines automate execution, handle errors/retries gracefully, scale computation resources dynamically, and guarantee reproducibility.

slides.headline: 🧠 Real-world Limitations
slides.body: • Feature Store: Centralized database (e.g. Feast) that stores engineered features, allowing both training and serving pipelines to access the same feature values.

revisionCards.title: Versioning
revisionCards.explanation:
**Definition**: Tracking versions of code, data, and model parameters to ensure reproducibility.

Data Version Control (DVC): Git-like tool designed to track massive dataset files and model weights.

Model Registry: Central database (e.g. MLflow) that stores model binaries, hyperparameters, and evaluation metrics.

slides.headline: 💡 Core Concept
slides.body:
• **Definition**: Tracking versions of code, data, and model parameters to ensure reproducibility.

• Data Version Control (DVC): Git-like tool designed to track massive dataset files and model weights.

• Model Registry: Central database (e.g. MLflow) that stores model binaries, hyperparameters, and evaluation metrics.

slides.headline: 💡 How it Works
slides.body:
• Commit code updates to Git.

• Store dataset hashes and tracking links using DVC.

• Log parameters, metrics, and model binaries in the Model Registry during training.

slides.headline: 🧠 Intuitive Analogy
slides.body: • **Analogy**: A time-travel system for ML: you can go back to any past experiment and recreate the exact same model with the exact same data.

slides.headline: 🧠 Commonly Asked Questions
